docs.title: ForensiX documentation
docs.text:
ForensiX is an end-to-end media forensics platform: it takes you from the first suspicious file to a calibrated, monitored detection service on your own infrastructure or any major cloud.

  • Detect manipulated and AI-generated images, video and voices with 38 commercially licensed detectors, including face swaps, lip-sync mismatches, cloned voices and physical inconsistencies. They all sit behind one API: forensix.load(name).predict(media) in Python, or POST /v1/detect over HTTP.
  • Prove what a file says about itself: C2PA Content Credentials, generator watermarks, metadata.
  • Adapt and trust the results on your media: fine-tune (including LoRA), calibrate to a false-alarm budget, and audit fairness.
  • Run it as an API and web console: locally, on Kubernetes, or on AWS, Google Cloud and Azure with one command or one click. Monitor it live.

docs.title: From data to production
docs.text: These pages are for engineers who build ForensiX into their products and pipelines. The top-level README is the model reference: per-model papers, licenses, preprocessing details and parity checks against upstream code.

docs.title: Top level: forensix
docs.text:
import forensix
Function Returns Description load(name, device="cpu", weights_path=None) detector Builds a detector, downloading and hash-checking its weights first. device is "cpu", "cuda" or "cuda:N". weights_path uses a local checkpoint instead of the registered one (required for models you train: avcons, avid, id-motion, person-detector; optional for physdf), or a fine-tune checkpoint, which is applied on top of the pretrained weights. finetune(model, dataset=None, real_media=None, fake_media=None, out=None, mode="norm", epochs=5, ...) (detector, report) Fine-tunes a pretrained image, audio or GenD video detector on labelled media and saves the checkpoint to out (Fine-tuning). list_models(family=None) list[str] Registered model names, sorted, optionally filtered by family. info(name) ModelSpec Family, license, source, paper, description and weight file of a model. download(name, force=False) Path \| None Fetches the model's weights and shared backbones into the cache, without building the model. None for models without registered weights. cache_dir() Path $FORENSIX_CACHE or ~/.cache/forensix. forensix.specialized (alias forensix.person) module Person-specialized models.

Unknown names raise KeyError with the list of available models.

docs.title: Prediction
docs.text:
forensix.Prediction is a frozen dataclass (forensix/types.py).

Attribute Type Description model str The detector's name. fake_prob float Score; higher means more likely fake. Not comparable across models. threshold float \| None Default decision threshold; None for scores without one. segment_fake_probs tuple[float, ...] Per-segment scores (audio windows, faces, frames or AV windows). May be empty. score_type str "probability" or "anomaly". details dict Model-specific evidence. Excluded from equality comparison. is_fake bool \| None fake_prob >= threshold, or None without a threshold. label str \| None "fake", "real" or None.

Models and their score conventions:

Models score_type threshold segment_fake_probs Notable details audio models probability 0.5 one per audio window none image models probability 0.5 none none gend, gend-pe, dfdet-clip, dfdc-selim, dfdc-wm probability 0.5 one per scored face none avad anomaly None none none syncnet anomaly (-confidence) None none offset_frames, confidence, min_dist, mean_dist_by_offset, tracks stablesyncnet probability (1 − sync probability) 0.5 none offset, sync probability per offset and per window avcons probability 0.5 one per AV window inconsistent segments (s), per-track results avid probability 0.5 none features, per-segment voice–face match, tracks id-face anomaly (1 − cosine similarity) 0.637 one per sampled frame similarity, frame_similarity, frame_time_s, other_enrolled_similarity id-motion anomaly (1 − similarity) EER threshold from training one per 4 s window window_similarity, window_start_s phys-* anomaly in [0, 1] None none constraints (measured value, expected range, violation), timeline, per-detector summaries physdf anomaly in [0, 1] None none constraints, localization, report, detectors, modalities, status person-detector probability from training (default 0.5) per frame (video) target_person, modality

docs.title: Audio detectors
docs.text:
det = forensix.load("nes2net-x-itw", device="cuda")
det.predict(audio, sample_rate=None) -> Prediction
det.predict_batch(inputs, sample_rate=None, batch_size=16) -> list[Prediction]
det.sample_rate   # 16000
det.window        # window length in samples (e.g. 64600 for AASIST)
det.threshold     # 0.5

audio is a path or a 1-D (or (n, channels)) float array. With an array, sample_rate is required. Paths libsndfile can't read (m4a, aac, mp4 and other video containers) are decoded with ffmpeg if it's on PATH.

docs.title: Image detectors
docs.text:
det = forensix.load("commfor", device="cuda")
det.predict(image) -> Prediction
det.predict_batch(images, batch_size=16) -> list[Prediction]
det.transform     # PIL image -> tensor, the model's upstream eval preprocessing

image is a path, a PIL image or an (H, W, 3) uint8 RGB array. Arrays of another dtype or shape raise ValueError.

docs.title: Video detectors
docs.text:
det = forensix.load("gend-pe", device="cuda")
det.predict(video_path) -> Prediction
det.predict_batch(video_paths) -> list[Prediction]   # loops over predict

A video with no detectable face scores exactly 0.5 for these models. Check len(pred.segment_fake_probs) == 0 to tell "no face" from a genuine 0.5.

docs.title: Audiovisual detectors
docs.text:
det = forensix.load("syncnet", device="cuda")
det.predict(video_path) -> Prediction     # needs a video stream and an audio stream

Raises ValueError if the file lacks either stream. Needs ffmpeg on PATH.

docs.title: Identity detectors
docs.text:
id-face (forensix.identity.face.FaceVerifier) and id-motion (forensix.identity.motion.MotionVerifier) compare media with enrolled people.

Method id-face id-motion enroll(name, media) photos and/or videos (paths or RGB arrays); returns {"name", "n_embeddings"} videos only; returns {"name", "n_windows"} predict(media, identity=name) Prediction Prediction verify(media, identity) the details dict, without building a Prediction same identify(media) [(name, similarity), ...], best first not available save_gallery(path) / load_gallery(path) .npz of enrolled embeddings same; galleries are tagged with the model and can't be mixed gallery.names(), gallery.remove(name) manage enrolled people same

verify raises ValueError("No face found") (or no tracked 4 s window, for id-motion) when the media has nothing to compare.

docs.title: Physics detectors
docs.text:
det = forensix.load("phys-voice")           # also phys-room (audio); phys-bloodflow, phys-motion, phys-lighting (video)
det.predict(path) -> Prediction             # audio detectors also take an array plus sample_rate=
det.load_priors("learned_priors.json")      # or a dict; None = packaged table, if any, else provisional ranges
det.analyze(frames, fps) / det.analyze(x, sr) -> dict   # the same evidence, from decoded media

physdf = forensix.load("physdf", weights_path="physdf_graph.safetensors")   # weights_path optional
physdf.predict(media, audio_path=None) -> Prediction    # video (uses its sound), audio, or video + separate audio

Report helpers in forensix.physics.report:

Function Description build_report(result) Builds the report dict from a physdf result (already done for you in details["report"]). to_markdown(report) The report as Markdown (also in details["report"]["markdown"]). verify_report(report, result) Re-derives every claim, the score and the verdict from the evidence; returns a list of problems (empty means it checks out). render_figures(result, out_dir) Draws the residual timeline; needs matplotlib. Returns the written paths.

docs.text: Command Description python -m forensix FILE [FILE ...] [--models a,b] [--device cuda] [--json] Scores files with the server's default models for each media type (or --models), plus provenance checks, and prints a line per model or JSON python scripts/fetch_samples.py [--out DIR] Downloads a labelled test kit of real and fake media (public domain, CC0 and MIT/Apache) with a SOURCES.md

docs.text: Name Description forensix.calibrate(model, real_media=None, fake_media=None, dataset=None, alpha=0.05, folds=5, seed=0, source="", score_type=None, device="cpu", **load_options) Scores labelled media (a dataset folder or ZIP, or real/fake lists) and fits a calibration. docs.title: Fine-tuning: forensix.finetune, forensix.finetuning
docs.text: Name Description forensix.finetune(model, dataset=None, real_media=None, fake_media=None, out=None, mode="norm", epochs=5, lr=None, batch_size=16, val_fraction=0.2, max_per_class=None, frames=16, augment=True, seed=0, device="cpu", cache_dir=None, lora_rank=8, lora_alpha=16, lora_dropout=0.05, lora_target_pattern=None) Fine-tunes and returns (detector, report): held-out AUC before (base_val_auc) and after (val_auc), best_epoch, per-epoch history, counts and warnings python -m forensix.finetuning MODEL --dataset DATA --out MODEL-ft.safetensors The same from the command line; also writes MODEL-ft.json finetuning.checkpoint_info(path) The checkpoint's metadata (model, mode, base weights hash, report), or None if path isn't a fine-tune checkpoint finetuning.apply(detector, path) Loads a checkpoint into a detector built with its pretrained weights (what forensix.load(..., weights_path=...) does) finetuning.trainable_parameters(network, mode) The parameters a mode trains (head, norm, full) finetuning.lora_targets(network, pattern=None), add_lora(...), merge_lora(network) LoRA through PEFT: choose layers, inject adapters, fold them back into plain layers (PEFT)

docs.title: Provenance: forensix.provenance
docs.text:
Name Description forensix.provenance.check(path, models=None, device="cpu", trust_anchors=None) Runs every applicable provenance check and combines them: {media, verdict, label, summary, findings, checks, skipped} (Provenance) forensix.load("c2pa", trust_anchors=pem_path) C2PA Content Credentials forensix.load("watermark-image"), forensix.load("watermark-audio") SD/SDXL/SVD and AudioSeal watermarks forensix.load("metadata") EXIF/XMP/PNG chunks and container tags provenance.watermark_image.match(bgr) Bit accuracy of each known generator message on an image

Each returns a Prediction with score_type="provenance", threshold=None and details holding verdict, label, summary and findings.

docs.title: Metrics: forensix.metrics
docs.text:
Fakes are the positive class, and higher scores mean more likely fake.

Function Returns roc_auc(fake_scores, real_scores) ROC-AUC, ties counted as ½ average_precision(fake_scores, real_scores) AP, same definition as scikit-learn compute_eer(fake_scores, real_scores) (eer, threshold), ASVspoof-compatible, including tie-breaking binary_summary(fake_scores, real_scores, threshold=0.5) dict with auc, ap, n_fake, n_real, and (if threshold is not None) balanced_acc, real_acc, fake_acc

docs.title: Deploying on AWS
docs.text:
This guide is for engineers putting the ForensiX server (API and web manager) on AWS. Pick a target, then deploy it in one of three ways: from the AWS console, with one command, or with one click in GitHub Actions. Everything the deploy creates is removed by the matching teardown.

Target What runs Pick it when ecs: ECS on Fargate CPU tasks, no servers to manage You want the simplest service, moderate volume, mostly images and audio ecs-gpu: ECS on EC2 GPU One NVIDIA L4 (g6.2xlarge) per task Video and audiovisual models at volume, still without Kubernetes eks: EKS Auto Mode Kubernetes, CPU nodes AWS manages and scales You run Kubernetes already, or want the same manifests as on other clouds eks-gpu: EKS Auto Mode, GPU Kubernetes, NVIDIA nodes launched on demand Kubernetes plus GPUs File What it is deploy/aws/ecs.yaml CloudFormation template: the whole ECS deployment in one stack deploy/aws/eks/ eksctl cluster config (Auto Mode), ALB ingress class, GPU node pool, EFS storage class deploy/kubernetes/overlays/eks, eks-gpu The Kubernetes manifests adapted to EKS deploy/aws/deploy.sh One command to deploy or tear down any target .github/workflows/deploy-aws.yml The same, as a one-click GitHub Actions workflow

docs.title: Before you start: the image
docs.text:
Every target runs the published image, ghcr.io/anas-rz/forensix:cpu-bundled or :gpu-bundled, with the default models baked in. The docker workflow publishes them when you push a version tag:

git tag v0.1.0 && git push origin v0.1.0     # builds and pushes cpu, gpu, cpu-bundled, gpu-bundled

GitHub creates the package as private. AWS can only pull it anonymously once you make it public (GitHub → your profile → Packages → forensix → Package settings → Change visibility). To keep it private, push the image to Amazon ECR instead and pass it with --image (or the image input):

aws ecr create-repository --repository-name forensix
aws ecr get-login-password | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin ACCOUNT.dkr.ecr.REGION.amazonaws.com
docker build -t ACCOUNT.dkr.ecr.REGION.amazonaws.com/forensix:cpu-bundled \
  --build-arg MODELS="dfdet-clip commfor nes2net-x-itw syncnet c2pa watermark-image watermark-audio metadata" .
docker push ACCOUNT.dkr.ecr.REGION.amazonaws.com/forensix:cpu-bundled

docs.title: Option 1: from the AWS console (ECS)
docs.text:
No tools needed. In the CloudFormation console:

  1. Create stack → Upload a template file → choose deploy/aws/ecs.yaml.
  2. Name the stack (e.g. forensix) and pick Compute: Fargate or GPU. The other parameters have working defaults.
  3. Acknowledge that the stack creates IAM roles, then Submit.
  4. When the stack reaches CREATE_COMPLETE (15–30 minutes), its Outputs tab has the web manager URL and the Secrets Manager names of the generated API and admin keys.

A "Launch Stack" button. To give others a one-click link, upload the template to an S3 bucket and link to the quick-create page:

aws s3 cp deploy/aws/ecs.yaml s3://YOUR-BUCKET/forensix/ecs.yaml
# https://console.aws.amazon.com/cloudformation/home?region=us-east-1#/stacks/quickcreate?stackName=forensix&templateURL=https://YOUR-BUCKET.s3.amazonaws.com/forensix/ecs.yaml

[![Launch Stack](https://s3.amazonaws.com/cloudformation-examples/cloudformation-launch-stack.png)](https://console.aws.amazon.com/cloudformation/home?region=us-east-1#/stacks/quickcreate?stackName=forensix&templateURL=https://YOUR-BUCKET.s3.amazonaws.com/forensix/ecs.yaml)

docs.title: Option 2: one command
docs.text:
Needs the AWS CLI v2 with credentials, and for EKS also eksctl and kubectl.

deploy/aws/deploy.sh ecs                     # or ecs-gpu, eks, eks-gpu
deploy/aws/deploy.sh ecs --destroy           # delete everything it created
Option Default Meaning --name forensix Stack or cluster name; deploy several side by side with different names --region AWS_REGION, else us-east-1 Region. GPU targets need L4/A10G capacity there --image ghcr.io/anas-rz/forensix:{cpu,gpu}-bundled Your image, e.g. from ECR --certificate-arn none ECS: an ACM certificate, to serve HTTPS (HTTP redirects to it) --admin-arn none EKS: an IAM user or role to make cluster admin, e.g. yours when GitHub Actions created the cluster

Rerunning the deploy updates in place: a new image, a changed parameter, or a fresh rollout.

When it finishes it prints the web manager URL and how to read the keys. The keys are generated in AWS Secrets Manager and never printed:

aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id <name from the output> --query SecretString --output text

Enter them under Settings in the web manager, or send X-API-Key to the API:

curl -H "X-API-Key: $KEY" -F file=@photo.jpg http://<load balancer>/v1/detect

docs.title: Option 3: one click in GitHub Actions
docs.text:
Actions → deploy-aws → Run workflow: pick the target, deploy or destroy, the name and the region. The workflow runs deploy/aws/deploy.sh and writes the URL and key commands to the run summary.

One-time setup: GitHub signs in to AWS with OpenID Connect, so no access keys are stored.

  1. Add GitHub as an identity provider in your AWS account (once per account):

    aws iam create-open-id-connect-provider --url https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com \
  --client-id-list sts.amazonaws.com

  2. Create a role that only this repository's aws environment can assume. Save as trust.json, replacing ACCOUNT:

    {
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Principal": {"Federated": "arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT:oidc-provider/token.actions.githubusercontent.com"},
    "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity",
    "Condition": {"StringEquals": {
      "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:aud": "sts.amazonaws.com",
      "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub": "repo:anas-rz/ForensiX:environment:aws"
    }}
  }]
}

    aws iam create-role --role-name forensix-deploy --assume-role-policy-document file://trust.json
aws iam attach-role-policy --role-name forensix-deploy --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AdministratorAccess

    A deploy creates VPCs, IAM roles, load balancers, EFS, ECS or EKS, so the role needs broad rights. In a shared account, use a dedicated account or replace AdministratorAccess with a policy limited to CloudFormation, EC2, ECS, EKS, ELB, EFS, IAM, Auto Scaling, Secrets Manager, CloudWatch Logs and SSM.

  3. In the repository: Settings → Environments → New environment aws (add required reviewers to approve each deploy), then Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret AWS_DEPLOY_ROLE_ARN = the role's ARN.

For EKS, pass your own IAM ARN as admin_arn so you can use kubectl on the cluster the workflow created.

docs.title: What gets deployed
docs.text:
Both platforms deploy the same design as the Kubernetes manifests.

  • One manager serves the web manager, dataset uploads, calibration and fairness jobs, and identity enrollment. It's the single writer of shared state.
  • Autoscaled inference replicas serve /v1/detect. They can't write shared state.
  • EFS holds the shared state: datasets, calibration versions, fairness reports and galleries. An activated calibration applies to every replica on its next request.
  • An Application Load Balancer routes management paths to the manager and everything else to the replicas. It health-checks /ready, so a task gets traffic only once its models are loaded.

ECS (deploy/aws/ecs.yaml):

  • Network: a new VPC with two public subnets. Tasks accept traffic only from the load balancer, and EFS only from the tasks.
  • Fargate: 4 vCPUs, 16 GiB and 100 GiB of ephemeral storage per task. The inference service scales from 2 to 6 tasks on CPU utilization.
  • GPU:
  • An Auto Scaling group of ECS GPU-optimized instances (g6.2xlarge by default, one task each), sized by an ECS capacity provider.
  • Inference scales on requests per task, because GPU work doesn't show up as CPU.
  • GPU tasks have no public IP. The instance pulls the image, and the bundled image needs no other downloads.
  • Keys and logs: both keys are generated in Secrets Manager and injected as secrets. Logs go to CloudWatch (/forensix/<stack>, 30 days).
  • Parameters: instance type, task counts, preloaded models, image, certificate and the allowed client CIDR. Set them in the console, or with aws cloudformation deploy --parameter-overrides.

EKS (deploy.sh eks):

  • Cluster: an Auto Mode cluster. AWS runs the nodes (Karpenter), the load balancer controller and the GPU drivers, so nodes appear when the HPA adds pods and go away when they're idle.
  • Storage: an EFS file system with mount targets in the cluster's private subnets, plus the efs-sc storage class and the EFS CSI driver add-on.
  • Keys: generated into the Secrets Manager secret <name>/forensix-keys, then copied into the forensix-keys Kubernetes Secret.
  • Workloads: the eks or eks-gpu overlay. Its Ingress becomes an internet-facing ALB, and for eks-gpu a gpu NodePool (g6, g6e or g5, one GPU per node) is added.

docs.title: HTTPS and a domain
docs.text:
• ECS: pass --certificate-arn (an ACM certificate in the same region). Port 80 then redirects to 443. Point a CNAME or a Route 53 alias at the LoadBalancerDns output.
  • EKS: add these annotations to the Ingress in your copy of the overlay, then point your DNS at the Ingress address:
  • alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/certificate-arn: <arn>
  • alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/listen-ports: '[{"HTTP": 80}, {"HTTPS": 443}]'
  • alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "443"

Until then, traffic, including API keys, is plain HTTP. Restrict who can reach it (ECS AllowedCidr, or alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/inbound-cidrs on EKS) or add HTTPS before using real keys.

docs.title: Costs and teardown
docs.text:
You pay for what runs: - Fixed: the load balancer and the EFS storage. - Per task or node: Fargate tasks or EC2/EKS nodes. GPU instances are the largest cost. - EKS only: the control plane and a NAT gateway.

--destroy (or the workflow's destroy action) deletes the stack or cluster, the EFS file system with your datasets and calibrations, and the keys. Copy anything you want to keep first, for example by downloading calibration tables from the web manager.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause and fix Tasks or pods stop with CannotPullContainerError / ImagePullBackOff The image isn't published or isn't public: see the image Load balancer returns 503 for a few minutes after deploy Models are loading; targets join once /ready returns 200 ECS GPU stack waits on the services No GPU capacity in the region or AZs, or an EC2 vCPU quota for G instances: request a quota increase or try another region EKS GPU pods stay Pending Same capacity or quota limit; kubectl describe nodeclaims shows why nodes didn't launch POST /v1/datasets or calibration returns 409 The request reached an inference replica; use the load balancer's URL, which routes management paths to the manager Logs ECS: aws logs tail --follow /forensix/<name>. EKS: kubectl -n forensix logs deploy/forensix-manager

  • The deploy script passes ShellCheck.

docs.title: Deploying on Azure
docs.text:
This guide is for engineers putting the ForensiX server (API and web manager) on Azure. Pick a target, then deploy it with the "Deploy to Azure" button, with one command, or with one click in GitHub Actions. Every deployment lives in its own resource group, so the teardown deletes that group.

Target What runs Pick it when aca: Container Apps, CPU Serverless containers on a dedicated D8 workload profile, HTTPS included The simplest service, moderate volume, mostly images and audio aca-gpu: Container Apps, GPU Serverless NVIDIA T4 per replica Video and audiovisual models without managing anything aks: AKS Kubernetes with the cluster autoscaler and managed NGINX ingress You run Kubernetes already, or want the same manifests as on other clouds aks-gpu: AKS, GPU Kubernetes plus an autoscaled T4 node pool Kubernetes plus GPUs File What it is deploy/azure/containerapps.bicep Bicep template: the whole Container Apps deployment deploy/azure/containerapps.json The same compiled to an ARM template, for the "Deploy to Azure" button deploy/azure/deploy.sh One command to deploy or tear down any target deploy/kubernetes/overlays/aks, aks-gpu The Kubernetes manifests adapted to AKS .github/workflows/deploy-azure.yml The same, as a one-click GitHub Actions workflow

docs.title: Before you start: the image
docs.text: Every target runs ghcr.io/anas-rz/forensix:cpu-bundled or :gpu-bundled, which have the default models baked in. Push a version tag (git tag v0.1.0 && git push origin v0.1.0) to publish them, then make the GHCR package public (details). To use a private registry (Azure Container Registry), pass --image and give the apps or cluster pull access (az containerapp registry set, az aks update --attach-acr).

docs.title: Option 1: Deploy to Azure (Container Apps)
docs.text:
1. Choose or create a resource group and a region. compute = gpu needs a serverless-GPU region such as westus3, swedencentral or australiaeast.
  2. Enter an API key and an admin key: long random strings, for example from python3 -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(30))".
  3. Review + create. When it finishes, the deployment's Outputs show the web manager and detection URLs.

The button deploys the JSON template from the main branch. After editing the Bicep file, regenerate the JSON with az bicep build --file deploy/azure/containerapps.bicep --outfile deploy/azure/containerapps.json.

docs.title: Option 2: one command
docs.text:
Needs the Azure CLI, logged in (az login) with a subscription selected. AKS also needs kubectl (az aks install-cli).

deploy/azure/deploy.sh aca                      # or aca-gpu, aks, aks-gpu
deploy/azure/deploy.sh aca --destroy            # delete the resource group
Option Default Meaning --name forensix Resource group and resource name prefix --location AZURE_LOCATION, else eastus Region. aca-gpu needs a serverless-GPU region; aks-gpu needs NCasT4_v3 quota --image ghcr.io/anas-rz/forensix:{cpu,gpu}-bundled Your image

Rerunning the deploy updates in place and keeps the keys. The deploy generates them once, stores them as Container Apps or Kubernetes secrets, and never prints them. The output shows how to read them:

az containerapp secret show -g forensix -n forensix-manager --secret-name api-key --query value -o tsv
curl -H "X-API-Key: $KEY" -F file=@photo.jpg https://<inference URL>/v1/detect

docs.title: Option 3: one click in GitHub Actions
docs.text:
Actions → deploy-azure → Run workflow: pick the target, deploy or destroy, the name and the region. The URLs and key commands appear in the run summary.

One-time setup: GitHub signs in to Microsoft Entra with OpenID Connect, so no client secret is stored.

SUB=$(az account show --query id -o tsv)
APP=$(az ad app create --display-name forensix-deploy --query appId -o tsv)
az ad sp create --id $APP
az role assignment create --assignee $APP --role Owner --scope /subscriptions/$SUB
az ad app federated-credential create --id $APP --parameters '{
  "name": "github-forensix-azure",
  "issuer": "https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com",
  "subject": "repo:anas-rz/ForensiX:environment:azure",
  "audiences": ["api://AzureADTokenExchange"]
}'

A deploy creates resource groups, clusters and role assignments for managed identities, so the app needs Owner, or Contributor plus User Access Administrator. In a shared tenant, scope it to a dedicated subscription.

In the repository, create the environment azure (Settings → Environments; add required reviewers to gate deploys). Then add these repository secrets: - AZURE_CLIENT_ID = $APP - AZURE_TENANT_ID = from az account show --query tenantId -o tsv - AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID = $SUB

docs.title: What gets deployed
docs.text:
Container Apps (aca, aca-gpu; deploy/azure/containerapps.bicep):

  • <name>-manager serves the web manager, dataset uploads, calibration and fairness jobs. It runs as exactly one replica, the single writer of shared state.
  • <name>-inference serves /v1/detect. It scales from 1 to 6 replicas on concurrent requests and can't write shared state.
  • Two URLs. Each app has its own HTTPS URL on azurecontainerapps.io. Open the web manager on the manager URL and send API traffic to the inference URL. (The manager also answers /v1/detect, which the web manager's Test page uses.) To put both behind one domain, front them with Azure Front Door or Application Gateway and route the management paths (see the Ingress) to the manager.
  • Compute:
  • CPU: the dedicated D8 workload profile, with one replica per node (7 vCPUs, 28 GiB). The Consumption profile tops out at 4 vCPUs and 8 GiB, too little for the default models.
  • GPU: the serverless Consumption-GPU-NC8as-T4 profile, with one T4, 8 vCPUs and 56 GiB per replica. Serverless GPUs need a quota request.
  • Shared state: an Azure Files share mounted at /data in both apps, owned by the image's user (uid 10001).
  • Probes: startup and readiness on /ready (up to 15 minutes for models to load), liveness on /health.
  • Logs: in a Log Analytics workspace.

AKS (aks, aks-gpu):

  • Cluster:
  • two to six Standard_D8s_v5 nodes, scaled by the cluster autoscaler;
  • Azure CNI overlay with the Cilium dataplane, which enforces the NetworkPolicy;
  • the application routing add-on, a managed NGINX ingress.
  • GPU: aks-gpu adds a gpu node pool of Standard_NC4as_T4_v3 (one to four nodes) and the NVIDIA device plugin. The pool has the nvidia.com/gpu.present=true label and nvidia.com/gpu taint the GPU overlay expects.
  • Workloads: the aks or aks-gpu overlay, with the shared volume on Azure Files (azurefile-csi). The keys are in the forensix-keys Kubernetes Secret.

docs.title: HTTPS and a domain
docs.text:
• Container Apps: HTTPS is on by default. Add a custom domain with a free managed certificate using az containerapp hostname add and az containerapp hostname bind.
  • AKS: the Ingress serves plain HTTP on its IP. Point a host at that IP and add a TLS certificate through the application routing add-on's Key Vault integration. Until then, restrict access or don't use real keys over it.

docs.title: Costs and teardown
docs.text:
• Container Apps CPU: at least one D8 node per running replica, so two at minimum (manager plus one inference replica).
  • Container Apps GPU: billed per second while replicas run.
  • AKS: the nodes (two or more D8s_v5, plus T4 nodes for GPU), the load balancer and the Azure Files share.

--destroy (or the workflow's destroy action) deletes the resource group, including the file share with your datasets and calibrations.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause and fix Revision fails with an image pull error The GHCR image isn't published or isn't public: see the image aca-gpu: workload profile not available or quota exceeded Use a serverless-GPU region and request Consumption-GPU-NC8as-T4 quota for Container Apps aks-gpu: node pool creation fails Request quota for the Standard NCASv3_T4 Family vCPUs in the region Replicas restart while loading Startup takes longer than the probe allows on a slow region; raise periodSeconds in the Bicep probes POST /v1/datasets returns 409 You sent it to the inference app; use the manager URL Logs az containerapp logs show -g RG -n <name>-manager --follow, or kubectl -n forensix logs deploy/forensix-manager

docs.text:
• The Bicep template compiles with az bicep build, with no linter warnings.
  • The deploy script passes ShellCheck.
  • The aks and aks-gpu overlay patches apply cleanly to the base manifests.

Deployments to an Azure subscription haven't been run from this repository yet. Try a non-production subscription first.

docs.title: Calibrating models on your data
docs.text:
A detector's raw score isn't a probability you can act on. On SDFVD, rine called every video real at its default threshold, while gend flagged a third of real videos. Calibration fixes the meaning of the score for your data, without retraining the model:

  • Calibrated probability: "0.92" means about 92% of media scoring like this were fake in your labelled data (Platt scaling).
  • A false-alarm guarantee: the decision threshold flags at most alpha (e.g. 5%) of real media like yours (split-conformal threshold, fitted on your real items only).
  • A verdict with confidence: fake, real, uncertain (the score fits both classes) or out_of_distribution (the score fits neither), from conformal p-values.

Calibration doesn't make a model better at telling real from fake: AUC is unchanged. If a model can't separate your data (the report's AUC is near 0.5), you need a different model, not a calibration.

The workflow: 1. Put your labelled media in the standard dataset format. 2. Calibrate, from Python (forensix.calibrate) or over HTTP (the server). 3. Read the report: AUC, out-of-fold false-alarm and detection rates, warnings. 4. Predict: calibrated scores and a confidence block on every prediction. 5. Check for drift on newly labelled data, and recalibrate when it fails.

docs.title: The dataset format
docs.text:
A dataset is a ZIP archive (or a folder) in one of two layouts.

Manifest (recommended): a manifest.csv at the root, with one row per file:

my_dataset/
├── manifest.csv
└── media/
    ├── interview7.mp4
    ├── interview7_swap.mp4
    └── ...

file,label,group,identity
media/interview7.mp4,real,interview-7,
media/interview7_swap.mp4,fake,interview-7,
photos/alice_01.jpg,real,,alice
Column Required Meaning file yes Path relative to the dataset root label yes real or fake. Also accepted: bonafide, genuine, authentic, 0 / spoof, deepfake, synthetic, manipulated, 1 group no Files that belong together: a real clip and fakes made from it, or one recording session. Cross-validation keeps a group in one fold, so near-duplicates can't flatter the report. Default: each file alone identity no The enrolled person the media claims to be, for identity models skin_tone, age, gender, attr_<name> no Demographic attributes for fairness reports

Folders: no manifest. Every file under real/ is real and every file under fake/ is fake (subfolders allowed).

my_dataset/
├── real/...
└── fake/...

Zip it with the folder at the top level or one level down; both work:

cd parent_dir && zip -r my_dataset.zip my_dataset

docs.title: What makes a good calibration set
docs.text:
• Media like what you'll score: same sources, platforms, compression and content. A calibration only holds for media exchangeable with it.
  • Enough real items. The conformal threshold needs at least 1/alpha − 1 real items (19 for 5%, 99 for 1%), or it never flags; the report warns you. A few hundred real items give stable rates.
  • Fakes from the generators you expect. The false-alarm guarantee needs no fakes at all, but the probabilities and the detection rate do.
  • Groups for related files, e.g. SDFVD's v12.mp4 and its face swap vs12.mp4.
  • Separate data for checking. Keep newly labelled media for drift checks rather than adding it to the calibration set straight away.

Uploads are validated: unknown labels, missing files, duplicates and files outside the dataset are listed as problems and skipped; a dataset with no usable items is rejected.

If a model ranks your real and fake media poorly (a low AUC), calibration can't fix that: fine-tune it on your data first, then calibrate the fine-tuned model.

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
import forensix

cal, report = forensix.calibrate("dfdet-clip", dataset="my_dataset.zip", device="cuda", alpha=0.05)
print(report["auc"], report["cv"]["conformal"], report["warnings"], report["skipped"])
cal.save("calibrations/dfdet-clip.json")

det = forensix.load("dfdet-clip", device="cuda", calibration="calibrations/dfdet-clip.json")
pred = det.predict("new.mp4")
pred.fake_prob                     # calibrated probability
pred.label                         # decision at the conformal threshold (≤ alpha false alarms)
pred.details["prediction_set"]     # ["fake"], ["real"], ["real", "fake"] or []
pred.details["p_real"], pred.details["p_fake"], pred.details["raw_score"]

forensix.calibrate also takes real_media=[...] and fake_media=[...] lists instead of a dataset, folds and seed for cross-validation, and score_type="raw" for scores that aren't probabilities (detected automatically for anomaly models such as syncnet). For scores you've already computed (e.g. scripts/eval_video_folder.py --scores-out), use forensix.calibration.calibrate_scores(model, scores, is_fake, groups) or scripts/recalibrate.py.

To build on an existing calibration with newly labelled scores of the same model:

from forensix.calibration import Calibration, update_calibration

base = Calibration.load("calibrations/dfdet-clip.json")
new, report = update_calibration(base, new_fake_scores, new_real_scores, window=2000)
new.save("calibrations/dfdet-clip.json")    # report: n_new_*, n_carried_*, AUC, CV, warnings

window caps the scores kept per class: all new scores stay, and older ones are subsampled. Without it, every old score is kept. The HTTP API below does the same with item-level bookkeeping: deduplication by file and lineage.

docs.title: HTTP API
docs.text:
All calibration data lives under the server's calibration_dir. Set it, or datasets and calibrations are lost on restart. Changing calibrations needs the admin key.

1. Upload the dataset:

curl -H "X-API-Key: $ADMIN" -F file=@my_dataset.zip -F name=platform-x-oct \
     http://localhost:8000/v1/datasets

{"id": "9249deec143c", "name": "sdfvd25", "layout": "manifest", "n_items": 50, "n_real": 25,
 "n_fake": 25, "n_groups": 25, "with_identity": 0, "problems": [], "n_problems": 0}

2. Start a calibration job for one or more models:

curl -H "X-API-Key: $ADMIN" -H "content-type: application/json" \
     -d '{"mode": "full", "datasets": ["9249deec143c"], "models": ["dfdc-wm", "dfdet-clip"], "alpha": 0.05}' \
     http://localhost:8000/v1/calibrations

There are three modes (Calibration modes has the details):

mode Fits on Use it for full (default) The given datasets, from scratch A first calibration; a clean rebuild on everything you have incremental The base version's items plus the given datasets Adding newly labelled data on top of previous calibrations refit The base version's items only; nothing is scored Changing alpha or folds Field Default Meaning mode "full" full, incremental or refit datasets required for full and incremental Dataset ids (dataset takes one id) models required Models to calibrate (fusion names work too) base_version the active version, else the latest incremental/refit: the version to build on window none (keep everything) incremental: max items per class. All new items stay; older ones are randomly subsampled only_if_drift false incremental: refit only if the new data fails the drift check against the base version level 0.01 Significance level of that drift check alpha the base's, else 0.05 Target false-alarm rate on real media folds 5 Cross-validation folds for the report seed 0 Seed for folds and window subsampling activate true Use the new version for predictions as soon as it's fitted score_types auto {"model": "raw"} for scores that aren't probabilities

The job scores every item with each model's raw (uncalibrated) output. Image and audio models batch the items, and videos are bounded like uploads. Scores are cached per dataset and model configuration, so a dataset is scored once per model however many calibrations use it. The job then fits, saves a new version and (by default) activates it. It returns 202 with a job id.

3. Poll the job:

curl -H "X-API-Key: $KEY" http://localhost:8000/v1/jobs/19a78650a8ef

While running, progress shows {"model": "dfdc-wm", "scored": 12, "total": 50}. When done, results has one report per model:

Real output: dfdc-wm calibrated on 25 real and 25 face-swapped SDFVD clips (pairs grouped), on CPU:

{
 "status": "done", "version": 1, "activated": true, "model": "dfdc-wm",
 "n_real": 25, "n_fake": 25, "n_skipped": 0, "score_type": "probability", "alpha": 0.05,
 "auc": 0.6656, "ap": 0.6891,
 "cv": {
  "raw":       {"threshold": 0.5, "balanced_acc": 0.58, "false_alarm_rate": 0.12, "detection_rate": 0.28, "ece": 0.3214},
  "platt":     {"balanced_acc": 0.60, "false_alarm_rate": 0.40, "detection_rate": 0.60, "ece": 0.0652},
  "conformal": {"alpha": 0.05, "balanced_acc": 0.56, "false_alarm_rate": 0.04, "detection_rate": 0.16},
  "prediction_sets": {"coverage_real": 0.96, "coverage_fake": 0.96, "single_label": 0.2, "both_labels": 0.8, "empty": 0.0}
 },
 "conformal_threshold": 0.7326,
 "warnings": ["fewer than 50 items in a class: probabilities and rates are rough"]
}

How to read it: - Probabilities: calibration error (ECE) fell from 0.32 to 0.07. - False alarms: the conformal threshold held them at 4% against a 5% target. - Ranking: AUC 0.67 says dfdc-wm separates this data poorly. That's why 80% of the prediction sets hold both labels: calibration made the model honest about its uncertainty, but didn't make it better. For this data, calibrate a stronger model (gend-pe reached AUC 0.96 on SDFVD).

Report field Meaning version, activated The saved version and whether it's now in use mode, parent, lineage How it was built: the mode, the version it built on, and every dataset in its history n_new, n_carried, n_dropped_old Items from this job's datasets, items carried over from the base version, and old items left out by window or replaced by a newer copy of the same file n_real, n_fake, n_skipped, skipped Items scored, and items the model couldn't score (wrong media type, no face, unreadable) auc, ap How well the model separates your data. Calibration doesn't change these cv.raw Out-of-fold results at the model's default threshold cv.platt Out-of-fold results deciding at calibrated probability ≥ 0.5, plus Brier score, log loss and ECE cv.conformal Out-of-fold results at the conformal threshold: false_alarm_rate should be near alpha cv.prediction_sets Coverage of the prediction sets, and how often they're single, double or empty conformal_threshold Raw score above which media is flagged warnings Too few real items for alpha, small classes, low AUC

4. Manage versions. Every fit is a new version; nothing is overwritten.

curl -H "X-API-Key: $KEY" http://localhost:8000/v1/calibrations/dfdc-wm                 # versions, active one
curl -H "X-API-Key: $KEY" http://localhost:8000/v1/calibrations/dfdc-wm/versions/1      # table + report
curl -X PUT -H "X-API-Key: $ADMIN" -H "content-type: application/json" \
     -d '{"version": 1}' http://localhost:8000/v1/calibrations/dfdc-wm/active           # roll back
curl -X PUT -H "X-API-Key: $ADMIN" -H "content-type: application/json" \
     -d '{"version": null}' http://localhost:8000/v1/calibrations/dfdc-wm/active        # raw scores again

A version's table is the standard calibration JSON. Save it to a file and it works with forensix.load(name, calibration=path), so a calibration fitted on the server can be used in batch jobs too.

5. Check for drift when you have newly labelled media. Upload it as another dataset, then:

curl -H "X-API-Key: $ADMIN" -H "content-type: application/json" \
     -d '{"dataset": "<new dataset id>"}' http://localhost:8000/v1/calibrations/check

The job scores the new data and tests it against each active calibration: false alarms above alpha, shifted real or fake scores, a dropped detection rate. recalibrate: true means at least one test failed. Then calibrate on data that includes the new media. If the new data's AUC has dropped, the model itself no longer works on it, and recalibrating won't help.

docs.title: Calibration modes
docs.text:
Every job creates a new version. Each version stores the exact items it was fitted on (file hash, label, group, raw score, source dataset), so later versions can build on it.

Full. Fits from scratch on the given datasets: one, or several at once ("datasets": [a, b]). A file that appears in two datasets is used once; a file labelled both real and fake is left out, with a warning. Use it for the first calibration of a model, and periodically to rebuild on exactly the data you trust.

Incremental. Starts from a base version: base_version, else the active version, else the latest. It combines the base's items with the new datasets' items:

  • Duplicates: a file the base already had (same SHA-256) takes its new label and score, so re-uploading corrected labels fixes them rather than doubling the file.
  • window: keeps at most that many items per class: all new items, plus a random subset of the old. The calibration then follows changing traffic instead of being dominated by old data. Without window, the calibration set only grows.
  • only_if_drift: checks the new data against the base version first. If none of the drift tests fail, no version is created and the result is "status": "skipped", with the drift report. Use this for scheduled updates: upload each week's labelled media and recalibrate only when it's needed.
  • Settings: alpha and the score type default to the base version's.
# weekly: add the newest labelled media, keep the 2,000 most recent items per class,
# and only create a new version if the old one no longer fits
curl -H "X-API-Key: $ADMIN" -H "content-type: application/json" \
     -d '{"mode": "incremental", "datasets": ["<this week>"], "models": ["dfdet-clip"],
          "window": 2000, "only_if_drift": true}' \
     http://localhost:8000/v1/calibrations

Refit. Re-fits the base version's items with new settings, such as a stricter alpha ({"mode": "refit", "models": ["dfdet-clip"], "alpha": 0.01}). Nothing is scored, so it takes seconds.

Lineage. GET /v1/calibrations/{model} lists every version with its mode, parent and datasets. For example (illustrative values):

{"version": 7, "mode": "incremental", "parent": 6, "datasets": ["oct", "nov", "dec"],
 "n_real": 1840, "n_fake": 1020, "n_new": 412, "n_carried": 2448, "auc": 0.93, "alpha": 0.05}

Same model only. Raw scores are only combined when they come from the same model configuration: the same registered weights or checkpoint file, and the same load options. Each version records this as fingerprint. If you change a model's checkpoint or options, an incremental or refit job on an older version fails with a clear error. Run a full calibration instead; the datasets are rescored with the new configuration.

docs.title: Predictions with confidence
docs.text:
With a calibration in use, every /v1/detect result for that model reads:

Real output for two SDFVD clips that weren't in the calibration set (dfdc-wm, version 1 above):

// v30.mp4 (real)
{"score": 0.531, "threshold": 0.669, "label": "real", "calibration": "v1",
 "confidence": {"fake_probability": 0.531, "verdict": "uncertain", "prediction_set": ["real", "fake"],
                "p_real": 0.423, "p_fake": 0.5, "alpha": 0.05, "calibration": "v1"}}
// vs30.mp4 (its face swap)
{"score": 0.707, "threshold": 0.669, "label": "fake", "calibration": "v1",
 "confidence": {"fake_probability": 0.707, "verdict": "fake", "prediction_set": ["fake"],
                "p_real": 0.038, "p_fake": 0.962, "alpha": 0.05, "calibration": "v1"}}
Field Meaning score Calibrated fake probability, at the calibration set's fake rate threshold, label Decision at the conformal threshold: at most alpha of real media like the calibration set is labelled fake calibration Version in use ("v3", or "config" for a table from the server config) confidence.verdict fake or real: the score fits only that class. uncertain: it fits both (the model can't tell). out_of_distribution: it fits neither (unlike the calibration data, so check it by hand) confidence.p_real, confidence.p_fake Conformal p-values: how typical the score is among real and among fake calibration items confidence.prediction_set The classes with p-value above alpha. Each true class is included with probability at least 1 − alpha

label and verdict answer different questions. label is the decision with a false-alarm guarantee; verdict says how sure the evidence is. A good triage rule: act automatically only on verdict: fake, send uncertain and out_of_distribution to a person, and pass real.

These guarantees hold for media exchangeable with the calibration data. When your traffic changes, run a drift check.

Next step: check that false alarms are even across groups with a fairness report.

docs.title: Docker, Kubernetes and cloud
docs.text:
This guide is for engineers deploying the ForensiX server (API and web manager) as containers: locally with Docker Compose, on Kubernetes, or on a managed cloud service. For the design of a large-scale service (queues, worker pools, thresholds, monitoring), see Deployment at scale.

File What it is Dockerfile The server image: CPU or GPU, optionally with model weights baked in compose.yaml, compose.gpu.yaml Docker Compose, CPU and an NVIDIA GPU override deploy/forensix.env.example Keys and settings as environment variables deploy/kubernetes/ Kustomize base plus cpu and gpu overlays .github/workflows/docker.yml CI: tests, image builds, publishing to GHCR on version tags deploy/aws/ AWS: ECS (Fargate or GPU) and EKS Auto Mode, one command or one click (Deploying on AWS) deploy/gcp/ Google Cloud: Cloud Run (CPU or L4) and GKE Autopilot (Deploying on Google Cloud) deploy/azure/ Azure: Container Apps (CPU or T4) and AKS (Deploying on Azure)

docs.title: The image
docs.text:
docker build -t forensix:cpu .
docker build -t forensix:gpu --build-arg TORCH_INDEX=https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu124 .
docker build -t forensix:cpu-bundled --build-arg MODELS="dfdet-clip commfor nes2net-x-itw syncnet" .
Build arg Default Meaning TORCH_INDEX CPU wheels PyTorch wheel index; cu124 (or the version matching your driver) for NVIDIA GPUs MODELS none Models whose weights are downloaded, verified and baked into the image PYTHON_VERSION 3.12 Base image Python

Bundled or not. - Bundled images (MODELS=...) start without downloading anything and can run with no network access, which is what you want for production. Every container starts from the same verified files. Each CLIP-sized model adds about 1.2–1.6 GB. - Plain images download weights on first use into /opt/forensix/cache. Mount a volume there so they survive restarts.

Bake the same models you preload and use as defaults. If a request needs a model that isn't baked in, the server tries to download it. On a read-only cache that fails with an error naming the fix, and the server logs a warning at startup for default models that aren't preloaded.

Inside the image: - Server: python -m forensix.server on port $PORT (default 8000), under tini, as non-root user 10001. - Logs: JSON lines on stdout (LOG_FORMAT=json; set text for humans). - Writable paths: /data (datasets, calibrations, identity galleries) and /tmp. Everything else can be read-only. - Health: a Docker HEALTHCHECK on /health. - Shutdown: in-flight requests get GRACEFUL_TIMEOUT seconds (default 30) after SIGTERM.

Configuration comes from a JSON file (FORENSIX_SERVER_CONFIG or --config) and/or FORENSIX_SERVER_<FIELD> environment variables for any field in the server configuration. Lists can be comma- or space-separated; dicts are JSON:

docker run -p 8000:8000 -v forensix-data:/data \
  -e FORENSIX_SERVER_API_KEY=... -e FORENSIX_SERVER_ADMIN_KEY=... \
  -e FORENSIX_SERVER_PRELOAD="commfor dfdet-clip" -e FORENSIX_SERVER_THRESHOLDS='{"dfdet-clip": 0.71}' \
  forensix:cpu-bundled

docs.title: Docker Compose
docs.text:
cp deploy/forensix.env.example .env        # set FORENSIX_SERVER_API_KEY and _ADMIN_KEY
docker compose up -d --build               # http://localhost:8000/ui/
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.gpu.yaml up -d --build    # NVIDIA GPU host
docker compose logs -f

Compose runs the container read-only with dropped capabilities and a /tmp tmpfs. Two named volumes keep state across restarts: data (calibrations, datasets, galleries) and cache (weights).

docs.title: Kubernetes
docs.text:
kubectl create namespace forensix
kubectl -n forensix create secret generic forensix-keys --from-env-file=deploy/forensix.env
kubectl apply -k deploy/kubernetes/overlays/cpu       # or overlays/gpu
kubectl -n forensix get pods -w

docs.title: What gets deployed
docs.text:
On Kubernetes the shared storage is a ReadWriteMany volume (Filestore on GKE, EFS on EKS, Azure Files on AKS). On ECS it's EFS; on Cloud Run, a Cloud Storage bucket; on Container Apps, an Azure Files share.

  • The manager owns the web UI, dataset uploads, calibration jobs and identity enrollment. It runs as a single replica, so shared state has exactly one writer.
  • Inference replicas serve /v1/detect and scale horizontally. With admin_endpoints: false they refuse writes to shared state (HTTP 409). They read the shared volume on every request, so an activated calibration or a new enrollment takes effect on all replicas immediately, without restarts.
  • Ingress routes management paths to the manager and the rest to the replicas. The UI's Test page calls /v1/detect, so it uses the replicas too.
Object Notes ConfigMap forensix-config server.json, shared settings. preload should match the models baked into the image Secret forensix-keys FORENSIX_SERVER_API_KEY, FORENSIX_SERVER_ADMIN_KEY (you create it) PVC forensix-data ReadWriteMany; set your RWX storage class in the overlay Probes startupProbe on /ready (up to 15 min to preload models), readinessProbe on /ready, livenessProbe on /health Security Restricted Pod Security Standard: non-root, read-only root filesystem, no privilege escalation, all capabilities dropped, RuntimeDefault seccomp, no service-account token NetworkPolicy Inbound port 8000; outbound DNS only. Needs a bundled image (no weight downloads) HPA Inference on CPU utilization (CPU overlay); see below for GPU PodDisruptionBudget At least one inference replica during node drains Prometheus Pods carry prometheus.io/scrape annotations for /metrics

Overlays: - cpu: the cpu-bundled image, with your RWX storage class and host name. - gpu: the gpu-bundled image, one nvidia.com/gpu per pod for both deployments, GPU node selector and toleration, and device: cuda. It needs the NVIDIA device plugin (GKE and AKS GPU pools include it; on EKS install the NVIDIA GPU operator).

Copy an overlay and edit the image registry, host, TLS secret and storage class for your cluster.

Sizing. - CPU pods: request 4 CPUs and 12 GiB, with a 16 GiB limit; that holds the four default models with headroom. - GPU pods: a 24 GB L4 fits the defaults. CPU-side work (decoding, face detection) still matters there, so keep 4+ CPUs per GPU pod. - Autoscaling on GPU: GPU pods don't produce useful CPU-utilization signals. Scale them on request rate instead, e.g. rate(forensix_requests_total[2m]) through prometheus-adapter or KEDA.

Startup time. A new replica takes minutes to load models (more on CPU). The HPA scales down slowly (10-minute window) so replicas don't flap. Pre-pull the image on GPU node pools if your platform supports it (e.g. GKE image streaming).

docs.title: Managed clouds
docs.text:
Each cloud has a one-command, one-click deployment that sets all of this up:

  • AWS: ECS on Fargate or GPU instances, or EKS Auto Mode.
  • Google Cloud: Cloud Run (CPU or L4), or GKE Autopilot.
  • Azure: Container Apps (CPU or T4), or AKS.
GKE EKS AKS RWX storage class Filestore CSI (standard-rwx) EFS CSI driver (efs-sc) Azure Files (azurefile-csi) GPU nodes L4 node pool (g2-standard-8), node selector cloud.google.com/gke-accelerator: nvidia-l4 g6.2xlarge (L4) node group + NVIDIA GPU operator Standard_NC4as_T4_v3 / NC A100 pools Registry Artifact Registry ECR ACR Ingress GKE Ingress or ingress-nginx AWS Load Balancer Controller or ingress-nginx Application Gateway or ingress-nginx

The base Ingress targets ingress-nginx (its upload size and timeout annotations matter for dataset ZIPs). On other controllers, set the equivalent body-size and read-timeout limits.

docs.title: Cloud Run (no cluster)
docs.text:
Deploying on Google Cloud automates this, with a separate manager service and shared storage.

A single container works on Cloud Run, with CPU or an NVIDIA L4 GPU:

gcloud run deploy forensix --image REGION-docker.pkg.dev/PROJECT/forensix/forensix:gpu-bundled \
  --gpu 1 --gpu-type nvidia-l4 --cpu 8 --memory 32Gi --no-cpu-throttling \
  --min-instances 1 --max-instances 4 --concurrency 8 --timeout 900 \
  --set-env-vars FORENSIX_SERVER_DEVICE=cuda,FORENSIX_SERVER_PRELOAD="dfdet-clip commfor nes2net-x-itw syncnet" \
  --set-secrets FORENSIX_SERVER_API_KEY=forensix-api-key:latest,FORENSIX_SERVER_ADMIN_KEY=forensix-admin-key:latest
  • Port: Cloud Run sets PORT, which the server uses.
  • Instances: --min-instances 1 avoids cold starts, which take minutes to load models. --no-cpu-throttling keeps calibration jobs running between requests.
  • State: the container filesystem is lost when an instance stops, so calibrations need storage. Either mount a Cloud Storage bucket at /data (Cloud Run volume mounts), or keep calibration on a separate always-on manager and run Cloud Run instances as prediction-only (FORENSIX_SERVER_ADMIN_ENDPOINTS=false) with the same bucket mounted.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
• Metrics: /metrics (Prometheus text format):
  • server: forensix_ready, forensix_uptime_seconds, forensix_models_loaded;
  • per model: forensix_requests_total, forensix_errors_total, forensix_cache_hits_total, forensix_busy_seconds_total, forensix_load_seconds, forensix_batches_total, forensix_batched_items_total;
  • calibration: forensix_jobs{status}, forensix_calibration_active_version{model}.

Mean latency per model is rate(busy_seconds_total) / rate(requests_total). Turn the endpoint off with metrics: false. - Logs: JSON lines with time, level, logger, message, ready for Cloud Logging, CloudWatch, Loki or Elasticsearch. - Health: /health (process up) and /ready (preloaded models in memory). - Web UI: the Overview page shows the instance it's served from. On Kubernetes that's the manager, so use Prometheus for fleet-wide numbers.

docs.title: Security checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] API and admin keys set, from a Secret manager, never in images or ConfigMaps.
  • [ ] TLS terminated at the Ingress or load balancer; plain HTTP only inside the cluster.
  • [ ] Bundled image plus the NetworkPolicy: no egress from pods that decode untrusted media.
  • [ ] Read-only root filesystem, non-root user, dropped capabilities (all in the manifests).
  • [ ] Images rebuilt regularly for ffmpeg, OpenCV and Python security fixes; scan them in your registry.
  • [ ] /data access restricted. It holds identity galleries (biometric data) and your labelled datasets.
  • [ ] Upload and dataset size limits (max_upload_mb, max_dataset_mb) and Ingress body limits set to what you need.

docs.title: What's been verified
docs.text:
• Server runtime, run locally as the container runs it:
  • environment-only configuration, PORT, JSON logs;
  • --warm-only filling a cache with verified, stamped files, and exiting 1 on a model that can't load;
  • serving from a read-only cache, with an actionable error for missing weights;
  • prediction-only replicas refusing writes;
  • /metrics;
  • graceful SIGTERM shutdown;
  • a manager and a replica sharing a calibration directory (automated test).
  • Kubernetes manifests: both overlays were rendered with a Python implementation of the Kustomize steps used here, and their links checked (selectors, Services, Ingress backends, volumes, ConfigMap and PVC references, the GPU patch, the restricted security settings).
  • Not yet: building the image (this repo's development machine has no Docker access) and applying the manifests to a cluster. Run docker compose up --build and kubectl apply -k --dry-run=server on your side, or let CI build the image on the next pull request.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
ForensiX has four building blocks: a registry of models, a loader that builds detectors with verified weights, detectors that share one calling convention per input type, and the Prediction every detector returns.

forensix.load("gend-pe", device="cuda")
   │
   ├─ registry.get_spec("gend-pe")          → ModelSpec (family, license, weights URL + SHA-256, builder)
   ├─ hub.fetch(spec.weights)                → ~/.cache/forensix/weights/gend-pe-l.safetensors (hash-checked)
   └─ spec.builder(path, device="cuda")      → detector object
                                                 │
detector.predict("clip.mp4")  ───────────────────┘→ Prediction(model, fake_prob, threshold, segment_fake_probs,
                                                               score_type, details)

docs.title: Registry and ModelSpec
docs.text:
Each model module calls register(ModelSpec(...)) when forensix is imported. A spec holds:

Field Meaning name The string you pass to forensix.load, e.g. "gend-pe" family audio, image, video, audiovisual, identity, physics or specialized builder (weights_path, device) -> detector weights A WeightFile(url, sha256, filename), or None for models that need no weights or that you train yourself extra_weights Shared files the builder fetches itself, e.g. a CLIP backbone used by several models license, source, paper, description Provenance. Read license before you ship a model (Licensing) 
import forensix
forensix.list_models()            # every registered name
forensix.list_models("video")     # one family
forensix.info("gend-pe").license  # provenance for one model

docs.title: Weights and the cache
docs.text:
forensix.load(name) calls forensix.download(name), which fetches every file in the spec into the cache and checks its SHA-256 hash. A file whose hash doesn't match is deleted and downloaded again, and a download whose hash doesn't match raises an error. Nothing unverified is loaded.

  • Location: $FORENSIX_CACHE if set, otherwise ~/.cache/forensix. Weights live under weights/.
  • Size: about 18 GB for every model. The large ones are the CLIP/PE-based models (1.2–1.6 GB each), the XLS-R audio models (1.2 GB each), stablesyncnet (1.5 GB) and dfdc-selim (1.8 GB).
  • Hashing cost: hashing a 1.6 GB file takes a few seconds. After a successful check, <file>.verified records the hash, size and modification time, and later loads trust an unchanged file without rehashing it. A changed size or mtime triggers a full check. Set FORENSIX_VERIFY_HASH=always to rehash on every load.
  • Load once: building a model still takes seconds (library imports, initialization), so load once per process and reuse the detector.
  • Your own checkpoints: forensix.load(name, weights_path="my.safetensors") skips the download and hash check for the model's own weights. Shared backbones are still fetched.

Checkpoints are read with torch.load(weights_only=True) or safetensors, so loading weights never runs pickled code.

docs.title: Detectors by input type
docs.text:
Detectors of one input type share a calling convention:

Family Input to predict Base class Batch call audio file path (any format libsndfile or ffmpeg reads, including video containers), or a waveform array plus sample_rate= forensix.audio.detector.AudioDetector predict_batch(inputs, sample_rate=None, batch_size=16) image file path, PIL image, or (H, W, 3) uint8 RGB array forensix.image.detector.ImageDetector predict_batch(images, batch_size=16) video video file path forensix.video.detector.VideoDetector predict_batch(videos) (a loop) audiovisual video file path with an audio track (needs ffmpeg) none predict_batch(videos) (a loop) physics video path, audio path, or both (physdf) forensix.physics.base predict_batch(inputs) identity media path plus identity= (after enroll) none none specialized media path or array PersonDetector none

Only the audio and image detectors truly batch on the GPU. Video, audiovisual and physics predict_batch calls are loops over predict, so for throughput, run several worker processes (Deployment).

docs.title: What each type does with your media
docs.text:
• Audio: converted to mono and resampled to 16 kHz, then cut into the model's window (4.04 s for AASIST-family models). Short clips are repeat-padded. Long clips are cut into consecutive windows, with the last one aligned to the end. The clip score is the mean window score.
  • Image: never resized or re-encoded before the model's own upstream preprocessing, because the traces these detectors look for don't survive resampling. Several models score only a central crop (224 or 256 px) of a large image.
  • Video: each model uses its upstream frame sampling and face pipeline: typically 32 evenly spaced frames, face detection (MTCNN or RetinaFace), alignment and per-face scores. Frames are decoded sequentially, so time grows with video length, but memory doesn't.
  • Audiovisual: the whole video is decoded at 25 fps and full resolution into memory, plus 16 kHz audio. Face tracks are built syncnet_python-style. Memory grows with resolution × duration: downscale and trim long inputs first (Deployment).
  • Physics: every frame of the first 30 s, downscaled to a 640 px long side, because physiological signals need every frame.

docs.title: Prediction
docs.text:
Every detector returns a frozen forensix.Prediction:

Field Meaning model Model name fake_prob The score. Higher always means more likely fake. threshold The model's default decision threshold, or None when the score has no natural one score_type "probability" (a softmax/sigmoid output in [0, 1]) or "anomaly" (distance from real behaviour; may be unbounded or negative) segment_fake_probs Per-segment scores: audio windows, faces, frames or AV windows, depending on the model details Structured evidence: per-model measurements, timelines, reports is_fake, label fake_prob >= threshold and "fake"/"real"; None when threshold is None

Two rules follow, and they cause most integration mistakes:

  1. Scores are not comparable across models. A fake_prob of 0.4 from rine and 0.4 from gend mean different things. Compare models by AUC/EER, and choose thresholds per model on data like yours (Interpreting scores).
  2. The default threshold is often wrong for your data. On the SDFVD benchmark, rine scored every video below 0.5 (it called all fakes real) despite an AUC of 0.745.

docs.title: Families and their evidence
docs.text:
Family Question it answers Needs audio Is this speech synthetic or converted? Speech image Is this image generated by a GAN or diffusion model? A whole generated image (not a face swap in a real photo) video Is this face manipulated (swap, reenactment)? A visible face audiovisual Do the voice and the lips belong together? A talking face with its audio track physics Does the media obey physics (pulse, head motion, lighting, voice, room)? A few seconds of face or speech identity Is this really person X? Reference media of X specialized Is this real media of person X? (a tiny model trained only for X) Real media of X to train on

No single family covers every attack. A face swap keeps in-sync lips and real physics in the untouched parts of the frame, while a voice clone has no face to check. See Choosing detectors.

docs.title: Deployment at scale
docs.text:
ForensiX is a Python library with an optional HTTP server (HTTP server). The server suits synchronous calls at moderate volume: one process per GPU, models kept in memory. This guide covers the next step: a service that scores large volumes of media reliably, cheaply and auditably, with queues and worker pools. It is written for the engineers who will design and run that service. A pool of forensix.server instances behind a load balancer is one way to build the worker pools below.

The worker code below was run end to end with real models. The queue and autoscaling sections are patterns to adapt. The container image and Kubernetes manifests are in the repo; see Docker, Kubernetes and cloud for what has been verified.

  • Architecture
  • Input limits
  • Workers
  • Packaging
  • Sizing and scaling
  • Decisions, thresholds and review
  • Monitoring
  • Security
  • Audit and reproducibility
  • Launch checklist

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
┌──────────────┐
 uploads ──────▶│  API / intake │── store original (object storage), compute SHA-256
                └──────┬───────┘
                       │ job {media_uri, sha256, priority}
                       ▼
                ┌──────────────┐    cache hit (same sha256 + same model versions)
                │  job queue    │───────────────────────────────────────────┐
                └──────┬───────┘                                            │
        ┌──────────────┼──────────────────┬─────────────────┐               │
        ▼              ▼                  ▼                 ▼               │
 ┌────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐  ┌───────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐         │
 │ probe +    │ │ face-video  │  │ audio pool    │ │ AV pool      │         │
 │ normalize  │ │ pool (GPU)  │  │ (GPU)         │ │ (GPU, RAM)   │         │
 │ (CPU)      │ │ gend-pe ... │  │ nes2net-x-itw │ │ syncnet ...  │         │
 └────────────┘ └──────┬──────┘  └──────┬────────┘ └──────┬───────┘         │
                       └─────────────────┼─────────────────┘                 │
                                         ▼                                   │
                                ┌─────────────────┐                          │
                                │ results store    │◀────────────────────────┘
                                │ (scores+versions)│
                                └────────┬────────┘
                                         ▼
                                ┌─────────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐
                                │ decision layer   │────▶│ human review │
                                │ thresholds, rules│     │ queue        │
                                └─────────────────┘     └──────────────┘

Design principles:

  • Asynchronous. Video models take seconds per clip on a GPU and minutes on a CPU. Accept a job, return an ID, and deliver results by callback or polling. Never run inference inside a web request.
  • Pools by model group. Each pool is a set of identical worker processes with models loaded once at startup. Pools scale independently: audio-only traffic shouldn't wait behind video.
  • Normalize first. One cheap CPU step probes the media and caps resolution and duration before any GPU work (Input limits).
  • Scores, then decisions. Workers produce raw scores with full provenance. A separate decision layer applies thresholds and rules from versioned configuration, so you can change a threshold without rescoring anything.
  • Idempotent by content. Key results by (input SHA-256, model, weights hash). Re-uploads and retries cost nothing.

docs.title: Input limits
docs.text:
Some code paths read whole files into memory. Bound every input before it reaches a model.

Path Reads Memory and time Limit to apply Video models (gend-pe etc.) 32 evenly spaced frames, decoded sequentially Memory small; time grows with length Fine for long files, but see coverage below Audiovisual models Every frame at 25 fps, full resolution, all in RAM, plus audio About 155 MB per second at 1080p, so a 1-minute 1080p clip is about 9 GB Downscale to ≤ 720p and cut to ≤ 60 s segments Physics models Every frame of the first 30 s, downscaled to 640 px Bounded (about 1 GB at 30 fps) Content after 30 s is ignored: segment long files Audio models The whole file, at 16 kHz mono Small (≈ 4 MB per minute) Segment very long recordings for latency id-face 2 frames per second, up to 120 Bounded Content after 60 s is ignored: segment

Coverage on long videos. Video models spread 32 frames over the whole file. On a 10-minute video that's one frame every 19 s, so a short manipulated segment can be missed. Split long media into 30–60 s segments, score each segment, and keep per-segment results, then flag on the most suspicious segment.

A normalization step with ffmpeg (used by the worker below):

ffmpeg -nostdin -v error -y -i input -t 60 -vf "scale=-2:'min(720,ih)'" \
       -c:v libx264 -crf 18 -c:a aac -b:a 192k normalized.mp4

Re-encoding changes pixels. The detectors were tested on compressed media, and CRF 18 is close to visually lossless, but measure your thresholds on media that went through the same normalization. For segments, use -ss START -t 60 per segment.

docs.title: Workers
docs.text:
A worker is a long-running process that loads its models once and then scores jobs one at a time. This one probes the input, normalizes video, runs only the models that apply (no audio track means no audio or AV models), and returns a record with provenance:

"""ForensiX scoring worker: one process, models loaded once, one job at a time."""

import hashlib
import importlib.metadata
import json
import subprocess
import tempfile
import time
from pathlib import Path

import forensix

MAX_SECONDS = 60          # longer media is split into segments before it reaches this worker
MAX_HEIGHT = 720


def sha256_file(path) -> str:
    h = hashlib.sha256()
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        for chunk in iter(lambda: f.read(1 << 20), b""):
            h.update(chunk)
    return h.hexdigest()


def probe(path) -> dict:
    """Stream types and duration, via ffprobe."""
    out = subprocess.run(
        ["ffprobe", "-v", "error", "-show_entries", "stream=codec_type:format=duration",
         "-of", "json", str(path)], capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=30, check=True).stdout
    info = json.loads(out)
    kinds = {s["codec_type"] for s in info.get("streams", [])}
    return {"video": "video" in kinds, "audio": "audio" in kinds,
            "duration_s": float(info.get("format", {}).get("duration", 0) or 0)}


def normalize(src, workdir) -> Path:
    """Cap duration and resolution so memory per job is bounded."""
    dst = Path(workdir) / "input.mp4"
    subprocess.run(
        ["ffmpeg", "-nostdin", "-v", "error", "-y", "-i", str(src), "-t", str(MAX_SECONDS),
         "-vf", f"scale=-2:'min({MAX_HEIGHT},ih)'", "-c:v", "libx264", "-crf", "18",
         "-c:a", "aac", "-b:a", "192k", str(dst)],
        check=True, timeout=300)
    return dst


class Worker:
    def __init__(self, video_models, audio_models, av_models, device="cuda"):
        self.models = {}
        for group, names in (("video", video_models), ("audio", audio_models), ("av", av_models)):
            for name in names:
                self.models[name] = (group, forensix.load(name, device=device))
        self.versions = {"forensix": importlib.metadata.version("forensix")}
        for name in self.models:
            w = forensix.info(name).weights
            self.versions[name] = w.sha256[:16] if w else "no-weights"

    def run(self, media_path) -> dict:
        record = {"input_sha256": sha256_file(media_path), "versions": self.versions, "results": {}}
        info = probe(media_path)
        record["input"] = info
        with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
            path = normalize(media_path, tmp) if info["video"] else Path(media_path)
            for name, (group, detector) in self.models.items():
                if (group == "video" and not info["video"]) or (group == "audio" and not info["audio"]) \
                        or (group == "av" and not (info["video"] and info["audio"])):
                    record["results"][name] = {"status": "not_applicable"}
                    continue
                start = time.perf_counter()
                try:
                    p = detector.predict(path)
                    result = {"status": "ok", "score": p.fake_prob, "score_type": p.score_type,
                              "default_threshold": p.threshold, "n_segments": len(p.segment_fake_probs)}
                    if group == "video" and not p.segment_fake_probs:
                        result["status"] = "no_face"
                except Exception as e:          # decode failures, no face track, ...
                    result = {"status": "error", "error": repr(e)[:500]}
                result["seconds"] = round(time.perf_counter() - start, 2)
                record["results"][name] = result
        return record

For a video with sound, run on CPU with dfdc-wm, aasist and syncnet:

{
 "input_sha256": "…",
 "versions": {"forensix": "0.1.0", "dfdc-wm": "651ca679c582501b", "aasist": "51d2d9cf0738172f", "syncnet": "961e8696f888fce4"},
 "results": {
  "dfdc-wm": {"status": "ok", "score": 0.032, "score_type": "probability", "default_threshold": 0.5, "n_segments": 24, "seconds": 49.4},
  "aasist":  {"status": "ok", "score": 0.109, "score_type": "probability", "default_threshold": 0.5, "n_segments": 2, "seconds": 1.0},
  "syncnet": {"status": "ok", "score": -0.535, "score_type": "anomaly", "default_threshold": null, "n_segments": 0, "seconds": 76.9}
 },
 "input": {"video": true, "audio": true, "duration_s": 8.1}
}

For an audio file, the video and AV models report "not_applicable".

Connect the worker to your queue (SQS, Pub/Sub, Kafka, Redis, Celery) with a loop: take a job, download the media to local disk, call worker.run, write the record, acknowledge the job.

Rules for workers:

  • Load once. Building a model takes seconds: library imports, initialization, and hash checks of weight files that have no .verified stamp yet. Never load per request.
  • Processes, not threads. Detectors keep state (networks, face detectors) and aren't designed for concurrent calls. Run one detector instance per process, and scale with processes.
  • Timeouts per job. Run each job under a hard timeout: a watchdog that kills and restarts the worker process. A Python-level timeout can't interrupt a stuck decoder.
  • Limit CPU threads. Set OMP_NUM_THREADS / torch.set_num_threads to the worker's share of the cores. Otherwise several workers fight over every core.
  • Retry errors, not results. Retry on infrastructure errors (OOM, killed worker). A "no_face" or decode error is a result: store it, don't retry it forever.
  • Spawn, don't fork, with CUDA. If one parent process starts the workers, use multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").

docs.title: Packaging
docs.text:
The repo ships a production Dockerfile, Compose files and Kubernetes manifests; Docker, Kubernetes and cloud covers them. In short:

  • Bake weights into the image (--build-arg MODELS="..."), so a new node starts without downloading anything and the running service never needs the network. Baking runs python -m forensix.server --warm-only, which loads each model once, so lazily fetched helper files (face detectors, landmark models) are included, with verified hash stamps.
  • One image per pool keeps images small. Bake the models that pool preloads and uses as defaults.
  • Match the CUDA build to your nodes with --build-arg TORCH_INDEX=....
  • Lazy helper files. phys-lighting and physdf download the ICT-FaceKit meshes on their first prediction, not at load. If you serve them, run one prediction on a short sample video during the build or give them a writable cache. Verify the image with docker run --network none.
  • Your trained checkpoints (avcons, avid, id-motion, physdf, person-detector): COPY them into the image, or mount them read-only, and set weights in the server config.

docs.title: Per-model cost
docs.text:
Measured on one NVIDIA L4 (24 GB) with 2–6 s clips (SDFVD). Most of these were measured with 2–4 processes sharing the GPU, so treat them as upper bounds:

Model Seconds per clip Weights image models (8 frames per video) 0.06–0.5 (rine-ldm 2–2.7) 5 MB – 1.6 GB dfdc-wm ~1 312 MB dfdet-clip ~2.7 1.2 GB + 1.6 GB CLIP gend-pe, gend ~7 (shared GPU) 1.2 GB each dfdc-selim ~7 (shared GPU) 1.8 GB

Audio, audiovisual and physics models haven't been timed on a GPU yet. Measure them on your own media before sizing those pools.

docs.title: Workers per GPU
docs.text:
Video and audiovisual models spend much of each job on the CPU (decoding, face detection, tracking), so one process leaves the GPU idle.

  1. Start with 3 workers per 24 GB GPU and about 3 CPU cores per worker.
  2. Raise the count while GPU utilization rises and GPU memory fits; stop when per-job latency grows without throughput gains.
  3. Each worker holds its own copy of the model in GPU memory, which sets the ceiling.

docs.title: Autoscaling
docs.text:
• Scale each pool on its own queue depth (or age of the oldest job), not on CPU or GPU utilization. On Kubernetes, KEDA does this for most queue systems.
  • Keep a minimum of one warm worker per pool. Cold starts include pulling a multi-GB image and loading the models, which can take minutes. Images built by loading each model already contain the .verified stamps, so weights aren't rehashed at startup.
