  • Use separate queues per priority. User-facing checks shouldn't wait behind a bulk backfill.
  • Route by content. Use probe to send audio-only files only to the audio pool. A cheap face check (any face in a few frames?) avoids sending faceless videos to face models.

docs.title: Cutting cost
docs.text:
• Cache by content hash. Viral media gets uploaded many times.
  • Cascade. Run a fast model on everything (e.g. dfdet-clip), and send only uncertain cases to the slower ones. Measure the cascade's detection rate as a whole: the first stage's misses are never seen again.
  • Don't run models that can't help. Image detectors on face-swap video added little on SDFVD (AUC 0.56–0.75).

docs.title: Decisions, thresholds and review
docs.text:
Keep decision logic out of the workers, in versioned configuration:

# decision-config v7 (2026-10-26), thresholds set at 1% FPR on 12,000 real uploads (platform X)
rules:
  face_manipulation:
    model: dfdet-clip
    threshold: 0.71
  voice_clone:
    model: nes2net-x-itw
    threshold: 0.83
  lip_sync_mismatch:
    model: syncnet
    threshold: -2.0        # anomaly score = -confidence; flag when confidence < 2
action:
  any_rule_fires: human_review
  none_fire: pass
  • Set thresholds on real traffic from the deployment's own sources, at the false-alarm rate your review team can absorb (Interpreting scores). The defaults are wrong for many domains: on SDFVD, rine called every video real at 0.5.
  • Version the config and store its version with every decision, so any decision can be explained later.
  • Send uncertain or consequential cases to people, with the evidence: which check fired, its score and threshold, segment timelines, syncnet offset and confidence, the physdf report. The stablesyncnet weights license forbids fully automated decisions that adversely affect someone's legal rights (Licensing).
  • Feed reviewer verdicts back as labelled data for re-checking thresholds.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text:
Signal Why Alert when Score distribution per model (daily quantiles) Drift: new cameras, codecs or generators shift scores The 99th percentile on presumed-real traffic moves past the threshold Flag rate per rule Thresholds going stale; attacks Outside the expected band no_face / not_applicable / error rates Pipeline breakage, new formats Sudden change Latency per pool (p50, p95) and queue age Capacity SLA risk GPU utilization and memory per node Sizing Persistently below 50% (too few workers) or OOM kills Reviewer agreement with flags Real precision Precision falls

Regularly audit a random sample of unflagged media too. Monitoring only flagged items shows precision, never what you miss.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
The service decodes untrusted files with ffmpeg and OpenCV, two large C codebases with a history of decoder vulnerabilities. Treat every upload as hostile:

  • Sandbox the workers. Run as non-root (the Dockerfile does), with a read-only root filesystem, a writable temp directory only, and no network egress (weights are baked in, HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1).
  • Limit resources: CPU and memory limits per container, file-size caps at intake, a duration cap in normalization, and job timeouts.
  • Patch the decoders. Rebuild images regularly to pick up ffmpeg and OpenCV security fixes.
  • Never trust file extensions. Probe the streams.
  • Weights are integrity-checked. forensix.load verifies SHA-256 hashes, and checkpoints load with weights_only=True or safetensors, so a tampered checkpoint can't execute code. Keep the cache read-only at runtime.
  • Protect the gallery and scores. Identity galleries are biometric data, and stored scores reveal which media was flagged. Encrypt them at rest, restrict access, and set retention.

docs.title: Audit and reproducibility
docs.text:
Store with every result: - the input SHA-256 and, for segments, their start and end; - the ForensiX version and git commit (set it in the image, e.g. as an environment variable at build time); - the model name and weights hash (forensix.info(name).weights.sha256), or the checkpoint hash for models you trained; - the normalization parameters; - the decision-config version, the decision, and any reviewer action.

With these, any past decision can be re-derived exactly: same input, same code, same weights, same thresholds. Reprocessing after a model upgrade becomes a query: everything scored with the old weights hash.

docs.title: Launch checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Models chosen per threat (Choosing detectors) and evaluated on your own media (Evaluation).
  • [ ] Thresholds set on real traffic at a chosen false-alarm rate; config versioned.
  • [ ] Inputs normalized: resolution, duration, segmentation for long media.
  • [ ] Image built with baked weights; verified with --network none.
  • [ ] Workers: models loaded once, processes not threads, job timeouts, CPU threads limited.
  • [ ] Pools sized by measurement; autoscaling on queue depth; warm minimums.
  • [ ] Results keyed by content hash, with full provenance.
  • [ ] Human review for consequential decisions; reviewer feedback captured.
  • [ ] Monitoring on score drift, flag rates, error rates, latency; random audits of unflagged media.
  • [ ] Sandboxed decoding, no egress, patched images.
  • [ ] License review done (Licensing), including ‡ training-data terms and stablesyncnet restrictions if used.

docs.title: Fairness reports
docs.text: A detector that flags real people as fake more often when they have darker skin, are older, or are women causes real harm, and buyers and regulators (the EU AI Act, NIST's face-analysis guidance, procurement questionnaires) ask for evidence that it doesn't. A ForensiX fairness report measures false-alarm rates by skin tone, age and gender (and any other attribute you label) for any image, video or identity model, at the threshold the model actually runs at.

docs.title: What it measures
docs.text:
For each model and each attribute (for example gender), the report gives, per group:

Measure Meaning False-alarm rate Share of the group's real items the model flags as fake, with a 95% Wilson interval. The main number Detection rate Share of the group's fake items caught, when the dataset has fakes AUC Per-group ranking quality, when the group has both real and fake items Reliable Whether the group has at least min_group real items (default 30)

and a disparity across the reliable groups: the highest and lowest false-alarm rates, their difference and ratio, and a two-sided Fisher exact test of whether the gap could be chance (significant at p < 0.05). Groups below min_group are still shown, marked ⚠, but left out of the comparison: 1 false alarm in 8 people is not evidence of anything.

The threshold matters. Rates are measured at the model's operating point: its active calibration's threshold ("calibration vN"), else the server's configured threshold ("server config"), else the model default. The report records which was used. Re-run it after you recalibrate.

Provenance models (c2pa, watermarks, metadata) read file evidence, not faces, and are rejected.

docs.title: The dataset
docs.text:
Any ForensiX dataset with demographic columns in its manifest:

file,label,group,skin_tone,age,gender,attr_region
media/p001.jpg,real,p001,4,34,female,south-asia
media/p002.jpg,real,p002,9,61,male,west-africa
media/p002_swap.jpg,fake,p002,9,61,male,west-africa
Column Values Grouped as skin_tone Monk 1-10 or Fitzpatrick I-VI Monk 1-3 / 4-7 / 8-10; Fitzpatrick I-II / III-IV / V-VI age years, or a band such as 20-29 0-17, 18-29, 30-44, 45-59, 60+ (bands are kept as given) gender any label as given, lower-cased attr_<name> any label as given, reported as <name>

Real items drive the false-alarm rates, so a fairness set can be all real. Aim for at least 30, better 100+, real items per group; with 30 the interval on a 5% rate is roughly 1–17%.

docs.title: No skin-tone labels? Estimate them
docs.text:
With estimate_skin_tone on (the default) and no skin_tone column, ForensiX estimates each face's Individual Typology Angle (ITA, from the CIELAB colour of the cheeks and forehead, found with the YuNet face detector) and groups the dataset into terciles: lighter, middle and darker third. Faces that are greyscale, in profile or too small are left out.

Treat this as a proxy, not a measurement. Lighting, white balance and make-up move ITA a lot, so the tercile labels are relative to this dataset, never absolute skin types. Use annotated Monk labels for anything you publish. On FairFace, faces annotated Black fall in the darker third 55% of the time and in the lighter third 12%; that's useful for screening but noisy.

docs.title: A ready audit set: FairFace
docs.text: FairFace (CC BY 4.0) has real face photos annotated with age band, gender and race. scripts/build_fairface_set.py builds a balanced audit set (default 30 per race × gender cell, 420 images) from its validation split; the script's docstring has the download command. Race is FairFace's annotation and is reported as race. It is not skin tone.

docs.title: Running a report
docs.text:
Web manager: open Fairness, pick the dataset and models, and start. The report shows, per model and attribute, each group's false-alarm rate and interval against the overall rate, with disparity verdicts, and downloads as Markdown or JSON.

HTTP:

curl -X POST localhost:8000/v1/fairness -H "X-API-Key: $ADMIN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"dataset": "19065db78962", "models": ["commfor", "univfd"], "estimate_skin_tone": true, "min_group": 30}'
# → 202 {"id": "f6f17dfe2b81", ...}; follow GET /v1/jobs/{id}
curl localhost:8000/v1/fairness/f6f17dfe2b81?format=markdown -H "X-API-Key: $KEY" > fairness.md
Field Default Meaning dataset or datasets One dataset id, or several pooled models Image, video or identity models estimate_skin_tone true Estimate ITA terciles when there's no skin_tone column min_group 30 Real items a group needs to enter the disparity comparison attributes skin_tone, age, gender, race Which attributes to report

GET /v1/fairness lists saved reports. They are kept in the calibration directory with the datasets they came from.

Python:

from forensix.fairness import report, to_markdown

items = [{"label": "real", "attributes": {"gender": "female", "age": "34"}, "scores": {"commfor": 0.12}}, ...]
rep = report(items, {"commfor": {"threshold": 0.5, "threshold_source": "model default"}})
print(to_markdown(rep))

docs.title: Reading a report honestly
docs.text:
• A significant disparity is a finding: say which groups, by how much, at which threshold. Not significant means the data can't show a gap, not that there is none. Check how wide the intervals are.
  • False alarms depend on the images as much as the people: camera, compression and lighting differ between sources, so collect every group from comparable sources.
  • Recalibrating moves the threshold for everyone. Lowering one group's false alarms with a per-group threshold is a policy decision with legal implications; ForensiX doesn't do it for you.

Next step: take the calibrated, audited setup to production with Docker, Kubernetes and cloud.

docs.title: Deploying on Google Cloud
docs.text:
This guide is for engineers putting the ForensiX server (API and web manager) on Google Cloud. Pick a target, then deploy it from Cloud Shell, with one command, or with one click in GitHub Actions. The matching teardown removes everything the deploy created.

Target What runs Pick it when cloudrun: Cloud Run, CPU Serverless containers, HTTPS included, scale on requests The simplest service, moderate volume, mostly images and audio cloudrun-gpu: Cloud Run, GPU One NVIDIA L4 per instance Video and audiovisual models without managing anything gke: GKE Autopilot Kubernetes, nodes Google manages and scales You run Kubernetes already, or want the same manifests as on other clouds gke-gpu: GKE Autopilot, GPU Kubernetes, an L4 node per pod, created on demand Kubernetes plus GPUs File What it is deploy/gcp/deploy.sh One command to deploy or tear down any target deploy/kubernetes/overlays/gke, gke-gpu The Kubernetes manifests adapted to GKE Autopilot .github/workflows/deploy-gcp.yml The same, as a one-click GitHub Actions workflow

docs.title: Before you start: the image
docs.text:
Every target runs ghcr.io/anas-rz/forensix:cpu-bundled or :gpu-bundled, which have the default models baked in. Push a version tag (git tag v0.1.0 && git push origin v0.1.0) to publish them, then make the GHCR package public (details).

  • GKE pulls from GHCR directly.
  • Cloud Run only pulls from Artifact Registry (and Docker Hub), so the script creates an Artifact Registry remote repository named ghcr that proxies ghcr.io and caches the image in your region.

To use your own image instead, push it to Artifact Registry and pass --image.

docs.title: Option 1: from Cloud Shell
docs.text:
The button opens Cloud Shell with this repository cloned. gcloud and kubectl are already installed and signed in, so run:

gcloud config set project YOUR_PROJECT
deploy/gcp/deploy.sh cloudrun          # or cloudrun-gpu, gke, gke-gpu

docs.title: Option 2: one command
docs.text:
Needs the gcloud CLI, signed in with a project selected. GKE also needs kubectl and gke-gcloud-auth-plugin, installed with gcloud components install kubectl gke-gcloud-auth-plugin.

deploy/gcp/deploy.sh cloudrun                     # or cloudrun-gpu, gke, gke-gpu
deploy/gcp/deploy.sh cloudrun --destroy           # delete everything it created
Option Default Meaning --name forensix Prefix for services, the cluster, the bucket and the keys --project gcloud's current project Project to deploy into --region us-central1 Region. GPU targets need an L4 region, e.g. us-central1, us-east4, europe-west1, europe-west4 or asia-southeast1 --image ghcr.io/anas-rz/forensix:{cpu,gpu}-bundled Your image

Rerunning the deploy updates in place. It prints the URLs and how to read the keys, which are generated once in Secret Manager and never printed:

gcloud secrets versions access latest --secret forensix-api-key      # and forensix-admin-key
curl -H "X-API-Key: $KEY" -F file=@photo.jpg https://<inference URL>/v1/detect

docs.title: Option 3: one click in GitHub Actions
docs.text:
Actions → deploy-gcp → Run workflow: pick the target, deploy or destroy, the name and the region. The URLs and key commands appear in the run summary.

One-time setup: GitHub signs in with Workload Identity Federation, so no service account keys are stored.

PROJECT=your-project; NUMBER=$(gcloud projects describe $PROJECT --format 'value(projectNumber)')
gcloud iam workload-identity-pools create github --project $PROJECT --location global
gcloud iam workload-identity-pools providers create-oidc github --project $PROJECT --location global \
  --workload-identity-pool github --issuer-uri https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com \
  --attribute-mapping "google.subject=assertion.sub,attribute.repository=assertion.repository" \
  --attribute-condition "assertion.repository == 'anas-rz/ForensiX'"
gcloud iam service-accounts create forensix-deploy --project $PROJECT
gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding $PROJECT --role roles/owner \
  --member serviceAccount:forensix-deploy@$PROJECT.iam.gserviceaccount.com
gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding forensix-deploy@$PROJECT.iam.gserviceaccount.com \
  --project $PROJECT --role roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser \
  --member "principalSet://iam.googleapis.com/projects/$NUMBER/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/github/attribute.repository/anas-rz/ForensiX"

A deploy enables APIs and creates service accounts, buckets, secrets, services or clusters, so the account needs broad rights. In a shared project, replace roles/owner with Cloud Run Admin, Kubernetes Engine Admin, Storage Admin, Secret Manager Admin, Artifact Registry Admin, Service Account Admin, Service Account User, Project IAM Admin and Service Usage Admin.

In the repository, create the environment gcp (Settings → Environments; add required reviewers to gate deploys). Then add these repository secrets: - GCP_WORKLOAD_IDENTITY_PROVIDER = projects/NUMBER/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/github/providers/github - GCP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT = forensix-deploy@PROJECT.iam.gserviceaccount.com - GCP_PROJECT_ID

docs.title: What gets deployed
docs.text:
Cloud Run (cloudrun, cloudrun-gpu):

  • <name>-manager serves the web manager, dataset uploads, calibration and fairness jobs. It runs as exactly one instance with always-on CPU, so background jobs keep running between requests, and it's the single writer of shared state.
  • <name>-inference serves /v1/detect. It scales from 1 to 10 instances (1 to 4 on GPU) on concurrent requests and can't write shared state.
  • Two URLs. Each service has its own HTTPS URL on run.app. Open the web manager on the manager URL and send API traffic to the inference URL. (The manager also answers /v1/detect, which the web manager's Test page uses.) To put both behind one domain, add an external Application Load Balancer with serverless network endpoint groups and route the management paths (see the Ingress) to the manager.
  • Shared state: a Cloud Storage bucket, <project>-<name>-data, mounted at /data in both services. An activated calibration applies to the inference service on its next request.
  • Sizing: 4 vCPUs and 16 GiB per instance on CPU; 8 vCPUs, 32 GiB and an L4 on GPU. A startup probe on /ready waits up to 15 minutes for the models to load.
  • Identity and keys: both services run as a dedicated service account, <name>-run, that can read only the two keys and the bucket.

GKE Autopilot (gke, gke-gpu):

  • Cluster: a regional Autopilot cluster. Google provisions nodes for the pods the HPA asks for; gke-gpu pods each get an L4 node.
  • Workloads: the gke or gke-gpu overlay:
  • a Filestore volume (the standard-rwx class, 1 TiB minimum);
  • the GKE Ingress, which creates an external Application Load Balancer;
  • a BackendConfig with a 900-second timeout and health checks on /ready.
  • Keys: generated into Secret Manager (<name>-api-key, <name>-admin-key) and copied into the forensix-keys Kubernetes Secret.

docs.title: HTTPS and a domain
docs.text:
• Cloud Run: HTTPS is on by default on the run.app URLs. For your own domain, use Cloud Run domain mappings or a load balancer.
  • GKE: the Ingress serves plain HTTP on its IP. Point a host at that IP, then add a ManagedCertificate and the networking.gke.io/managed-certificates annotation to your copy of the overlay. Until then, restrict access or don't use real keys over it.

Cloud Run services allow unauthenticated invocation, so anyone can reach them, while ForensiX's own keys protect the API. If an organization policy forbids public services, redeploy with --no-allow-unauthenticated and call them with Google identity tokens.

docs.title: Costs and teardown
docs.text:
• Cloud Run: you pay per instance-second. The manager and one inference instance stay on, and GPU instances are billed while they run.
  • GKE: Autopilot bills pod resources, plus the cluster fee, the load balancer and Filestore. The 1 TiB Filestore minimum is a fixed monthly cost.

--destroy (or the workflow's destroy action) deletes the services or cluster, the bucket or Filestore volume with your datasets and calibrations, and the keys. The ghcr proxy repository is kept, since other deployments may share it. Delete it with gcloud artifacts repositories delete ghcr --location REGION.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause and fix Cloud Run: Image ... not found The GHCR image isn't published or isn't public, so the proxy can't fetch it: see the image Cloud Run GPU: quota error Request Total Nvidia L4 GPU allocation without zonal redundancy quota for Cloud Run in the region GKE GPU pods stay Pending No L4 capacity or quota in the region; kubectl describe pod shows the scale-up event GKE Ingress has no IP, or returns 502 for a while Load balancer provisioning takes about 5–10 minutes after the pods are ready POST /v1/datasets returns 409 You sent it to the inference service; use the manager URL Logs gcloud run services logs tail <name>-manager --region REGION, or kubectl -n forensix logs deploy/forensix-manager

docs.title: What's been verified
docs.text:
• The deploy script passes ShellCheck.
  • The gke and gke-gpu overlay patches apply cleanly to the base manifests.

Deployments to a Google Cloud project haven't been run from this repository yet. Try a non-production project first.

Next step: open the web manager's dashboard, then calibrate on your media.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
In about ten minutes you'll go from a fresh checkout to a running detection service: scoring files in Python, calling the API over HTTP, and working in the web console. Each step links to the page that covers it in depth. When you're ready for production, the same service deploys to AWS, Google Cloud or Azure with one command.

No install: try it in Google Colab

The get-started notebook runs everything on this page on a free Colab GPU, with sample media: detecting images, audio and video, provenance checks, uploading your own files, calibration, evaluation, the web manager inside Colab, and a fairness report.

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
You need Python 3.10 or newer and ffmpeg (Installation has the details and GPU notes).

git clone https://github.com/anas-rz/ForensiX.git
cd ForensiX
pip install -e ".[server]"        # the library, the HTTP server and the provenance checks

Model weights download on first use into ~/.cache/forensix/ and are checked against a SHA-256 hash. To fetch them ahead of time, for example before going offline, run python scripts/download_weights.py.

docs.title: 2. Score a file in Python
docs.text:
From the command line, python -m forensix FILE runs the right detectors and provenance checks for the file's media type. python scripts/fetch_samples.py downloads a small test kit of real and fake media to try it on.

import forensix

forensix.list_models("image")                  # ['clipdet', 'commfor', 'commfor-224', 'rine', ...]

detector = forensix.load("commfor")            # device="cuda" on a GPU
pred = detector.predict("photo.jpg")
pred.fake_prob, pred.label                     # (0.98, 'fake')

Every detector, whether for audio, images, video, lip sync, physics or identity, returns the same Prediction. Choosing detectors explains which detector catches which manipulation, and Interpreting scores explains what a score means.

Provenance checks read the evidence the file itself carries: Content Credentials, generator watermarks and metadata.

report = forensix.provenance.check("photo.jpg")
report["verdict"], report["summary"]           # ('no_decisive_evidence', 'No decisive provenance evidence (most files carry none; ...)')

docs.title: 3. Run the server
docs.text:
python -m forensix.server --preload commfor nes2net-x-itw

The first start downloads the preloaded models. Once it logs Uvicorn running on http://0.0.0.0:8000, the models are in memory and requests pay only for inference:

curl -F file=@photo.jpg http://localhost:8000/v1/detect
curl -F file=@clip.mp4 -F models=dfdet-clip,syncnet http://localhost:8000/v1/detect

Without models, the server picks the defaults for the media type: a detector plus the provenance checks. Before exposing the server, set an API key (--api-key, or api_key and admin_key in a config file). HTTP server covers the endpoints, configuration, batching and security. The interactive OpenAPI docs are at http://localhost:8000/docs.

For a repeatable setup, put the options in a JSON config. A calibration_dir keeps uploaded datasets, calibrations and fairness reports across restarts:

{
  "device": "cuda",
  "preload": ["commfor", "dfdet-clip", "nes2net-x-itw", "syncnet"],
  "calibration_dir": "/data/forensix/calibration",
  "api_key": "change-me",
  "admin_key": "change-me-too"
}

python -m forensix.server --config server.json

docs.title: 4. Use the web manager
docs.text:
Open http://localhost:8000/ui/. It's served by the same process and calls the same API, so anything you do there can be scripted. If you set keys, enter them under Settings first.

Overview is a live dashboard of the instance: requests, verdicts, latency, cache hits and resource use, for all models or one.

Test: drop in an image, video or audio file and pick models, or use the defaults. Each model shows its score against its threshold, and the provenance checks show what the file itself proves.

Models lists every registered detector: whether it's loaded, its license and its calibration. Load or unload models from here, and open one to see its versions and performance.

Calibration: upload a labelled dataset as a ZIP (real/ and fake/ folders, or a manifest.csv) and calibrate models on it. You get calibrated probabilities, a threshold for a target false-alarm rate, and confidence verdicts on every prediction. Calibration explains the dataset format and the full, incremental and refit modes.

Leaderboard: every model on commercially usable benchmarks, with 95% confidence intervals.

Fairness: false-alarm rates by skin tone, age and gender for face and identity models (Fairness reports).

docs.title: 5. Run it in a container
docs.text:
docker compose up -d --build                        # server and web manager on port 8000
kubectl apply -k deploy/kubernetes/overlays/cpu     # or overlays/gpu

Docker, Kubernetes and cloud covers images, GPUs, persistence and autoscaling, and Deployment at scale covers running ForensiX over large volumes of media.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Recipes: working code for common tasks, such as checking a talking-head video across modalities, finding the fake part of a long recording, or choosing a threshold.
  • Evaluating on your data: measure detectors on your own media before you trust them.
  • Licensing and compliance: what the bundled licenses allow.

docs.title: Building these docs
docs.text:
The documentation is a MkDocs site with the Material theme:

pip install -e ".[docs]"
mkdocs serve          # live preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000 (use -a 127.0.0.1:8001 if the ForensiX server is running)
mkdocs build          # static site in site/

Next step: measure the models on your own media with Calibration.

If ForensiX saved you time, a GitHub star helps others find it.

docs.title: Provenance: credentials, watermarks and metadata
docs.text:
Detectors judge how media looks. Provenance checks read what the file carries: signed Content Credentials, invisible watermarks embedded by generators, and the metadata tools leave behind. They're cheap, they explain themselves, and when they find something it's stronger evidence than any classifier score. A signed "AI-generated" declaration or a generator's watermark is close to proof. Their silence, though, means nothing: most files carry no provenance at all, and the evidence is easy to strip.

Check Reads Can conclude License c2pa C2PA Content Credentials (images, video, audio) tampered after signing, AI-generated (declared), verified capture (with a trust list) MIT OR Apache-2.0 (c2pa-python) watermark-image The invisible watermark of Stable Diffusion 1.x, 2.x, SDXL and Stable Video Diffusion (images, video frames) watermark found, naming the generator MIT (vendored dwtDct from invisible-watermark) watermark-audio Meta's AudioSeal watermark (audio, or a video's sound) watermark found, its 16-bit message, and where in time MIT code and weights metadata EXIF, XMP, PNG text chunks; container and stream tags AI-generated (generator traces), edited, re-encoded, camera metadata ForensiX 
pip install -e ".[provenance]"     # c2pa-python and audioseal; the server extra includes them

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
import forensix

report = forensix.provenance.check("upload.jpg")      # every applicable check, combined
report["verdict"], report["label"], report["summary"]
# ('ai_generated', 'fake', 'Content Credentials from OpenAI declare AI-generated content (trainedAlgorithmicMedia).')
for f in report["findings"]:
    print(f["check"], f["severity"], f["message"])

pred = forensix.load("c2pa", trust_anchors="c2pa-trust-list.pem").predict("photo.jpg")
pred.details["verdict"], pred.details["signer"], pred.details["validation_state"]

Each check returns a Prediction with score_type="provenance" and no threshold. The evidence is in details:

Field Meaning verdict What the evidence says (tables below) label "fake", "real" or None. None is the common case: no decisive evidence either way summary One sentence for people findings Each piece of evidence: code, severity (strong decides on its own, moderate needs corroboration, info is context), message, evidence

fake_prob is 1.0 for fake, 0.0 for real and 0.5 otherwise, only so provenance can sit next to detector scores; read details. check() leads with the most decisive verdict across the checks (tampering, then declared AI or a watermark, then verified capture) and keeps every finding.

docs.title: C2PA Content Credentials
docs.text:
Verdict Label When tampered fake The credentials are signed, but the content's hash no longer matches: it changed after signing ai_generated fake The manifest or any ingredient declares AI content (IPTC trainedAlgorithmicMedia, compositeWithTrainedAlgorithmicMedia, compositeSynthetic) verified_capture real A trusted signer declares a capture (camera, film) and no AI appears anywhere in the history ai_enhanced — Declared algorithmic enhancement credentials_untrusted — Intact and signed, but the signer isn't on your trust list trusted_credentials — Trusted, but declares neither AI nor capture invalid_credentials — The credentials don't validate (bad signature, broken manifest) no_credentials — Nothing to verify (most files)

Trust. A signature proves who signed, not that they're honest: anyone can sign "this is a camera photo" with their own certificate. Without a trust list every signer is untrusted, so capture claims are never verified. Pass trust_anchors, a PEM bundle of the root certificates you trust (for example the C2PA conformance trust list, or your own camera fleet's CA):

forensix.load("c2pa", trust_anchors="/etc/forensix/c2pa-trust.pem")

On the server: "options": {"c2pa": {"trust_anchors": "/etc/forensix/c2pa-trust.pem"}}, or the FORENSIX_C2PA_TRUST_ANCHORS environment variable. AI declarations count whoever signed them. Nobody gains by falsely labelling their own media as AI, and they never vouch for authenticity.

C2PA credentials come from some cameras and phones (e.g. recent Leica, Sony, Google Pixel and Samsung Galaxy models), Adobe tools including Firefly, OpenAI's image generation, and other members of the Content Authenticity Initiative. Most social platforms still strip them on upload.

docs.title: Generator watermarks
docs.text:
Images (watermark-image): the Stable Diffusion reference code and Hugging Face diffusers embed a fixed message by default, with invisible-watermark's dwtDct method:

Generator Message Source Stable Diffusion 1.x the bytes StableDiffusionV1 (136 bits) CompVis scripts/txt2img.py Stable Diffusion 2.x the bytes SDV2 (32 bits) Stability scripts/txt2img.py SDXL, Stable Video Diffusion a 48-bit message Stability generative-models; diffusers StableDiffusionXLWatermarker

The decoder is a vectorized version of the vendored reference, equal to it bit for bit, and runs in about 60 ms on a 1024×1024 image. A message counts as found at ≥ 90% matching bits; by chance that's below one in a million. Videos are checked on 8 frames (median).

Measured robustness, on an SDXL-watermarked 1024×1024 image:

After Found? PNG, lossless WebP yes (100% of bits) JPEG quality 90–95 with full-resolution colour (4:4:4) yes JPEG with standard 4:2:0 colour, any quality; JPEG quality ≤ 80 no Resizing to half no

The watermark sits in the colour (U) channel, which ordinary JPEG subsamples. So the check finds files close to the generator's output (PNG downloads, many web UIs), not media that went through a social platform. Many hosted services and forks turn the watermark off.

Audio (watermark-audio): AudioSeal (Roman et al., ICML 2024) marks every sample. The detector gives the share of watermarked audio, a per-second timeline (a watermarked segment spliced into a real recording shows exactly where), and the 16-bit message. Checked here: - Parity: identical outputs to upstream AudioSeal.load_detector. - Detection: watermarked speech 1.0, clean 0.001. - Compression: the watermark survives MP3 at 128 kbit/s.

It's embedded by Meta's audio generation research tools and by anyone who adopts it; most voice cloning services don't use it.

Weights load from a pinned Hugging Face revision with SHA-256 checks. The checkpoint pickles its training config, so it's read with an unpickler that accepts only the specific data classes inside and refuses anything else (tested with a malicious checkpoint).

docs.title: Metadata
docs.text:
Finding Severity Examples Generator parameters strong Automatic1111 parameters chunk (steps, sampler, seed); ComfyUI prompt/workflow; InvokeAI, NovelAI chunks IPTC digital source type declares AI strong XMP Iptc4xmpExt:DigitalSourceType = trainedAlgorithmicMedia A generative tool in a software or encoder field strong EXIF Software: Midjourney v6; an MP4 encoder naming a video generator A statement of origin in a comment strong "Generated with Runway Gen-3", "created by Midjourney" A tool mentioned in free text moderate a description that names a generator in passing Editing software moderate Photoshop, Lightroom, GIMP, CapCut, Premiere EXIF thumbnail doesn't match the image moderate edited after capture without updating the thumbnail Audio and video tracks of different lengths moderate tracks edited or muxed separately (dubbing) Re-encoded by FFmpeg; no creation time; variable frame rate info most downloaded or processed video Camera or phone metadata info supporting, but easy to forge No metadata; a typical generator output size; a TTS-like audio format info weak context only

Verdicts: ai_generated (label fake), edited, re_encoded, capture_metadata, no_metadata, no_findings. Metadata never says real.

docs.title: On the server
docs.text:
The default models run all provenance checks that apply next to the detectors (the server config default_models lists them):

Media Provenance checks by default image c2pa, watermark-image, metadata video c2pa, watermark-image, metadata video with sound c2pa, watermark-audio, metadata audio c2pa, watermark-audio, metadata

They read the file as uploaded, even when the server re-encodes a long or large video for the detectors, because re-encoding would destroy credentials and metadata. Each result carries provenance: {verdict, summary, findings}, and its label is the check's own. On the dashboard, provenance has its own tile and chart; it isn't mixed into the detector outcomes. Provenance checks aren't calibrated, since there's no score to calibrate.

Without the provenance extra, c2pa and watermark-audio report unavailable (with the install command) while everything else runs.

Next step: pair provenance with calibrated detector scores: Calibration.

docs.title: Recipes
docs.text:
Copy-paste solutions to common tasks. Each recipe was run on CPU against the repo's test fixtures or the SDFVD videos, and the outputs shown are real. Swap device="cpu" for device="cuda" on a GPU.

# Recipe Models 1 Scan a folder of images into a CSV image 2 Check a face video video 3 Find which part of a long recording is fake audio 4 Check a talking-head video across modalities video, audio, audiovisual, physics 5 Pick a threshold for a target false-alarm rate any 6 Combine several detectors any 7 Verify that media shows a specific person identity 8 Train a tiny detector for one person specialized 9 Produce a physics forensic report physics 10 Score a large folder of videos in parallel video 11 Benchmark detectors on your own videos video, image

docs.title: 1. Scan a folder of images into a CSV
docs.text:
Image detectors batch on the GPU, so pass lists to predict_batch. Load one model at a time and free it before the next one: three CLIP-sized models at once need several GB.

import csv
from pathlib import Path

import forensix

paths = sorted(p for p in Path("photos").iterdir() if p.suffix.lower() in {".jpg", ".jpeg", ".png", ".webp"})
models = ["commfor", "clipdet", "univfd"]

scores = {}
for name in models:
    detector = forensix.load(name, device="cpu")
    scores[name] = [p.fake_prob for p in detector.predict_batch(paths, batch_size=16)]
    del detector

with open("image_scores.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    w = csv.writer(f)
    w.writerow(["file", *models])
    for i, p in enumerate(paths):
        w.writerow([p.name, *(f"{scores[m][i]:.4f}" for m in models)])

On the three real public-domain photos in tests/data:

file,commfor,clipdet,univfd
face2_public_domain.jpg,0.0123,0.2115,0.0001
face_public_domain.jpg,0.0022,0.1946,0.0000
other_face_public_domain.jpg,0.0001,0.2191,0.0000

Notes. - Image detectors look for whole generated images (GAN, diffusion). They are weak on face swaps inside real photos and video frames (SDFVD benchmark: AUC 0.56–0.75). - Don't resize or re-compress images before scoring. The detectors rely on traces that resampling destroys. - commfor is the strongest choice for modern diffusion images (trained on ~4,800 generators).

docs.title: 2. Check a face video
docs.text:
The face-based CLIP/PE detectors are the strongest video models in ForensiX (SDFVD AUC 0.92–0.96). Each returns a video score and one score per scored face.

import forensix

detector = forensix.load("dfdet-clip", device="cuda")
pred = detector.predict("clip.mp4")

if not pred.segment_fake_probs:
    print("no face found: the 0.5 score means nothing")
else:
    print(pred.fake_prob, pred.label, f"{len(pred.segment_fake_probs)} faces scored")

On SDFVD's face-swapped vs1.mp4: 0.8128 fake 32 faces scored (about 2 minutes on CPU, about 3 s on an L4).

Notes. - gend-pe ranked first on SDFVD (AUC 0.956), but at the default 0.5 threshold it flagged 24% of real videos. dfdet-clip is better balanced at 0.5 (89% of reals and 76% of fakes right). See recipe 5 to set your own threshold. - Every video model returns exactly 0.5 when it finds no face. Always check segment_fake_probs before trusting the score.

docs.title: 3. Find which part of a long recording is fake
docs.text:
Audio detectors cut long clips into windows and return one score per window. This maps the window scores back to timestamps. The windows follow split_windows: consecutive, with the last one aligned to the end of the clip.

import forensix
from forensix.audio.io import load_audio

path = "call_recording.wav"          # any audio format, or a video file (needs ffmpeg)
detector = forensix.load("aasist")
pred = detector.predict(path)

sr, window = detector.sample_rate, detector.window
n = len(load_audio(path, sr))
starts = list(range(0, max(n - window, 0) + 1, window))
if len(pred.segment_fake_probs) > len(starts):
    starts.append(n - window)        # the last window is aligned to the end
for s, p in zip(starts, pred.segment_fake_probs):
    flag = "  <-- suspicious" if p >= detector.threshold else ""
    print(f"{s / sr:6.2f}s - {(s + window) / sr:6.2f}s  fake_prob={p:.3f}{flag}")
print("clip:", pred.fake_prob, pred.label)

On the 10 s real CC0 speech fixture:

  0.00s -   4.04s  fake_prob=0.120
  4.04s -   8.07s  fake_prob=0.050
  5.96s -  10.00s  fake_prob=0.002
clip: 0.05715656653046608 real

Notes. - For real-world, compressed audio (phone calls, social media), use nes2net-x-itw or xlsr-aasist-df rather than aasist; they were built for out-of-domain audio. They need a GPU for reasonable speed (about 1.3 s per 4 s window on CPU). - nes2net-x-itw scores whole utterances up to 30 s, so its segments are 30 s chunks, not 4 s windows.

docs.title: 4. Check a talking-head video across modalities
docs.text:
Different attacks leave different evidence. A face swap shows up in the face models; a cloned voice in the audio models; a dubbed or lip-synced video in the sync models; physics checks look for violations of how real faces and voices behave. Run one model per question and read the answers side by side. Don't average them (recipe 6 explains why).

import forensix

video = "interview.mp4"
checks = {
    "face (gend-pe)": forensix.load("gend-pe", device="cuda"),
    "voice (nes2net-x-itw)": forensix.load("nes2net-x-itw", device="cuda"),   # reads the video's audio track
    "lip sync (syncnet)": forensix.load("syncnet", device="cuda"),
}
preds = {}
for question, detector in checks.items():
    try:
        p = preds[question] = detector.predict(video)
    except ValueError as e:              # e.g. no audio track, no face
        print(f"{question:24} not applicable: {e}")
        continue
    if p.score_type == "anomaly":
        print(f"{question:24} anomaly score {p.fake_prob:.3f} (no default threshold)")
    else:
        print(f"{question:24} {p.fake_prob:.3f} -> {p.label}")

if "lip sync (syncnet)" in preds:
    sync = preds["lip sync (syncnet)"]
    print("AV offset", sync.details["offset_frames"], "frames, confidence", sync.details["confidence"])

SyncNet's confidence is about 10 on a real, in-sync talking head (upstream's example clip). On an SDFVD clip with unrelated CC0 speech dubbed over it, it measured 0.54, with the best offset pinned at the edge of the search range (15 frames). That's what a mismatched voice looks like.

Notes. - The audiovisual models load the whole video into memory at full resolution. Downscale to 720p and trim to about a minute before scoring long videos (Deployment). - Face swaps keep the original, in-sync mouth, so lip-sync models pass them. Lip-sync generators keep the face, so face models may pass them. That's why you need both.

docs.title: 5. Pick a threshold for a target false-alarm rate
docs.text:
Default thresholds are rarely right for your data. If you have scores for real media like the media you'll check, set the threshold so that only a chosen share of real media is flagged:

import numpy as np

def threshold_at_fpr(real_scores, target_fpr):
    """Smallest threshold that flags at most target_fpr of the real scores."""
    return float(np.quantile(real_scores, 1 - target_fpr, method="higher")) + 1e-9

Applied to the SDFVD per-video scores in results/sdfvd_scores.csv, with a 5% target:

import csv
rows = list(csv.DictReader(open("results/sdfvd_scores.csv")))
is_fake = np.array([r["label"] == "fake" for r in rows])
for model in ["dfdet-clip", "rine"]:
    s = np.array([float(r[model]) for r in rows])
    t = threshold_at_fpr(s[~is_fake], 0.05)
    print(model, round(t, 4), "FPR", np.mean(s[~is_fake] >= t).round(3), "TPR", np.mean(s[is_fake] >= t).round(3))

dfdet-clip 0.6307 FPR 0.038 TPR 0.604
rine 0.0063 FPR 0.038 TPR 0.396

rine needs a threshold of 0.0063, not 0.5: its default threshold called every SDFVD video real.

Notes. - Fit the threshold on one set of real media and check it on another. Thresholds fitted and measured on the same data look better than they are. - With 53 real videos, as here, the measured false-alarm rate is only accurate to about ±5 points. For a 1% target you need thousands of real samples. - Anomaly scores (avad, syncnet, physdf) work the same way: they have no default threshold, so this recipe is how you get one.

docs.title: 6. Combine several detectors
docs.text:
Scores from different models live on different scales, so never average raw fake_probs. Normalize each model against its own real-media distribution first, then combine. This version converts each score to a z-score relative to real media, using 5-fold cross-validation so the normalization never sees the media it scores:

import numpy as np

def logit(p):
    p = np.clip(p, 1e-6, 1 - 1e-6)
    return np.log(p / (1 - p))

def fuse(scores, is_fake, n_folds=5, seed=0):
    """scores: (n_media, n_models) fake_probs. Returns one fused score per media item."""
    folds = np.random.default_rng(seed).permutation(len(scores)) % n_folds
    x, fused = logit(scores), np.zeros(len(scores))
    for k in range(n_folds):
        train, test = folds != k, folds == k
        real = x[train & ~is_fake]
        fused[test] = ((x[test] - real.mean(0)) / real.std(0)).mean(1)
    return fused

On SDFVD, fusing gend-pe, gend and dfdet-clip gave AUC 0.942, below gend-pe alone (0.956). The three models share a CLIP-style backbone and training set, so they make the same mistakes, and averaging dilutes the best one.

Notes. - Fusion helps when models catch different things, e.g. a face model plus a voice model plus a sync model on talking heads. It rarely helps among near-identical models. - Measure the fused score on held-out data, exactly as you would a single model. - For models that answer different questions (recipe 4), an OR over per-model thresholds ("flag if any check fires") is easier to explain than a fused number. Set each threshold with recipe 5 so the combined false-alarm rate stays where you want it.

docs.title: 7. Verify that media shows a specific person
docs.text:
id-face enrolls people from photos or videos and checks new media against them. It catches impersonation and poor face swaps. A good face swap of the person is built to look like them and passes, so pair it with a face-manipulation model (recipe 2).

import forensix

det = forensix.load("id-face")
det.enroll("armstrong", ["tests/data/face_public_domain.jpg"])       # photos and/or videos
det.enroll("aldrin", ["tests/data/other_face_public_domain.jpg"])
det.save_gallery("people.npz")                                        # det.load_gallery("people.npz") later

pred = det.predict("tests/data/face2_public_domain.jpg", identity="armstrong")
print(pred.label, pred.fake_prob, pred.details["similarity"], pred.details["other_enrolled_similarity"])
print(det.identify("tests/data/face2_public_domain.jpg"))

real 0.3878 0.6122 {'aldrin': 0.0583}
[('armstrong', 0.6121812462806702), ('aldrin', 0.058341484516859055)]

The Aldrin photo checked against Armstrong comes back fake. For videos, details["frame_similarity"] and details["frame_time_s"] show when the face stops being the person.

More in Identity and person models.

docs.title: 8. Train a tiny detector for one person
docs.text:
A person-detector is a ~23k-parameter model trained on CPU in seconds from one person's real media. Negatives are optional: without them, manipulated and impostor-like samples are synthesized.

from forensix.specialized import PersonDetector, train_person_model

det = train_person_model(
    "armstrong",
    real_media=["tests/data/face_public_domain.jpg"],
    negative_media=["tests/data/other_face_public_domain.jpg"],    # optional
    modality="image",                                              # image, audio, video, audiovisual or auto
)
det.save("armstrong.safetensors")

det = PersonDetector.load("armstrong.safetensors")    # or forensix.load("person-detector", weights_path=...)
print(det)
for f in ["face2_public_domain.jpg", "other_face_public_domain.jpg"]:
    p = det.predict(f"tests/data/{f}")
    print(f, p.label, p.fake_prob)

PersonDetector(person='armstrong', modality='image', params=23,301, threshold=0.500)
face2_public_domain.jpg real 0.1861
other_face_public_domain.jpg fake 0.9999

The same from the command line:

python scripts/train_person_model.py --person armstrong --real tests/data/face_public_domain.jpg \
    --fake tests/data/other_face_public_domain.jpg --modality image --out armstrong.safetensors
python scripts/train_person_model.py --load armstrong.safetensors --test tests/data/face2_public_domain.jpg

Notes. One training photo is a demo, not a deployment. Use dozens of varied real samples, and hold some back to measure false alarms (Identity guide).

docs.title: 9. Produce a physics forensic report
docs.text:
physdf runs every physics check and writes a report from the measured evidence. The single-constraint detectors (phys-voice, phys-room, phys-bloodflow, phys-motion, phys-lighting) expose the same evidence per constraint.

import forensix

pred = forensix.load("phys-voice").predict("tests/data/speech_cc0.flac")
print(pred.fake_prob, pred.score_type)                          # 0.0 anomaly
print(pred.details["constraints"]["f0_jump_rate_per_s"])
# {'expected_range_start': 2.0, 'worse': 'higher', 'prior': 'provisional', 'measured': 0.2584, 'violation': 0.0}

det = forensix.load("physdf")                                   # add weights_path= once you've trained the graph prior
pred = det.predict("interview.mp4")                             # a video (uses its sound), or an audio file
print(pred.details["report"]["markdown"])
pred.details["localization"]                                    # where and when constraints were violated

Read this before relying on physics scores. Until learned priors are fitted on real media, the expected ranges are provisional and hand-set. In testing, a real SDFVD clip that was looped three times and dubbed with unrelated speech scored 1.00 (report confidence: low), driven by blood-flow ranges. The looping itself may break the pulse signal, but provisional video ranges are known to fire on real video. Treat physics output as leads for a human reviewer until you have run scripts/calibrate_physics.py on real media like yours (Physics guide).

docs.title: 10. Score a large folder of videos in parallel
docs.text:
Video detectors spend much of their time decoding and finding faces on the CPU, so one process leaves a GPU idle. Run several worker processes, each with its own copy of the model:

import csv
import multiprocessing as mp
import sys
from pathlib import Path

MODEL, DEVICE, WORKERS = "dfdet-clip", "cuda", 3

_detector = None


def init_worker():
    global _detector
    import torch
    torch.set_num_threads(2)          # leave CPU cores for the other workers
    import forensix
    _detector = forensix.load(MODEL, device=DEVICE)


def score(path):
    try:
        pred = _detector.predict(path)
        return str(path), pred.fake_prob, len(pred.segment_fake_probs), ""
    except Exception as e:            # keep going on corrupt files; record why
        return str(path), None, 0, repr(e)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    folder, out = Path(sys.argv[1]), sys.argv[2]
    videos = sorted(p for p in folder.rglob("*") if p.suffix.lower() in {".mp4", ".mov", ".avi", ".mkv", ".webm"})
    ctx = mp.get_context("spawn")     # required for CUDA in child processes
    with ctx.Pool(WORKERS, initializer=init_worker) as pool, open(out, "w", newline="") as f:
        w = csv.writer(f)
        w.writerow(["file", "fake_prob", "n_faces", "error"])
        for row in pool.imap_unordered(score, videos):
            w.writerow(row)

Tested with dfdc-wm, 2 CPU workers, on 4 SDFVD videos.

Notes. - Each worker holds a full copy of the model in GPU memory, so size WORKERS by GPU memory. The SDFVD benchmark ran 2–4 processes on one 24 GB L4. - For a service rather than a one-off batch, see Deployment at scale.

docs.title: 11. Benchmark detectors on your own videos
docs.text:
Put real videos in one folder and fake ones in another, then:

python scripts/eval_video_folder.py --device cuda \
    --real my_data/real --fake my_data/fake --dataset my-data \
    --models gend-pe gend dfdet-clip dfdc-selim dfdc-wm commfor \
    --out results/my_data.json --scores-out results/my_data_scores.csv

It reports AUC, AP, EER and accuracy at each model's default threshold, saves after every model, and skips finished models when rerun. Image detectors score 8 evenly spaced frames per video (--frames). See Evaluating on your data for how to build a test set that measures what you think it measures.

docs.title: HTTP server
docs.text:
forensix.server serves every ForensiX detector over HTTP: images, video, audio, lip sync, physics and identity, with any combination of models per request. Models stay in memory between requests, so after the first load (or a preload at startup) a request pays only for inference.

This page is for developers who call the API and for operators who run it. For running it at scale behind a queue, see Deployment at scale.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
pip install -e ".[server]"
python -m forensix.server --device cuda --preload dfdet-clip commfor nes2net-x-itw syncnet --api-key "$KEY"

curl -H "X-API-Key: $KEY" -F file=@photo.jpg http://localhost:8000/v1/detect

{
  "id": "364cdd572d63440187b5cd489f40c7cf",
  "filename": "photo.jpg",
  "sha256": "d91631d7923a2b224406e0dc7496f97bb699399d16c9a80adde2b3b9c2ca06ef",
  "media": {"kind": "image", "has_audio": false, "duration_s": null, "bounded": null},
  "results": {
    "commfor": {
      "status": "ok", "family": "image", "score": 0.0022, "score_type": "probability",
      "threshold": 0.5, "label": "real", "n_segments": 0, "cached": false, "seconds": 0.183
    }
  },
  "seconds": 0.197
}

Interactive API docs (OpenAPI) are at http://localhost:8000/docs, and the web manager (test, load, calibrate and monitor models) at http://localhost:8000/ui/.

docs.title: Endpoints
docs.text: Method and path Auth Purpose GET /health none Liveness: the process is up GET /ready none Readiness: preloaded models are in memory (503 while loading) POST /v1/detect user Score one file POST /v1/detect/batch user Score several files concurrently GET /v1/models[?family=video] user Every registered model: family, license, loaded, available, defaults GET /v1/models/{name} user One model POST /v1/models/{name}/load admin Load and warm up a model now DELETE /v1/models/{name} admin Unload a model GET /v1/identities?model=id-face user Enrolled people POST /v1/identities/{identity}?model=id-face admin Enroll a person from photos, videos or (for id-voice) recordings (files) DELETE /v1/identities/{identity}?model=id-face admin Remove a person GET /v1/stats user Per-model load time, calls, errors, cache hits, latency, batch size GET /v1/server user Server settings without secrets: version, device, limits, defaults, persistence GET /v1/benchmarks[?model=name] user Benchmark results from benchmarks_dir GET /ui/ none The web manager (static page; its API calls use your keys) GET /v1/telemetry?window=3600[&model=name] user Recent predictions and resource use of this instance, bucketed for the dashboard (in memory, since start) GET /v1/leaderboard none (public_leaderboard) The leaderboard: every model on commercially usable benchmarks, with intervals GET /metrics none Prometheus metrics: aggregate counters only (Observability) POST /v1/datasets admin Upload a labelled dataset (ZIP) for calibration (Calibration) GET /v1/datasets, GET /v1/datasets/{id} user Uploaded datasets and their validation summary DELETE /v1/datasets/{id} admin Delete a dataset POST /v1/calibrations admin Start a job that calibrates models on a dataset POST /v1/calibrations/check admin Start a job that checks active calibrations against new data (drift) GET /v1/jobs, GET /v1/jobs/{id} user Job status, progress and reports GET /v1/calibrations, GET /v1/calibrations/{model} user Calibration versions per model and the one in use GET /v1/calibrations/{model}/versions/{n} user A fitted table and its report PUT /v1/calibrations/{model}/active admin Switch, roll back or turn off a model's calibration POST /v1/fairness admin Start a fairness report: false-alarm rates by skin tone, age and gender on a dataset GET /v1/fairness, GET /v1/fairness/{id}[?format=markdown] user Saved fairness reports

docs.title: POST /v1/detect
docs.text:
Multipart form:

Field Default Meaning file required An image, video or audio file. The type is detected from the content, not the extension. models by media type Comma-separated model names, e.g. gend-pe,syncnet. identity none The enrolled person to check against, for identity models (id-face and id-motion on faces, id-voice on speech). details false Include each model's evidence (Prediction.details): sync offsets, physics constraints, reports, similarities. segments false Include per-segment scores: audio windows, faces, frames.

Without models, the server runs the defaults for the media type:

Media Default models image commfor, c2pa, watermark-image, metadata video without sound dfdet-clip, c2pa, watermark-image, metadata video with sound dfdet-clip, nes2net-x-itw, syncnet, c2pa, watermark-audio, metadata audio nes2net-x-itw, c2pa, watermark-audio, metadata

The provenance checks (c2pa, watermark-*, metadata) read the file as uploaded and return provenance: {verdict, summary, findings}. See Provenance.

Change them with default_models in the config.

docs.title: Per-model results
docs.text:
Every requested model gets an entry in results, with a status:

status Meaning Other fields ok Scored score, score_type, threshold, label, n_segments, cached, seconds, calibration (version in use or null), confidence (when calibrated), optional segments and details no_face A video model found no face. Its score is the meaningless 0.5, and label is null as ok not_applicable The model can't score this media (an image model on audio), or an identity model got no identity reason unavailable The model needs weights you train (avcons, avid, id-motion, person-detector) and none are configured reason error The model failed on this file (undecodable stream, no face track for AV models, ...) error

One model failing never fails the request. Request-level errors: 401 wrong or missing key, 404 unknown model name, 400 empty file, 413 file too large, 415 not an image, video or audio file.

Reading scores. score is the model's fake_prob: higher means more likely fake. Raw scores are not comparable across models. threshold is the configured override or the model's default, and label applies it. With a calibration in use, score is a calibrated probability, threshold the calibration's (with a false-alarm guarantee), and confidence gives the verdict and p-values (Calibration). Anomaly-type models (syncnet, avad, physics) have threshold: null and label: null until you configure a threshold for them. See Interpreting scores; defaults are often wrong for a new domain.

docs.title: Batch
docs.text:
curl -H "X-API-Key: $KEY" -F files=@a.jpg -F files=@b.jpg -F files=@c.jpg \
     -F models=commfor http://localhost:8000/v1/detect/batch

Returns {"results": [<one /v1/detect response per file>]}. A file that fails as a whole (unsupported type, too large) gets {"filename", "error", "status_code"} in its place. The files run concurrently, so image and audio models score them in shared batches.

docs.title: Identities
docs.text:
# enroll (admin key): photos and/or videos
curl -H "X-API-Key: $ADMIN" -F files=@alice1.jpg -F files=@alice_interview.mp4 \
     http://localhost:8000/v1/identities/alice
# check media against alice, together with a face-manipulation model
curl -H "X-API-Key: $KEY" -F file=@new.mp4 -F identity=alice -F models=id-face,dfdet-clip \
     http://localhost:8000/v1/detect

Galleries persist to gallery_dir (one .npz per identity model) and are reloaded at startup. Without gallery_dir, they live in memory only. Galleries hold face embeddings, which are biometric data: protect the directory accordingly (Licensing).

docs.title: Python client
docs.text:
import requests

API, KEY = "http://localhost:8000", "..."

def detect(path, models=None, **form):
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        r = requests.post(f"{API}/v1/detect", headers={"X-API-Key": KEY}, files={"file": f},
                          data={"models": ",".join(models) if models else None, **form},
                          timeout=600)   # video on many models can take minutes on CPU
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()

result = detect("interview.mp4", models=["gend-pe", "syncnet"], details="true")
for name, res in result["results"].items():
    print(name, res["status"], res.get("score"), res.get("label"))

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Settings are layered: defaults, then a JSON file (--config or FORENSIX_SERVER_CONFIG), then FORENSIX_SERVER_<FIELD> environment variables, then command-line flags. PORT and HOST set the bind address, LOG_FORMAT=json switches to JSON log lines, and GRACEFUL_TIMEOUT sets the seconds in-flight requests get on shutdown.

Field Default Meaning device "cpu" cpu, cuda or cuda:N preload [] Models loaded and warmed up at startup; /ready turns 200 when they're in memory warmup true Run one synthetic prediction after loading image and audio models max_loaded 8 Models in memory at once; the least recently used one is unloaded beyond this weights {} Checkpoints for models you trained: {"avcons": "/models/avcons.safetensors"} thresholds {} Decision thresholds replacing model defaults: {"dfdet-clip": 0.71, "syncnet": -2.0} calibrations {} Fixed calibration tables per model: {"syncnet": "/cal/syncnet.json"}. A version fitted and activated through the API takes precedence (Calibration) options {} Model options passed to forensix.load: {"aasist": {"clip_score": "first"}} fusions {} Fusion tables (forensix.fusion) served as models under these names: {"av-fusion": "/f/av.json"}. A fusion applies only to media all its members can score default_models see above Models per media type: keys image, video, video+audio, audio max_batch 16 Largest dynamic batch for image and audio models (1 disables batching) batch_wait_ms 5 How long a request waits for others to join its batch result_cache_size 10000 Cached results per (file hash, model); 0 disables max_upload_mb 500 Larger uploads get 413 max_video_seconds 60 Longer videos are trimmed to this before scoring max_video_height 720 Taller videos are downscaled to this before scoring gallery_dir none Where identity galleries are saved calibration_dir none (temporary) Where uploaded datasets, fitted calibration versions and job records are kept. Set it, or they're lost on restart max_dataset_mb 20000 Largest dataset ZIP, and largest size once extracted api_key none Required for user endpoints when set (X-API-Key header or Authorization: Bearer) admin_key none Required for load/unload and enrollment when set; falls back to api_key tmp_dir system temp Where uploads are written while being scored benchmarks_dir the repo's results/ Benchmark result JSONs shown in the UI; "" disables ui true Serve the web manager at /ui/ admin_endpoints true Serve endpoints that change shared state (datasets, calibrations, identities). Set false on scaled-out inference replicas; they still pick up calibrations and galleries from the shared directories (Kubernetes) metrics true Prometheus metrics at /metrics public_leaderboard true Serve /v1/leaderboard without an API key (it's published benchmark data)

Example server.json:

{
  "device": "cuda",
  "preload": ["dfdet-clip", "commfor", "nes2net-x-itw", "syncnet", "id-face"],
  "thresholds": {"dfdet-clip": 0.71, "nes2net-x-itw": 0.83, "syncnet": -2.0},
  "weights": {"avcons": "/models/avcons.safetensors"},
  "gallery_dir": "/data/galleries",
  "max_loaded": 6
}

FORENSIX_SERVER_API_KEY=... FORENSIX_SERVER_PRELOAD=commfor,dfdet-clip python -m forensix.server --config server.json

Lists in environment variables can be comma-separated or JSON; dicts are JSON.

docs.title: Where time goes
docs.text:
Measured on CPU (this repo's dev machine):

Step Cost What the server does about it import forensix and model libraries (transformers) 3–9 s, once per process Paid at startup, before /ready Verifying weight hashes 4.5 s per 1.6 GB file, every load Verified files get a stamp (hash, size, mtime), so unchanged files aren't rehashed: dfdet-clip + clipdet weights went from 7.0 s to 0.0 s on reload Building the model 0.1–10 s Done once; models stay loaded (preload, max_loaded) First inference (CUDA kernels, lazy imports) varies warmup runs one synthetic prediction for image and audio models Inference commfor image 0.18 s; aasist 10 s clip 1.2 s; dfdc-wm 8 s video ~50 s; syncnet ~80 s (CPU) GPU, batching, parallel models Same file again 1 ms Result cache keyed by file hash and model

Video and audiovisual models are slow on CPU. Use a GPU for them; see Choosing detectors for measured GPU times.

docs.title: Concurrency model
docs.text:
• One process per device. Models load once and requests share them through threads, so memory isn't duplicated. Don't run uvicorn --workers N: each worker would load every model again. To use several GPUs, run one server per GPU (CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0, =1, ...) behind a load balancer.
  • Per-model locks. Detectors aren't designed for concurrent calls, so each model scores one request (or one batch) at a time. Different models run in parallel. A video-with-sound request runs its video, audio and sync models concurrently.
  • Dynamic batching. Concurrent requests to the same image or audio model are grouped into one forward pass (up to max_batch, waiting at most batch_wait_ms). With 16 images sent at once on CPU, a batch took 3.1 s vs 3.9 s one by one; the gain is larger on GPU. /v1/stats shows mean_batch_size.
  • Bounded inputs. Videos over max_video_seconds or max_video_height are re-encoded first, because audiovisual models hold every frame in memory. media.bounded reports it.

docs.title: Tuning
docs.text:
• Preload the models you serve, and set max_loaded to fit them all in GPU memory.
  • Set OMP_NUM_THREADS to the CPU cores you want the server to use.
  • Raise batch_wait_ms (e.g. 20) when throughput matters more than single-request latency.
  • Put frequently re-uploaded content behind the result cache, or a shared cache keyed by sha256.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• Keys. Set api_key, and a separate admin_key for loading models and changing galleries. Terminate TLS at a reverse proxy (nginx, a cloud load balancer); the server speaks plain HTTP.
  • Untrusted media. Uploads are decoded by ffmpeg, OpenCV and PIL. Run the server as a non-root user, in a container with no network egress (bake weights into the image), with memory limits, and keep images patched (Deployment: Security).
  • Limits. max_upload_mb, max_video_seconds and max_video_height bound the work per request. Put a request timeout and rate limit in the proxy.
  • Integrity. Weights are hash-verified (stamps are invalidated when a file's size or mtime changes; set FORENSIX_VERIFY_HASH=always to rehash on every load), and checkpoints load without unpickling code.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Requests are synchronous. A long video on several heavy models can take minutes on CPU. Set client timeouts accordingly. For sustained heavy traffic, put a queue in front of workers (Deployment at scale).
  • No per-model timeout. A decoder that hangs on a malformed file holds a thread. Use the proxy's request timeout, and restart the process if /health stops answering.
  • Long media is trimmed to max_video_seconds. Score long recordings in segments on the client side if the whole file matters.
  • Video models' "no face" score. A 0.5 with no faces is reported as no_face, not as a result.

Next step: run it on your infrastructure or cloud: Docker, Kubernetes and cloud.

docs.title: Web manager
docs.text:
The ForensiX server includes a web manager. Use it to test files, load and unload models, calibrate them on your data, and watch how models perform. Open it at http://<server>:8000/ui/; the server root redirects there.

pip install -e ".[server]"
python -m forensix.server --config server.json      # then open http://localhost:8000/ui/

It's a static page served by the server (forensix/server/static/). It has no build step and loads nothing from the internet, so it also works on air-gapped deployments. Everything it shows comes from the HTTP API, so anything you do in the UI can be scripted.

docs.title: Pages
docs.text: Page What you can do Leaderboard Every model on commercially usable benchmarks (below): AUC with 95% intervals as a forest plot, EER, false-alarm and detection rates at a fixed threshold, speed; run details, caveats and a copyable reproduce command; pending benchmarks; a throughput table Overview A live dashboard of this server (below): requests, outcomes, latency, cache and resource use over the last 15 minutes to 24 hours, for all models or one; loaded models and recent jobs. Refreshes every 5 seconds Models Every registered detector, with search and filters by family and loaded state: whether it's loaded, needs trained weights, or has a calibration in use, and which media types it's a default for. Load or unload it Model (click a model) Description, license and paper; runtime statistics; every calibration version (mode, what it was built on, datasets, counts, AUC) with activate, roll back and turn off; the performance of the selected version; benchmark results Test Drop an image, video or audio file, pick models (or use the server's defaults for the media type), optionally an identity, then score it. Each model shows its score on a meter with the threshold, the decision, the confidence verdict when calibrated, per-segment scores, and optionally the full evidence Calibration Upload labelled datasets (with progress) and see their validation; start full, incremental or refit calibrations; start drift checks; follow jobs live, with progress and per-model reports Fairness Start a fairness report on a dataset with demographic columns; per model and attribute, each group's false-alarm rate with its interval against the overall rate, disparity verdicts and warnings; download as Markdown or JSON Settings API and admin keys (kept in this browser only), theme (system, light, dark), and the server's configuration

docs.title: The overview dashboard
docs.text:
Filters sit in one row at the top and apply to everything below them: a time range (15 min, 1 hour, 6 hours, 24 hours) and a model (all, or one). They're remembered in the browser, and a link can carry them, e.g. /ui/#/overview?window=900&model=dfdc-wm.

Panel Shows Status strip Ready, device, uptime, models in memory, calibrated models, version Tiles Requests, flagged fake (share of decided), uncertain, error rate, latency p50 (with p95), cache hit rate; most with a trend sparkline Requests over time Stacked columns per time bucket, by outcome: real, fake, uncertain / no decision, error Latency p50 and p95 per bucket, for requests computed by a model (cache hits excluded). Pick a model for its own latency; "all models" mixes fast and slow ones Outcomes by model Each model's share of real, fake, uncertain and error Requests by model, Media types Volume per model and per media type (hidden when one model is selected) Score distribution With one model selected: its live scores (calibrated probabilities when calibrated) and its threshold Provenance evidence Verdicts of the provenance checks (C2PA, watermarks, metadata), with a tile counting files that carry AI evidence. Kept apart from the detector outcomes Memory, CPU, GPU memory Resident memory, CPU (100% = one core) and, on GPU servers, allocated and reserved GPU memory, sampled every 10 s Models in memory, Recent jobs As before, with unload buttons

Outcomes come from the calibrated verdict when a model is calibrated, otherwise from its label at the threshold. Uncertain / no decision covers uncertain and out-of-distribution verdicts, anomaly scores without a threshold, and videos without a face.

Data comes from GET /v1/telemetry?window=…&model=…. It's held in memory: the last 50,000 model runs and 24 hours of resource samples. It starts empty when the server starts, and covers this one instance. For a fleet, or for history beyond a restart, use the Prometheus metrics at /metrics.

Every chart has a tooltip on hover, and the main ones have a Table view.

docs.title: The leaderboard
docs.text:
One tab per benchmark, plus Speed. Links can open a tab: /ui/#/leaderboard?b=asvspoof2019-la.

  • Forest plot: each model's AUC (dot) and 95% interval (line). The shaded band is the leader's interval: a model whose line reaches into it is tied with the leader, because the data can't separate them. The line at 0.5 is chance. Benchmarks without saved per-item scores show EER instead (lower is better).
  • Table: rank, AUC [95% CI], EER, false alarms (real media flagged) and detections (fakes caught) at the fixed threshold with their intervals, seconds per item, and "vs #1". Footnotes flag corrected values and timings measured on a shared GPU.
  • Run details: dataset, license, archive hash, hardware, date, commit and result files, then caveats and the exact command to reproduce.
  • Not run yet / not included: benchmarks waiting to be run (with their commands), and benchmarks left out because of their license.

The same data is in LEADERBOARD.md and at GET /v1/leaderboard (Evaluation: the leaderboard).

docs.title: Reading model performance
docs.text:
A model's page shows the performance of a calibration version on its own calibration data, measured out of fold (each item scored by a calibration fitted without it):

  • AUC: how well the model separates real from fake on your data. Calibration doesn't change it; a low AUC means you need a different model.
  • False alarms: the share of real items flagged at the conformal threshold. It should be close to the target alpha.
  • Fakes caught: the detection rate at that threshold.
  • Calibration error (ECE): raw → calibrated. Lower means the probabilities can be taken at face value.
  • Certain verdicts: how often the verdict is fake or real rather than uncertain.
  • Score distribution: raw scores of real and fake calibration items, with the decision threshold. Overlap is where the model can't tell them apart. Table view shows the counts.
  • Out-of-fold decisions: balanced accuracy, false alarms, detection rate, ECE and Brier score for three rules: the model's default threshold, calibrated probability ≥ 0.5, and the conformal threshold.

Benchmarks lists results found in the server's benchmarks_dir: any JSON with a models dictionary of metrics, as written by scripts/eval_*.py. By default that's the repo's results/ folder, so the SDFVD and ASVspoof results appear on each model's page.

docs.title: Access
docs.text:
The page itself has no secrets, so it loads without a key. Every call it makes uses the keys you enter in Settings: the API key for reading and testing, and the admin key for loading models, uploading datasets and changing calibrations. They're kept in the browser's localStorage and sent as the X-API-Key header. Use HTTPS through a reverse proxy when the server isn't on localhost. Turn the UI off with "ui": false in the server config.

Next step: upload a labelled dataset and calibrate a model on your media.

docs.title: Evaluating a deepfake detector: a buyer's checklist
docs.text:
This checklist is for teams choosing a deepfake detection product or vendor: trust and safety, fraud, identity verification, newsrooms, compliance and procurement. It's vendor-neutral. Ask every vendor these questions, including us, and keep the answers for your risk file.

Each question says what a good answer looks like. The last column says where ForensiX answers it, so you can check our answers the same way.

docs.title: Licensing and data
docs.text: Ask A good answer ForensiX Can we use the models commercially? Under which licenses? A license per model and per weight file, in writing. "Proprietary" alone isn't an answer for open models underneath Models, Licensing What were the models trained on, and was that data licensed for this use? Named datasets and their terms. Many public deepfake datasets are research-only Listed per model; models without commercially usable weights are left out Do you keep or train on our media? No, or only with a contract that says so. Self-hosting removes the question Self-hosted: media stays on your infrastructure

docs.title: Accuracy you can verify
docs.text: Ask A good answer ForensiX How accurate is it on media like ours? An evaluation on your data, or a way to run one yourself. Vendor benchmarks alone don't transfer Evaluating on your data What are the confidence intervals on the published numbers? Intervals, dataset sizes and the exact test sets. A single accuracy figure hides how small most test sets are Leaderboard: 95% intervals, sizes, reproduce commands What happens with a generator it has never seen? Results on held-out generators, plus a way to adapt to new ones Public benchmarks today (a multi-generator image set is pending); adapt with fine-tuning What is the false-alarm rate at the threshold you'll actually run? A rate at a stated threshold, and a way to set the threshold for your tolerance Calibration: a threshold for your false-alarm target How does it behave after compression, resizing or re-recording? Results on platform-processed media, since that is what you'll score Evaluate on your own pipeline's output; interpreting scores

docs.title: Decisions you can defend
docs.text: Ask A good answer ForensiX Does a score mean a probability? Calibrated probabilities on data like yours, or a clear statement that scores aren't probabilities Calibration What does it do when it can't tell? An explicit "uncertain" outcome rather than a forced yes or no Prediction sets: real, fake, or both What evidence comes with a result? More than a number: which frames, which segment, which signal Per-segment scores, evidence details, provenance findings Does it check provenance (C2PA, watermarks)? Yes, and it reports what was found and what wasn't Provenance

docs.title: Fairness and compliance
docs.text: Ask A good answer ForensiX Do false alarms differ by skin tone, age or gender? A report per group with intervals, on data you can inspect, and a way to rerun it on your population Fairness reports Which regulations does this help with, and which does it not? A specific, modest answer. Be wary of "fully compliant" claims for any regulation Tools for transparency and audit evidence; compliance stays your organization's responsibility

docs.title: Operating it
docs.text: Ask A good answer ForensiX Where does it run? Can it run in our cloud or on-premises? Your choice of environment, including air-gapped Local, Kubernetes, AWS, Google Cloud, Azure What are latency and cost per item, on what hardware? Measured numbers with the hardware named Seconds per item on the leaderboard; measure on your hardware How do we know when accuracy drifts? Monitoring plus a drift check on newly labelled data Web manager dashboard, drift checks Who reviews borderline cases? A workflow for human review; detectors should support people, not replace them Uncertain outcomes and evidence for reviewers

docs.title: Red flags
docs.text:
• "99% accurate" with no dataset, no interval and no threshold.
  • No way to test on your own data before you buy.
  • Unclear training-data licenses, or none at all.
  • "Compliant with [regulation]" as a product feature.
  • A yes or no with no evidence, and no way to say "uncertain".

docs.title: Choosing detectors
docs.text: No detector catches every manipulation. Choose by what was manipulated and what evidence is left in the media, then confirm on data like yours.

docs.title: By threat
