docs.text: Threat What changed Detectors that can see it Detectors that can't Face swap in a video The face region; the rest is real footage gend-pe, gend, dfdet-clip (best measured), dfdc-selim, dfdc-wm; id-face / id-motion if you have references; person-detector Lip-sync models (the mouth stays in sync); image detectors (only a small part of the frame is generated) Fully generated image (diffusion, GAN) Every pixel commfor (broadest training), rine-ldm (diffusion), clipdet, univfd, rine, safe Face models, unless the image is a face Cloned or converted voice The speech nes2net-x-itw, xlsr-aasist-df (real-world audio), xlsr-aasist, aasist, rawgat-st; phys-voice, phys-room Face and image models Dubbed video, voice replaced The audio track syncnet, stablesyncnet, avcons, avad, avid (voice doesn't fit the face); the audio models Face models Lip-sync generation (Wav2Lip-style) The mouth region, driven by new audio avad, avcons, face models; syncnet and stablesyncnet only if the sync is imperfect Generators trained against a SyncNet can pass the sync models Voice swap + lip-sync Audio and mouth avid (identity mismatch), audio models, id-face with references Sync models (the sync is good) Impersonation of a known person The identity id-face, id-motion, person-detector Detectors without references can't know who it should be Spliced or edited recording A segment Window/segment scores of audio models, phys-room (room or microphone change), avcons localization, physdf localization Clip-level scores alone

docs.title: Face-swap video: SDFVD
docs.text:
Full write-up: benchmark.md. 53 real and 53 face-swapped clips (one face-swap tool), on an L4 GPU.

Model AUC EER Balanced acc. at 0.5 Comment gend-pe 0.956 0.132 0.859 Best ranking; flags 24% of reals at 0.5 gend 0.919 0.170 0.811 Flags 32% of reals at 0.5 dfdet-clip 0.916 0.151 0.821 Best balanced at 0.5; fastest of the three dfdc-selim 0.761 0.321 0.566 Catches 19% of fakes at 0.5 rine (image, whole frames) 0.745 0.340 0.500 Calls everything real at 0.5 dfdc-wm 0.699 0.396 0.594 other image models 0.56–0.72 Not face-swap detectors

The top three are within statistical noise of each other on 106 videos. The gap between them and everything else is real.

docs.title: Other families
docs.text: Audio, image, audiovisual and identity models have published results (see the README Models tables), and their implementations are checked against upstream code, but they haven't yet been benchmarked by ForensiX on held-out data. The evaluation scripts are ready: Evaluating on your data.

docs.title: Practical defaults
docs.text: Situation Start with Social-media video of a face dfdet-clip (balanced at 0.5) or gend-pe (best ranking, set your own threshold) Video call or interview with sound gend-pe + nes2net-x-itw + syncnet (recipe 4) Phone call or voice note nes2net-x-itw Image upload commfor Protecting specific people id-face with enrolled references, plus a face-manipulation model Explaining a decision to a non-expert physdf report and syncnet offset/confidence, as supporting evidence (with calibrated priors)

docs.title: Cost
docs.text:
Measured on an NVIDIA L4 during the SDFVD run. Times are per video (2–6 s clips), and most were measured with other models sharing the GPU, so they are upper bounds:

Model Seconds per video Weights on disk image models (8 frames) 0.06–0.5 (rine-ldm 2–2.7) 5 MB – 1.6 GB (CLIP backbones are shared) dfdc-wm ~1 312 MB dfdet-clip ~2.7 1.2 GB + CLIP gend-pe, gend ~7 (shared GPU) 1.2 GB each dfdc-selim ~7 (shared GPU) 1.8 GB

On CPU, expect around 1–2 minutes per short video for the CLIP-based video models and about 6 s for dfdc-wm.

docs.title: Working in Google Colab
docs.text:
New to ForensiX? Start with the get-started notebook: it installs ForensiX, downloads sample media, and walks through detection, calibration, evaluation and the web manager.

Notebook What it does Get started (source) Detect, provenance, calibrate, evaluate, web manager and fairness on sample media Benchmark on SDFVD (source) Every image and video detector on the SDFVD face swaps Train and test (source) Train the models that ship without weights, then benchmark them

Training and large evaluations run on Colab GPUs. This guide sets up a workflow where the repo lives on Google Drive, survives disconnects, and syncs with GitHub.

docs.title: Which GPU
docs.text:
GPU VRAM Use for T4 16 GB Small evaluations; works for everything, but slowest L4 24 GB Default. Evaluations and most training; good speed per compute unit A100 40/80 GB Long training runs (physdf, avid, id-motion at full size)

Video evaluation is limited by CPU work (decoding, face detection), not by the GPU, so an A100 barely beats an L4 there. The SDFVD benchmark ran 2–4 processes at once on one L4 to keep it busy.

docs.title: One-time setup
docs.text:
1. GitHub token: create a fine-grained personal access token with access to only this repository, with Contents: Read and write.
  2. Colab secret: in Colab, open 🔑 Secrets, add the token (e.g. as GITHUB_TOKEN_FORENSIX), and turn on notebook access for it.

docs.title: Each session
docs.text:
# 1. Drive, secrets, cache location
from google.colab import drive, userdata
import os
drive.mount('/content/drive')
tok = userdata.get('GITHUB_TOKEN_FORENSIX').strip()
os.environ['GITHUB_TOKEN_FORENSIX'] = tok
os.environ['FORENSIX_CACHE'] = '/content/drive/MyDrive/forensix_cache'   # weights survive sessions

# credentials for git in this runtime only (the runtime's disk is wiped when it ends)
path = os.path.expanduser('~/.git-credentials')
with open(path, 'w') as f:
    f.write(f'https://x-access-token:{tok}@github.com\n')
os.chmod(path, 0o600)

%%bash
set -e
git config --global credential.helper store
git config --global user.name  "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
cd /content/drive/MyDrive
[ -d ForensiX ] || git clone https://github.com/anas-rz/ForensiX.git
cd ForensiX
git config core.fileMode false     # Drive changes file permissions; without this every file shows as modified
git pull
pip install -q -e .

Push from the notebook after reviewing your changes:

%%bash
cd /content/drive/MyDrive/ForensiX
git status && git add -A && git commit -m "Describe the change" && git push

docs.title: Where to put data
docs.text: What Where Why Repo /content/drive/MyDrive/ForensiX Survives disconnects; syncs with GitHub Weights cache /content/drive/MyDrive/forensix_cache ~18 GB, downloaded once Feature caches from extract Drive The expensive step; resumable Datasets /content/ (local disk) Drive is slow for many small reads; download again each session Results results/ in the repo on Drive Saved after every model; committed with the write-up

docs.title: Common errors
docs.text: Error Cause could not read Username for 'https://github.com' The repo is private and git has no credentials: run the credentials cell. Invalid username or token The token is empty, wrong or expired. The secret name in userdata.get must match the one in 🔑 Secrets exactly. HTTP 404 from the GitHub API with a valid token The token wasn't given access to this repository. Every file shows as modified Run git config core.fileMode false. A run stops when the session drops Rerun the same command: evaluation and extract steps resume.

docs.title: Claude Code in Colab
docs.text:
Claude Code can run in Colab's terminal, next to the GPU:

curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
cd /content/drive/MyDrive/ForensiX && claude      # log in with /login each session

Its session starts without your local context, so give it a self-contained prompt: the goal, the paths, the exact commands, and any rules, e.g. "write results to files, never commit". Its settings live on the runtime's disk and are wiped when the runtime ends.

docs.title: Evaluating on your data
docs.text: Published accuracy rarely survives a change of data. Before trusting a detector, measure it on media like yours. This guide covers the evaluation scripts, the metrics, and how to build a test set that measures what you think it measures.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
All scripts use forensix.metrics, with fakes as the positive class:

Metric Answers Notes AUC (ROC-AUC) How often does a random fake score above a random real? Threshold-free. 0.5 is chance. The main number for comparing models. AP (average precision) Precision averaged over recall levels Sensitive to class balance EER The error rate where false alarms equal misses Threshold-free; standard in audio anti-spoofing (ASVspoof-compatible implementation) Balanced accuracy Mean of real and fake accuracy at the model's default threshold Shows whether the default threshold suits your data Real acc / fake acc Share of reals called real / fakes called fake at the threshold 1 − real acc is the false-alarm rate 
from forensix.metrics import binary_summary, compute_eer
binary_summary(fake_scores, real_scores, threshold=0.5)
# {'auc': ..., 'ap': ..., 'balanced_acc': ..., 'real_acc': ..., 'fake_acc': ..., 'n_fake': ..., 'n_real': ...}
eer, eer_threshold = compute_eer(fake_scores, real_scores)

docs.title: Evaluation scripts
docs.text:
Script Data Models eval_video_folder.py Any two folders of videos (real, fake) video, image (on frames) eval_deepfake_eval_2024.py Deepfake-Eval-2024 (in-the-wild, gated, CC BY-SA 4.0) any family; --modality video/audio/image eval_asvspoof2019_la.py ASVspoof 2019 LA eval (ODC-By) audio; pooled and per-attack EER build_image_eval_set.py + eval_image.py ForensiX's license-clean image set (Open Images + 4 permissive generators) image; per generator, PNG and JPEG conditions eval_identity.py references/<person>/, queries/<person>/{real,fake}/ identity; real vs fake and real vs impostor calibrate_physics.py eval Stored physics measurements physics; per detector and per constraint

All of them write a JSON of metrics, and most also write a per-file scores CSV, which you need for thresholds and fusion. The folder script is the most general:

python scripts/eval_video_folder.py --device cuda \
    --real data/real --fake data/fake --dataset my-set \
    --models gend-pe dfdet-clip commfor \
    --out results/my_set.json --scores-out results/my_set_scores.csv

It saves after each model and skips models already in --out, so a dropped session resumes where it stopped. To use a big GPU fully, run several copies with disjoint --models lists and separate --out files, then merge them; the scores don't change.

docs.title: Building a fair test set
docs.text:
Most surprising benchmark results come from the test set, not the model.

  • Match formats between classes. If all fakes are PNG and all reals JPEG, a detector can score well by spotting PNG. SDFVD pairs each fake with its source clip at the same resolution, frame rate and codec; the ForensiX image set re-encodes fakes at the reals' JPEG quality. Check codec, resolution, duration, bitrate and container per class before trusting any number.
  • Match content. Fakes of talking heads against reals of landscapes measure scene recognition. Use reals and fakes of the same kind of content, ideally the same sources.
  • Keep sources apart. Don't let the same person, video or recording session appear in both data used to choose thresholds and data used to report results.
  • Cover several generators. One face-swap tool says little about the next one. Report per generator when you can.
  • Process like production. If production media is re-encoded by a platform, re-encode the test set the same way.
  • Check licenses. For commercial work, prefer test sets with commercially usable licenses: SDFVD (CC BY 4.0), ASVspoof 2019 (ODC-By), Deepfake-Eval-2024 (CC BY-SA 4.0, evaluation only), or the ForensiX image set. FaceForensics++, Celeb-DF, DFDC and FakeAVCeleb have research-only terms.

docs.title: How much data you need
docs.text:
Confidence intervals shrink slowly. On SDFVD (53 + 53 videos), the 95% interval on AUC was about ±0.04 for the best models and about ±0.1 for models near AUC 0.7, so differences of a few points meant nothing. Rough guide:

Per class AUC 95% CI at AUC 0.9 (Hanley–McNeil) What it can tell apart 50 ±0.06 Good vs. useless models 250 ±0.03 Models 5+ AUC points apart 1,000 ±0.014 Models 2–3 AUC points apart

Bootstrap your own intervals: resample reals and fakes separately, with replacement, and recompute the metric a few thousand times. To compare two models, bootstrap the difference on the same resamples (a paired bootstrap), as benchmark.md does.

docs.title: The leaderboard
docs.text:
Results become public through the leaderboard: LEADERBOARD.md, the web manager's Leaderboard page, and GET /v1/leaderboard. All three come from one module, forensix/leaderboard.py, which recomputes every number from the raw result files. Nothing is typed in by hand.

Metric How AUC 95% CI Stratified bootstrap (reals and fakes resampled separately, 2,000 times, seed 0) from per-item scores; Hanley–McNeil when only a summary exists False alarms, detections At a fixed threshold (0.5 on fake_prob; "any violation" for physics), with Wilson 95% intervals EER From per-item scores, else the run's summary (with an approximate binomial interval) Speed Seconds per item on the recorded hardware; the Speed tab shows measured throughput Tied with #1 The model's interval overlaps the leader's

Adding a benchmark run: 1. Run the evaluation with --out and --scores-out. Per-item scores are what make the intervals and rates possible; the eval scripts now save them at full precision. 2. Put both files in results/ and add an entry to results/leaderboard.json: name, task, license, dataset URL and archive hash, hardware, date, commit, reproduce command, caveats. Only benchmarks whose license allows commercial use belong there; list others under excluded with the reason. 3. Run python scripts/build_leaderboard.py. It rewrites LEADERBOARD.md and the snapshot the server ships (forensix/server/static/leaderboard.json, used when results/ isn't present, e.g. in containers). A test fails if LEADERBOARD.md is out of date with results/.

The pending benchmarks (Deepfake-Eval-2024, the ForensiX image set) are listed with their exact commands; once their result files exist, they appear automatically.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
Write results up like benchmark.md: - the dataset, its license and how the fakes were made; - the hardware, date, ForensiX commit and software versions; - AUC with confidence intervals, EER, and accuracy at the threshold; - the exact reproduce command; - caveats: sample size, generators covered, protocol choices.

Keep the raw per-file scores. They let you recompute any metric later without rerunning the models.

Next step: if accuracy on your media falls short, fine-tune; if it ranks well, calibrate.

docs.title: Extending ForensiX
docs.text:
ForensiX adds models one at a time, and every model goes through the same steps:

  1. Find it and check its licenses.
  2. Implement it and verify parity with upstream.
  3. Register it in the Python API.
  4. Evaluate it.

This guide shows how, using univfd (forensix/image/univfd/__init__.py) as the worked example.

docs.title: 1. Check licenses first
docs.text:
Do this before writing any code. ForensiX ships only components that can be used commercially:

  • Code: the upstream repo's license, plus any code it borrows. SAFE's network was rewritten because upstream copied unlicensed NPR code.
  • Weights: their own license if they have one. Weights linked from a licensed repo but hosted elsewhere with no separate license are accepted, marked with an asterisk (MIT*), and explained in the README.
  • Inherited licenses: the backbone the weights were fine-tuned from, and preprocessing models the pipeline needs. SPAI was rejected because its weights derive from a non-commercial backbone. InsightFace and DeepfakeBench preprocessing were replaced with MTCNN or MediaPipe.
  • Reject NC, ND, research-only or unlicensed components. Record why in the README, so nobody checks the same model twice.

docs.title: 2. Implement the network
docs.text:
Put the model in forensix/<family>/<model>/, with the upstream license file next to it:

forensix/image/univfd/
├── __init__.py      # network, detector, build(), register()
└── LICENSE          # upstream license, verbatim
  • Vendor or rewrite: copy upstream network code verbatim where its license allows, keeping parameter names so released checkpoints load unchanged. Rewrite from the paper where it doesn't.
  • Pin upstream: pin the upstream commit (_COMMIT) and the weight file's SHA-256.
  • No new heavy dependencies: if upstream needs fairseq, librosa, scikit-image or similar, reimplement the small part you need (see forensix/audio/xlsr.py).
  • Preprocessing must match upstream's evaluation pipeline: resize or not, crop size, normalization, interpolation. Most parity bugs live here.

docs.title: 3. Wrap it in a detector
docs.text:
Subclass the base class for the input type and implement one method:

Base class Implement Gets forensix.audio.detector.AudioDetector _fake_probs(windows) (batch, window) float tensor at 16 kHz forensix.image.detector.ImageDetector _fake_probs(batch) Batch of tensors from your transform forensix.video.detector.VideoDetector _score(video_path) Returns (video_prob, per_segment_probs) 
class UnivFDDetector(ImageDetector):
    def _fake_probs(self, batch: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        # upstream label convention: 1 = fake
        return self.network(batch).sigmoid().flatten()

Families without a base class (audiovisual, identity, physics) implement predict(...) returning a Prediction directly. Follow the conventions: - higher fake_prob means more fake; - threshold=None and score_type="anomaly" for scores without a natural cut-off; - evidence in details.

docs.title: 4. Register it
docs.text:
def build(weights_path: Path, device: str = "cpu") -> UnivFDDetector:
    network = UnivFD(clip_vit_l14())
    network.fc.load_state_dict(torch.load(weights_path, map_location="cpu", weights_only=True))
    return UnivFDDetector("univfd", network, TRANSFORM, device=device)


register(
    ModelSpec(
        name="univfd",
        family="image",
        builder=build,
        weights=WeightFile(url=..., sha256="4771...", filename="univfd-fc.pth"),
        extra_weights=(CLIP_VIT_L14,),            # shared backbone, fetched by download()
        license="MIT (code, linear head). Backbone: OpenAI CLIP ViT-L/14, MIT; ...",
        source=f"https://github.com/WisconsinAIVision/UniversalFakeDetect/tree/{_COMMIT}",
        paper="https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.10174",
        description="Linear probe on frozen CLIP ViT-L/14 image embeddings, ...",
    )
)

Then: - import the module in the family's __init__.py, so registration happens on import forensix; - add the license file to [tool.setuptools.package-data] in pyproject.toml; - load checkpoints with weights_only=True (forensix.hub.torch_load allows the numpy types some upstream checkpoints carry) or safetensors. Never unpickle arbitrary objects; - reuse shared backbones (forensix/image/clip.py, forensix/audio/xlsr.py, the face detectors in forensix/video/) instead of adding another copy.

docs.title: 5. Verify parity with upstream
docs.text:
Run upstream's own evaluation code and ForensiX's on the same inputs, and compare the outputs. Every model in the README Verification table has a row like:

Model Check Result univfd ForensiX (HF CLIP) vs upstream (OpenAI clip package) on PNG/JPEG/grayscale images of 180×150 to 1024×768 max fake_prob diff 1.1e-6
  • Check preprocessing, network and end-to-end output separately, so a mismatch points to its cause.
  • Use inputs that exercise the edge cases: small images, grayscale, odd sizes, short clips, no face.
  • Explain any remaining difference (fp16 vs fp32, OpenCV versions, a replaced face detector).
  • Use public-domain or CC0 test media (tests/data/).

docs.title: 6. Test
docs.text:
Add tests in tests/test_<family>.py: - registration and forensix.info fields; - output shape, range and label convention on a tiny or toy input; - edge cases: an empty or short input, no face, corrupt files; - for trainable models, a synthetic-data test that training actually learns (tests/training/).

Keep tests fast: build toy networks, or mark tests that need large weights.

docs.title: 7. Document and evaluate
docs.text:
• Add a row to the family's table in the README, with the license marks (*, †, ‡) and published results, plus a model paragraph: paper, code, what changed from upstream and why, speed.
  • Run the family's evaluation script and record the result (Evaluation).
  • Update Choosing detectors if the model changes the recommendation.

docs.title: Adding a family
docs.text: A new family (the planned multimodal and graph-based families) needs: - a package forensix/<family>/ imported in forensix/__init__.py; - a base class if its models share an input type and batching logic; - a family name added to the comment in forensix/registry.py; - an evaluation path: an existing script with a new --modality, or a new script; - a row in the status table.

docs.title: Fine-tuning on your data
docs.text:
This guide takes a pretrained detector from your labelled data to a service on AWS, Google Cloud or Azure. It covers fine-tuning, measuring the result, calibrating it, packaging it and deploying it. It's for engineers whose media differ from what the public models were trained on: a new generator, a camera pipeline, a language, a compression chain.

To train the models that ship without weights (avcons, avid, id-motion, physdf, person-detector), see Training models instead.

docs.title: Fine-tune or calibrate?
docs.text:
Problem Fix Needs Scores rank real and fake well on your data, but thresholds or probabilities are off Calibrate Hundreds of labelled items; no training The model misses a generator or manipulation it has never seen, or flags your real media Fine-tune, then calibrate Hundreds to thousands of labelled items per class, a GPU

Measure first (step 2): if the AUC on your data is already high, calibration alone is enough.

docs.title: The whole path
docs.text:
1. Data: three labelled sets in the ForensiX dataset format: one to train on, one to calibrate, and one to test.
  2. Baseline: score the test set with the pretrained model.
  3. Fine-tune: python -m forensix.finetuning MODEL --dataset train.zip --out MODEL-ft.safetensors.
  4. Evaluate: score the test set again with the checkpoint, and compare.
  5. Calibrate the fine-tuned model on the calibration set.
  6. Serve it locally with the checkpoint and calibration.
  7. Package both into an image on top of the published one.
  8. Deploy that image to AWS, Google Cloud or Azure with the usual one command or one click.

docs.title: What can be fine-tuned
docs.text:
Family Models What a training sample is Image commfor, commfor-224, univfd, rine, rine-ldm, safe, clipdet An image, with light augmentation (flips, mild JPEG recompression) Audio aasist, aasist-l, rawgat-st, nes2net-x, nes2net-x-itw, xlsr-aasist, xlsr-aasist-df A random window of a clip, with random gain Video gend, gend-pe, dfdet-clip An aligned face crop. Crops are extracted once per video and cached; a video's score is the mean over its faces, as in production

Other video, audiovisual, physics and identity models aren't supported by the fine-tuner. Most of them are calibrated rather than trained, or have their own training scripts.

Modes (--mode) set how much of the network changes:

Mode Trains Use when Default learning rate head The final classifier layer A few hundred items per class; a quick, safe first try 1e-3 norm (default) Normalization layers' scales and shifts, plus the head ("LN-tuning", as GenD and dfdet-clip were trained) Hundreds to a few thousand items per class 1e-4 lora Low-rank adapters on every Linear layer, plus the head, via Hugging Face PEFT (pip install peft) When norm plateaus and you have more data: near-full capacity at low memory. See PEFT 2e-4 full Every parameter Many thousands of items per class and a large GPU 1e-5

head and norm checkpoints store only the tensors they changed, from kilobytes to a few megabytes. They load on top of the pretrained weights, so the base model's license and weights still apply.

docs.title: 1. Data
docs.text:
Use the same format as calibration: a ZIP or folder with real/ and fake/ folders, or a manifest.csv with file,label,group (format).

  • Three separate sets. Fine-tuning holds out part of its data to choose the best epoch, which makes that part optimistic. Calibrate on a second set and report results on a third that neither step has seen.
  • Groups. Put a real clip and the fakes made from it, or one person's or one session's media, in the same group. The fine-tuner splits by group, so near-duplicates can't leak between training and held-out data. Split your three sets by group too.
  • Match production. Use the same sources, resolutions, compression and platforms as the media you'll score. Get real media from the same channels as the fakes, or the model learns the channel instead of the manipulation.
  • Balance. Classes are reweighted automatically, but each class still needs variety: many generators and many sources.
  • Licenses. Your training data's license carries into the checkpoint's use. For commercial use, train only on data you're allowed to use commercially (see Licensing and compliance).

docs.title: 2. Baseline
docs.text:
Score the test set with the pretrained model:

python scripts/eval_video_folder.py --real test/real --fake test/fake --models dfdet-clip \
  --device cuda --out results/test_base.json

For images and audio, forensix.calibrate("commfor", dataset="test.zip") reports the AUC, or use scripts/eval_image.py. If the AUC is already high, calibrate instead of fine-tuning.

docs.title: 3. Fine-tune
docs.text:
python -m forensix.finetuning dfdet-clip --dataset train.zip --out models/dfdet-clip-ft.safetensors \
  --mode norm --epochs 5 --device cuda --cache-dir face_cache/

import forensix

det, report = forensix.finetune("commfor", dataset="train.zip", out="models/commfor-ft.safetensors",
                                mode="norm", epochs=5, device="cuda")
report["base_val_auc"], report["val_auc"], report["best_epoch"], report["warnings"]
Option Default Meaning --dataset or --real / --fake A dataset ZIP or folder, or two folders of files --mode norm head, norm, lora or full (above); lora options in PEFT --epochs 5 Passes over the training data. The best epoch on held-out data is kept --lr by mode Learning rate (AdamW) --batch-size 16 Lower it if the GPU runs out of memory --val-fraction 0.2 Share held out (by group) to score each epoch --max-per-class all Cap for a quick trial run --frames 16 Video: frames sampled per video for face crops --cache-dir temporary Video: keep face crops so reruns skip extraction (put it on persistent storage) --no-augment Turn augmentation off

What it does: - It first scores the held-out part with the base model, then again after every epoch, and keeps the best epoch. - If no epoch beats the base model, the checkpoint keeps the base weights and the report says so. - Next to the checkpoint it writes MODEL-ft.json, with the AUC before and after, every epoch's loss and held-out AUC, the item counts and warnings.

Where to run it:

Where How Google Colab pip install -e . in a GPU runtime, as in the Colab guide. Keep --cache-dir and --out on Drive Your GPU machine pip install -e ., then the command above A cloud GPU VM, from the published image docker run --gpus all -v $PWD:/work -w /work ghcr.io/anas-rz/forensix:gpu python -m forensix.finetuning commfor --dataset train.zip --out models/commfor-ft.safetensors on an AWS g6.xlarge, a GCP g2-standard-8 or an Azure NC4as_T4_v3 VM with NVIDIA drivers (each cloud's deep learning VM images include them)

The image runs as user 10001, so the mounted folder must be writable by it (chmod a+w models face_cache).

docs.title: 4. Evaluate
docs.text:
Score the same test set with the checkpoint, writing to a separate results file:

python scripts/eval_video_folder.py --real test/real --fake test/fake --models dfdet-clip \
  --weights dfdet-clip=models/dfdet-clip-ft.safetensors --device cuda --out results/test_ft.json

Compare the AUC, the false-alarm rate on real media and the detection rate with the baseline. Also check what the model must keep doing well, such as public benchmarks (Evaluating on your data): fine-tuning on one generator can cost accuracy on others. If you have demographic labels, run a fairness report on real faces before and after.

docs.title: 5. Calibrate
docs.text:
Fit the calibration on the calibration set, loading the fine-tuned model:

cal, report = forensix.calibrate("dfdet-clip", dataset="calibration.zip", device="cuda",
                                 weights_path="models/dfdet-clip-ft.safetensors")
cal.save("models/dfdet-clip-ft.calibration.json")

A calibration belongs to one set of weights. Recalibrate whenever you fine-tune again. Once deployed, you can instead calibrate in the web manager; the server fingerprints the weights, so a calibration fitted to other weights is refused.

docs.title: 6. Serve it locally
docs.text:
{
  "device": "cuda",
  "preload": ["dfdet-clip", "commfor"],
  "weights": {"dfdet-clip": "models/dfdet-clip-ft.safetensors"},
  "calibrations": {"dfdet-clip": "models/dfdet-clip-ft.calibration.json"}
}

python -m forensix.server --config server.json        # or FORENSIX_SERVER_WEIGHTS='{"dfdet-clip": "..."}'

In Python, use forensix.load("dfdet-clip", weights_path=..., calibration=...).

docs.title: 7. Package
docs.text:
deploy/Dockerfile.finetuned adds your models/ folder to a published image and points the server at it:

docker build -f deploy/Dockerfile.finetuned -t forensix:gpu-ft \
  --build-arg BASE=ghcr.io/anas-rz/forensix:gpu-bundled \
  --build-arg WEIGHTS='{"dfdet-clip": "/opt/forensix/models/dfdet-clip-ft.safetensors"}' \
  --build-arg CALIBRATIONS='{"dfdet-clip": "/opt/forensix/models/dfdet-clip-ft.calibration.json"}' \
  .                     # the folder that contains models/

Use a *-bundled base (cpu-bundled for CPU targets), because the checkpoint loads on top of the pretrained weights baked into it.

docs.title: 8. Deploy
docs.text:
Push the image to your cloud's registry, then deploy it with the same one command or one-click workflow as the stock image, passing the image:

Cloud Push Deploy AWS aws ecr create-repository --repository-name forensix; aws ecr get-login-password \| docker login --username AWS --password-stdin ACCOUNT.dkr.ecr.REGION.amazonaws.com; tag and push ACCOUNT.dkr.ecr.REGION.amazonaws.com/forensix:gpu-ft deploy/aws/deploy.sh ecs-gpu --image ACCOUNT.dkr.ecr.REGION.amazonaws.com/forensix:gpu-ft (AWS) Google Cloud gcloud artifacts repositories create forensix --repository-format docker --location REGION; gcloud auth configure-docker REGION-docker.pkg.dev; tag and push REGION-docker.pkg.dev/PROJECT/forensix/forensix:gpu-ft deploy/gcp/deploy.sh cloudrun-gpu --image REGION-docker.pkg.dev/PROJECT/forensix/forensix:gpu-ft (Google Cloud) Azure az acr create -g RG -n REGISTRY --sku Basic; az acr login -n REGISTRY; tag and push REGISTRY.azurecr.io/forensix:gpu-ft deploy/azure/deploy.sh aca-gpu --image REGISTRY.azurecr.io/forensix:gpu-ft, after giving the apps or cluster pull access (Azure)

The GitHub Actions workflows (deploy-aws, deploy-gcp, deploy-azure) take the same image in their image input. Redeploying with a new image rolls the services over to it. The shared data (datasets, calibration versions made in the web manager) stays.

docs.title: Retraining over time
docs.text:
• Detect drift: when new labelled media arrives, run a drift check in the web manager (Calibration → Check for drift) or with scripts/recalibrate.py.
  • Recalibrate first: if the ranking still holds, recalibrating is enough.
  • Fine-tune again: if the AUC on new data drops, fine-tune again on the old and new training data together. Give the checkpoint a new name, repeat steps 4–8, and keep each run's MODEL-ft.json report with the image tag it went into.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom Cause and fix "No epoch beat the base model" The base model already does well on this data (calibrate instead), the training data is too small or too different from the held-out part, or the learning rate is off. Try head mode, more data, or --lr 3× lower or higher Held-out AUC rises, then falls Overfitting. Fewer epochs (the best one is kept anyway), head instead of norm, or more data CUDA out of memory Lower --batch-size, or use head/norm instead of full Video: "no face in ..." The face detector found no face in the sampled frames. Those videos are skipped; check that they show a face The served model behaves like the base model The server didn't get the checkpoint: GET /v1/server lists the models with custom weights under trained_weights; also check that the path exists inside the container "fine-tunes X, not Y" The checkpoint belongs to a different model; checkpoints only load into the model they were trained from

Next step: for the large CLIP and ViT models, try LoRA adapters; or go straight to deployment.

docs.title: Identity and person models
docs.text:
Most detectors judge media on its own. Identity-based detectors also know who the media claims to show, and compare it with reference media of that person. This fits person-of-interest protection: executives, public figures, or customers who enrolled for verification. It needs nothing about how a fake was made.

ForensiX has three tools for this:

Tool Question Enroll from Needs training? id-face Does the face look like the person? Photos and/or videos No (SFace weights) id-motion Does the person move and emote like the person? Videos only Yes, once, on many people (Colab) person-detector Is this real media of this one person? Their real media (any modality) Yes, per person, seconds on CPU

docs.title: What each one catches
docs.text:
Attack id-face id-motion person-detector A different person claiming to be X Yes Yes Yes Poor face swap of X Often Yes Often Good face swap of X, with an actor's motion No: built to look like X Yes: the motion is the actor's Depends on the training data Reenactment of X driven by someone else No Yes Depends Real X in unusual conditions (lighting, age) May false-alarm May false-alarm May false-alarm

A good face swap is designed to pass face recognition. Use id-face together with a face-manipulation detector (gend-pe, dfdet-clip), and with id-motion where you have videos of the person.

docs.title: id-face
docs.text:
import forensix

det = forensix.load("id-face")                        # CPU is fine
det.enroll("alice", ["alice_passport.jpg", "alice_interview.mp4"])
det.save_gallery("people.npz")

pred = det.predict("new_video.mp4", identity="alice")
pred.is_fake                                  # True when similarity < 0.363 (fake_prob > 0.637)
pred.details["similarity"]                    # median over frames of the best-matching face
pred.details["frame_similarity"]              # per sampled frame (2 per second, up to 120 frames)
pred.details["frames_without_face"]
pred.details["other_enrolled_similarity"]     # {"bob": 0.72} means it looks more like bob

det.identify("unknown.jpg")                   # [("alice", 0.61), ("bob", 0.12)]

How it works: - Detection and embedding: YuNet finds faces and 5 landmarks, OpenCV aligns each face to 112×112, and SFace embeds it. The 0.363 cosine threshold is OpenCV Zoo's, which gives 99.40% on LFW. - Enrollment: each frame contributes its largest face. In videos, frames whose face disagrees with the rest (another person, a bad detection) are dropped. - Verification: in each frame, the face that looks most like the person is kept (the mean of its top-3 similarities to the references). The clip score is the median over frames, which resists a few bad frames, while the per-frame timeline shows a face switching mid-video.

Enrollment tips: - Use 5–20 references covering different angles, lighting, ages and expressions. One passport photo works but is brittle. - Enroll from video when you can: it gives many frames, filtered for consistency. - Re-enroll as people age or change appearance. - Galleries hold embeddings, not images, but they are still biometric data. Store and delete them under the rules that apply to you (GDPR, BIPA and similar).

docs.title: id-motion
docs.text:
det = forensix.load("id-motion", weights_path="id_motion.safetensors")   # train it first
det.enroll("alice", ["alice_interview1.mp4", "alice_interview2.mp4"])
pred = det.predict("new.mp4", identity="alice")
pred.details["window_similarity"], pred.details["window_start_s"]       # per 4 s window
  • Features: head rotation, translation and their velocities, plus MediaPipe's 52 expression blendshapes, at 25 fps. These describe behaviour, not the face's shape.
  • Model: a temporal network embeds every 4 s window. It is trained contrastively on real videos of many people, with each person's positives taken from different videos, so it learns the person rather than the recording.
  • Data needs: a few seconds of natural, talking behaviour in both the references and the query. Several reference videos in different settings work best. Short clips, or a person who barely moves, give weak evidence.
  • Training: on VoxCeleb2 dev on Colab (Training). The decision threshold is the equal-error point measured on held-out people.

docs.title: person-detector
docs.text:
A tiny model (~23k parameters) trained for one person, on CPU, in seconds. Without negatives, it synthesizes manipulated and impostor-like samples from the real ones.

from forensix.specialized import train_person_model

det = train_person_model("alice", real_media=alice_files, negative_media=other_people_files,
                         modality="video", epochs=30)
det.save("alice.safetensors")
forensix.load("person-detector", weights_path="alice.safetensors").predict("new.mp4")
  • modality is image, audio, video, audiovisual or auto; one model covers one modality.
  • use_peft=True (default) adapts a base model with LoRA. pretrain_base_model builds that base from general real/fake data; without it, a fresh base is used.
  • Real negatives (other people, known fakes of the person) beat synthetic ones. Add them when you have them.
  • Hold out some of the person's real media and measure the false-alarm rate on it before relying on the model. A few training samples give an overconfident model.

docs.title: Evaluating identity detectors
docs.text:
scripts/eval_identity.py enrolls each person from references/<person>/, then scores their real queries (should pass), their fakes (should be flagged) and other people's real queries claimed as them (impostors):

DATA/references/<person>/*        reference photos or videos
DATA/queries/<person>/real/*      genuine media of the person
DATA/queries/<person>/fake/*      deepfakes of the person (optional)

python scripts/eval_identity.py --data /content/id_eval --models id-face id-motion \
    --weights id-motion=id_motion.safetensors --out results/identity.json

There's no commercially usable deepfake benchmark with per-person references. VoxCeleb2 test (CC BY 4.0) alone already measures the impostor rate and the false-alarm rate on real media.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: Requirement Notes Python ≥ 3.10 Tested on 3.13 PyTorch ≥ 2.0 CPU works for everything; a CUDA GPU is strongly recommended for video, audiovisual and XLS-R audio models ffmpeg on PATH Required for audiovisual models, and for audio in formats libsndfile can't read (m4a, aac, audio inside video files) Disk About 18 GB for every model's weights; much less if you load only some RAM 8 GB is enough for one model at a time; audiovisual models need more on long or high-resolution videos (input limits)

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/anas-rz/ForensiX.git
cd ForensiX
pip install -e ".[dev]"            # dev adds pytest

On a GPU machine, install the CUDA build of PyTorch first, following pytorch.org, so pip doesn't pull in a CPU-only build.

ffmpeg:

sudo apt-get install ffmpeg        # Debian/Ubuntu
brew install ffmpeg                # macOS

The eval extra (pip install -e ".[eval]") is only needed to build the image evaluation set with diffusion models.

docs.title: Check it works
docs.text:
import torch, forensix

print(torch.cuda.is_available())
print(forensix.list_models())

pred = forensix.load("aasist").predict("tests/data/speech_cc0.flac")
print(pred)            # a small model; downloads 1.3 MB on first use

Run the test suite with pytest tests. Some tests download model weights on their first run, and tests that need ffmpeg are skipped without it.

docs.title: The weights cache
docs.text:
Weights download on first use into ~/.cache/forensix/weights/, and their SHA-256 hashes are checked. A .verified stamp next to each file lets later loads skip rehashing it while the file is unchanged (FORENSIX_VERIFY_HASH=always forces a full check). To put the cache somewhere else (a bigger disk, a shared volume, Google Drive):

export FORENSIX_CACHE=/data/forensix_cache

Pre-fetch weights instead of downloading on first use:

python scripts/download_weights.py                    # every model
python scripts/download_weights.py gend-pe syncnet    # some models
python scripts/download_weights.py --family video     # one family

docs.title: Offline and air-gapped machines
docs.text:
Some models fetch helper files the first time they run, not when they load: face detectors and landmark models (RetinaFace, YuNet, MediaPipe), and the ICT-FaceKit meshes used by phys-lighting. All of them go through the same verified cache, so the reliable way to fill a cache for an offline machine is to load and run every model you need once, on a connected machine:

# warm_cache.py: run on a connected machine with FORENSIX_CACHE set
import forensix

AUDIO = "tests/data/speech_cc0.flac"
IMAGE = "tests/data/face_public_domain.jpg"
VIDEO = "sample_talking_head.mp4"     # any short video of a face, with sound

needs_your_weights = {"avcons", "avid", "id-motion", "person-detector"}
for name in forensix.list_models():
    if name in needs_your_weights:
        continue
    family = forensix.info(name).family
    detector = forensix.load(name)
    if family == "identity":
        detector.enroll("warmup", [IMAGE])
        detector.predict(IMAGE, identity="warmup")
    elif family == "audio" or name in {"phys-voice", "phys-room"}:
        detector.predict(AUDIO)
    elif family == "image":
        detector.predict(IMAGE)
    else:
        detector.predict(VIDEO)
    print("ok", name)

Then copy the whole $FORENSIX_CACHE directory to the offline machine and set FORENSIX_CACHE there. Before you depend on it, test with networking disabled. For models you train, ship the checkpoint file and pass weights_path=.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause and fix RuntimeError: Checksum mismatch The download was corrupted, or the upstream file changed. Delete the file and retry. If it persists, the upstream host changed the file; open an issue rather than editing the hash. ValueError: Can't decode ... ffmpeg isn't installed Install ffmpeg. ValueError: ... needs both a video and an audio stream Audiovisual models need a video with sound. person-detector requires a trained checkpoint (and similar for avcons, avid, id-motion) These models ship without weights. Train them (Training) and pass weights_path=. A video scores exactly 0.5 No face was found. Check pred.segment_fake_probs (empty when no face was found). OpenCV prints setPreferableTarget Targets are not supported Harmless warning from OpenCV 5's DNN module (used by id-face). MediaPipe / TensorFlow Lite log lines Harmless; set GLOG_minloglevel=2 to hide them. CUDA out of memory Load one large model at a time, del it before the next, and reduce batch_size for image and audio models.

docs.title: Interpreting scores
docs.text: A detector's output is evidence, not a verdict. This guide explains what each part of a Prediction means, and how to turn scores into decisions you can defend.

docs.title: The three kinds of score
docs.text:
score_type threshold Models Meaning "probability" a number (usually 0.5) audio, image, video, stablesyncnet, avcons, avid, person-detector The model's softmax or sigmoid output. In [0, 1], but not calibrated: 0.8 doesn't mean "80% chance of fake". "anomaly" None avad, syncnet, phys-*, physdf Distance from how real media behaves. There's no natural cut-off: choose one on your own real data. syncnet's score is -confidence, so it's usually negative. "anomaly" a number id-face (0.637), id-motion 1 − similarity to the enrolled person. The threshold comes from face verification (LFW) or training, not from deepfake data.

In every case, higher means more likely fake, so ranking metrics (AUC, EER) work the same way for all of them.

docs.title: Why the default threshold often fails
docs.text:
A model's default threshold of 0.5 fits the data it was trained on. On other data, the score distributions shift. On the SDFVD face-swap benchmark:

Model AUC Real correct at 0.5 Fake correct at 0.5 What happened rine 0.745 100% 0% Every score below 0.5; highest fake 0.384 dfdc-selim 0.761 94% 19% Scores too low on this face-swap tool gend 0.919 68% 94% Scores too high on real faces dfdet-clip 0.916 89% 76% Reasonably balanced

A model can rank well (good AUC) and still make bad yes/no decisions at its default threshold. Treat the default as a placeholder.

docs.title: Choosing a threshold
docs.text:
1. Collect real media like the media you'll check: same sources, platforms, compression, resolution, languages. Real data is much easier to get than fakes, and it's what sets the false-alarm rate.
  2. Decide the false-alarm rate you can afford: for example 1% of real uploads sent to human review.
  3. Set the threshold at that quantile of the real scores (recipe 5).
  4. Measure the detection rate on fakes, if you have any, at that threshold. Measure it on media not used to set the threshold.
  5. Re-check periodically. New cameras, codecs and platforms shift real-media scores too.

Sample size matters. To confirm a 1% false-alarm rate to within about ±0.5 points, you need roughly 1,500 real samples; to within ±0.2 points, about 10,000.

docs.title: Segments and localization
docs.text:
segment_fake_probs breaks a score down:

Models One segment per Use audio (most) 4.04 s window (recipe 3) Find the fake part of a long recording nes2net-x-itw 30 s chunk Coarse localization video models scored face crop Spot one bad face among good ones; empty means no face found avcons AV window When audio and face stop matching id-face sampled frame (2 per second) When the face stops being the person id-motion 4 s window Same, for behaviour person-detector (video) frame Same, for the per-person model

Physics detectors put their timelines in details["timeline"], and physdf puts segments in details["localization"]["segments"], each with a start and end in seconds, the constraint and the face or voice node involved.

Clip-level scores average over segments, so a short manipulation in a long clip can be diluted below the threshold. If short edits matter, also flag on max(segment_fake_probs), with its own threshold chosen the same way.

docs.title: details
docs.text:
details holds structured evidence, and its keys depend on the model (API reference). The most useful ones:

  • syncnet: offset_frames (best audio shift; real clips are usually within ±3 frames, and an offset at ±15 means no good alignment was found), confidence (about 10 on a clean real clip, under 1 when audio and lips don't match), mean_dist_by_offset (the full curve).
  • id-face: similarity, frame_similarity, frame_time_s, frames_without_face, and other_enrolled_similarity, which tells you when the face looks more like someone else in your gallery.
  • Physics detectors: constraints[name] with measured, expected_range_start, worse (whether higher or lower is suspicious), violation (0–1) and prior (provisional or learned).
  • physdf: report (verdict, findings, counter-evidence, and Markdown), localization, status (which checks ran).

docs.title: Reporting results to people
docs.text:
• Report the score with the model name and threshold, never a bare "87% fake".
  • Say what the model checks: "the face region shows manipulation artefacts" (gend-pe) is a different claim from "the voice doesn't match the lip movements" (syncnet).
  • A low score is not proof of authenticity. It means this model found nothing. Models miss manipulations they weren't trained for.
  • Keep a human in the loop for consequential decisions. The stablesyncnet weights license forbids fully automated decisions that affect someone's legal rights (Licensing).

docs.title: Licensing and compliance
docs.text:
The ForensiX framework itself (library, server, web console, deployment templates, scripts) is MIT-licensed (LICENSE). The models are licensed separately, as below.

ForensiX includes only code and weights whose licenses allow commercial use. That doesn't mean every deployment is automatically fine. This page lists what to check. It's engineering guidance, not legal advice: have counsel review a commercial deployment.

docs.title: Three layers
docs.text:
Layer What governs it Where to look Code The license in each model's directory forensix/<family>/<model>/LICENSE* Weights The weights' own license, or the repo's when the authors give none forensix.info(name).license; README Models tables Training data The dataset's terms, which may or may not carry over to the weights README footnote ‡ 
for name in forensix.list_models():
    print(name, "|", forensix.info(name).license)

docs.title: Marks in the Models tables
docs.text: Mark Meaning What to do * (e.g. MIT*) The weights are linked from a permissively licensed repo but hosted elsewhere, with no separate license. Applies to xlsr-aasist, xlsr-aasist-df, avad, syncnet. Generally treated as covered by the repo license; flag it in your license review. † Built on OpenAI CLIP ViT-L/14 (MIT). OpenAI's model card lists "any deployed use case" as out of scope. That's an intended-use statement, not a license term. Note it in your risk assessment. ‡ Trained on data with research-only or non-commercial terms: FaceForensics++, DFDC, ForenSynths, LRS2, VGGFace2 and others. Whether those terms carry over to trained weights is legally unsettled. The main open question for commercial use. Get a legal opinion; prefer models you train yourself on permissive data where it matters. § stablesyncnet: CreativeML Open RAIL++-M Use-based restrictions apply; see below.

docs.title: stablesyncnet and use-based restrictions
docs.text:
stablesyncnet's weights are under OpenRAIL++-M. Commercial use is allowed, but the license's use restrictions (paragraph 5 and Attachment A) apply, and you must pass them on to your users. Two matter for forensics. The weights may not be used: - for fully automated decision-making that adversely affects someone's legal rights; - to generate information for administration of justice, law enforcement, immigration or asylum processes.

In those settings, use syncnet (MIT), which performs the same check. The full text is in forensix/audiovisual/stablesyncnet/LICENSE-WEIGHTS-OpenRAIL++-M.txt.

docs.title: Models you train
docs.text: avcons, avid, id-motion, physdf and person-detector are ForensiX code (no third-party restrictions beyond their frozen components), trained by you. The weights' terms then depend on your training data: - VoxCeleb2, LibriSpeech: CC BY 4.0. Attribution required; for VoxCeleb2, video copyright stays with the owners. - Your own customers' media: your contracts and privacy law decide. - Frozen components: SyncNet (MIT*), ECAPA-TDNN (Apache-2.0), DINOv2 (Apache-2.0), MediaPipe (Apache-2.0), ICT-FaceKit (MIT).

docs.title: Provenance components
docs.text: Component License c2pa-python (C2PA SDK) MIT OR Apache-2.0 invisible-watermark dwtDct code (vendored in forensix/provenance/imwatermark/) MIT AudioSeal code and detector weights MIT (weights MIT since 2024-04-02)

docs.title: Evaluation datasets
docs.text:
Evaluating on a dataset is a use of it too. ForensiX's benchmarks use commercially usable data:

Dataset License SDFVD CC BY 4.0 ASVspoof 2019 LA ODC-By 1.0 Deepfake-Eval-2024 CC BY-SA 4.0, evaluation only, gated ForensiX image eval set Open Images CC BY 2.0 photos + generators whose outputs allow commercial use

FaceForensics++, Celeb-DF, DFDC, FakeAVCeleb, DeepSpeak and most other deepfake datasets have non-commercial or research-only terms.

docs.title: Biometric and privacy law
docs.text:
Identity features process biometric data: - id-face: face embeddings. - id-motion: behavioural embeddings. - avid and the audio models: voice.

Consent, retention limits and deletion rights may apply (GDPR, BIPA, CCPA and similar). Galleries (.npz) store embeddings, not images, but embeddings are still biometric data.

docs.title: Before shipping
docs.text:
• [ ] List the exact models in production and their forensix.info(name).license.
  • [ ] Review the ‡ training-data question for each, with counsel.
  • [ ] If stablesyncnet is used: no automated adverse legal decisions, no justice or immigration use, and the restrictions passed on to users.
  • [ ] Attribution for CC BY data you trained or evaluated on.
  • [ ] Biometric consent and retention for identity features.
  • [ ] A human review step for consequential decisions.

docs.title: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT)
docs.text:
This guide is for engineers who want to adapt the large detectors (CLIP- and ViT-based image and video models, wav2vec-style audio models) to their own media without training hundreds of millions of parameters. It uses LoRA from Hugging Face's PEFT library (pip install peft, Apache-2.0), and goes from development to a deployed service.

It builds on Fine-tuning on your data, which covers the data, evaluation, calibration and deployment steps shared by every fine-tuning mode. This page covers what's specific to LoRA.

docs.title: What LoRA does here
docs.text:
LoRA (low-rank adaptation) leaves each pretrained weight matrix W frozen and learns a small correction B·A beside it, where A and B have rank r (4–16). The layer then computes with W + (alpha / r)·B·A. ForensiX adds these adapters to every Linear layer except the classifier head, and trains them together with the head.

norm (default) lora full What changes Normalization scales and shifts, plus the head Low-rank corrections to every Linear layer, plus the head Everything Trained parameters, dfdet-clip (CLIP ViT-L) ~0.1M 1.8M at rank 4 ~300M Can learn Shifts in the features' statistics New feature directions: unseen generators, new artifacts Anything, given enough data Data needed per class Hundreds Hundreds to thousands Many thousands GPU memory Low Low: frozen weights need no gradients or optimizer state High Checkpoint, dfdet-clip Under 1 MB 7.1 MB at rank 4 1.2 GB Serving cost Same as the base Same as the base: adapters are merged into the weights Same as the base

Use LoRA when norm stops improving and you have more data, or when the model has to pick up a kind of manipulation the pretrained features don't separate. It's the closest thing to full fine-tuning that fits on a Colab T4.

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
pip install peft                     # or: pip install -e ".[finetune]"

PEFT is only needed to train. Loading and serving a LoRA checkpoint doesn't import it, so deployment images stay as they are.

docs.title: 2. Data and baseline
docs.text: Use the same three labelled sets (train, calibrate, test) and the same baseline as for any fine-tuning: Data and Baseline.

docs.title: 3. Train
docs.text:
python -m forensix.finetuning dfdet-clip --dataset train.zip --mode lora \
  --lora-rank 8 --lora-alpha 16 --epochs 5 --device cuda \
  --cache-dir face_cache/ --out models/dfdet-clip-lora.safetensors

import forensix

det, report = forensix.finetune("univfd", dataset="train.zip", mode="lora", lora_rank=8, lora_alpha=16,
                                epochs=5, device="cuda", out="models/univfd-lora.safetensors")
report["base_val_auc"], report["val_auc"], report["lora"]   # {'rank': 8, 'alpha': 16, 'scaling': 2.0, 'n_targets': ...}
Option Default Meaning --lora-rank 8 Rank r of each adapter. Higher learns more and needs more data; 4–16 is the useful range --lora-alpha 16 Scale numerator: corrections are multiplied by alpha / r. Keep alpha ≈ 2r and tune the learning rate instead --lora-dropout 0.05 Dropout on the adapter input, against overfitting --lora-targets every Linear but the head Regex of module names to adapt (below) --lr 2e-4 Learning rate; 1e-4–5e-4 works for LoRA

All other options (--epochs, --batch-size, --val-fraction, --frames, --cache-dir) work as in Fine-tune. The held-out split is scored before training and after every epoch. The best epoch is kept, and if no epoch beats the base model the checkpoint leaves the base weights unchanged.

Choosing targets. To see a model's layer names:

det = forensix.load("dfdet-clip")
[n for n, m in det.network.named_modules() if m.__class__.__name__ == "Linear"][:6]
# ['backbone.encoder.layers.0.self_attn.k_proj', '...v_proj', '...q_proj', '...out_proj', '...mlp.fc1', '...mlp.fc2']
Goal --lora-targets Every Linear layer (default): most capacity (omit) Attention only, a common LoRA setting with fewer parameters '(q_proj\|v_proj)$' Only the last layers of a 24-layer ViT, for small datasets 'layers\.(1[6-9]\|2[0-3])\.'

The CNN models (safe, aasist and others) have few Linear layers. For them, the default also adapts the Conv2d layers. With --lora-targets, any matching Linear or Conv2d layer gets an adapter.

Hyperparameters that usually work: - Rank 8, alpha 16, learning rate 2e-4, 3–10 epochs. - If the held-out AUC climbs and then falls, use fewer epochs, rank 4, more dropout or more data. - If it never climbs, raise the learning rate (5e-4) or the rank, or check that the training and held-out data come from comparable sources.

docs.title: 4. How the checkpoint works
docs.text:
1. PEFT injects the adapters (peft.inject_adapter_in_model), and only the adapters and the head are trained.
  2. After the best epoch is restored, each adapter is merged into its layer (W ← W + (alpha / r)·B·A) and PEFT's wrapper is removed. The returned detector is a plain model running at the base model's speed.
  3. The checkpoint stores the head and, for each adapted layer:
  4. A and B for Linear layers, which is what keeps it small;
  5. the merged correction for convolutions.

The metadata records the rank, alpha and scaling. 4. forensix.load(model, weights_path=checkpoint) builds the pretrained model and adds the corrections with plain tensor math. No PEFT is needed at load time; the test suite checks this by loading with PEFT blocked.

from forensix.finetuning import checkpoint_info
checkpoint_info("models/dfdet-clip-lora.safetensors")["lora"]   # {'rank': 8, 'alpha': 16, 'dropout': 0.05, 'scaling': 2.0}

docs.title: 5. Evaluate and calibrate
docs.text:
Same as any checkpoint. Evaluate on the test set with --weights, then calibrate the LoRA model on the calibration set:

python scripts/eval_video_folder.py --real test/real --fake test/fake --models dfdet-clip \
  --weights dfdet-clip=models/dfdet-clip-lora.safetensors --device cuda --out results/test_lora.json

cal, report = forensix.calibrate("dfdet-clip", dataset="calibration.zip", device="cuda",
                                 weights_path="models/dfdet-clip-lora.safetensors")
cal.save("models/dfdet-clip-lora.calibration.json")

Compare against the base model and, if you trained one, the norm checkpoint. LoRA is only worth its larger checkpoint if it beats norm on the test set.

docs.title: Training on cloud GPUs
docs.text:
The published gpu image has ForensiX and PyTorch but not PEFT. Add it when you start the container:

docker run --gpus all -e HOME=/tmp -v $PWD:/work -w /work ghcr.io/anas-rz/forensix:gpu \
  sh -c "pip install --user -q peft && python -m forensix.finetuning dfdet-clip --dataset train.zip \
         --mode lora --cache-dir face_cache --out models/dfdet-clip-lora.safetensors"

Run it on any GPU VM with NVIDIA drivers: AWS g6.xlarge, Google Cloud g2-standard-8, or Azure NC4as_T4_v3. In Colab, pip install peft in a GPU runtime. Keep --cache-dir and --out on persistent storage (Drive, a mounted bucket or a disk), because face-crop extraction is the slow part and is reused across runs.

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
A LoRA checkpoint deploys exactly like any other fine-tune checkpoint, and the serving image doesn't need PEFT:

  1. Serve locally: add "weights": {"dfdet-clip": "models/dfdet-clip-lora.safetensors"} and the calibration to the server config (details).

  2. Package: build deploy/Dockerfile.finetuned on a *-bundled base. The adapters are applied on top of the pretrained weights baked into it.

    docker build -f deploy/Dockerfile.finetuned -t REGISTRY/forensix:gpu-lora \
  --build-arg BASE=ghcr.io/anas-rz/forensix:gpu-bundled \
  --build-arg WEIGHTS='{"dfdet-clip": "/opt/forensix/models/dfdet-clip-lora.safetensors"}' \
  --build-arg CALIBRATIONS='{"dfdet-clip": "/opt/forensix/models/dfdet-clip-lora.calibration.json"}' .
docker push REGISTRY/forensix:gpu-lora

  3. Deploy with your cloud's one command or one-click workflow, passing the image:

    Cloud Command AWS deploy/aws/deploy.sh ecs-gpu --image ACCOUNT.dkr.ecr.REGION.amazonaws.com/forensix:gpu-lora (AWS) Google Cloud deploy/gcp/deploy.sh cloudrun-gpu --image REGION-docker.pkg.dev/PROJECT/forensix/forensix:gpu-lora (Google Cloud) Azure deploy/azure/deploy.sh aca-gpu --image REGISTRY.azurecr.io/forensix:gpu-lora (Azure)

    Deploy has the registry setup for each cloud.

The merge happens once at load, so latency and memory are the same as the base model's. When you retrain, build a new image tag and redeploy, then recalibrate: the server refuses a calibration fitted to other weights.

docs.title: Beyond LoRA
docs.text: PEFT has other methods (IA³, LoHa, LoKr, DoRA and more). forensix.finetuning supports LoRA, because LoRA merges cleanly into the weights and keeps checkpoints small and PEFT-free at serving time. To experiment with another method: 1. Inject it into det.network with PEFT yourself and train with your own loop. 2. Merge it (for example with the method's merge on each layer). 3. Save with forensix.finetuning.save(det, path, "full", report). That gives a full checkpoint, which loads anywhere like the others.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom Cause and fix mode='lora' needs PEFT pip install peft in the training environment (not needed for serving) "no Linear or Conv2d layers match" The --lora-targets regex matches no layer names; list them as shown above The held-out AUC drops after the first epoch Overfitting: rank 4, --lora-dropout 0.1, fewer epochs, or more data. The best epoch is kept regardless CUDA out of memory Lower --batch-size, target attention only ('(q_proj\|v_proj)$'), or a lower rank. Training on CUDA already uses mixed precision The loaded model scores like the base model The run kept the base weights (see the report's warnings), or the server isn't using the checkpoint (trained_weights in GET /v1/server)

Next step: once it's deployed, watch it in the web manager's dashboard.

docs.title: Physics forensics
docs.text:
Learned detectors recognize the fingerprints of generators they were trained on. Physics detectors work the other way round: they measure physically meaningful quantities (pulse, head motion, lighting, voice production, room acoustics), compare them with how real faces and voices behave, and say which physical constraint was broken. The output is evidence a person can check, not just a number.

The README physics section describes every measurement and its verification. This guide covers using them.

docs.title: The detectors
docs.text:
Detector Input Constraint Needs phys-bloodflow video One heart drives the pulse in all facial skin ≥ 6 s of a steady, visible face phys-motion video The head is a rigid body with inertia; the jaw is a hinge ≥ 2 s of a tracked face at ≥ 20 fps phys-lighting video One light field lights the face, and it follows the scene ≥ 2 s of a tracked face phys-voice audio Voice production stays within anatomical limits ≥ 1.5 s of voiced speech phys-room audio One room and one microphone ≥ 6 s of speech with pauses physdf video, audio, or both All of the above, plus a learned graph prior across face, pulse, light and voice Whatever the parts need

All of them return score_type="anomaly" with no default threshold. The score is the violation (0–1) of the most-violated constraint, because one clearly broken physical law is evidence on its own. Constraints that don't apply to a clip (for example jaw coupling when the mouth never moves) are listed in details but left out of the score.

docs.title: Reading the evidence
docs.text:
pred = forensix.load("phys-room").predict("voice_note.wav")
for name, c in pred.details["constraints"].items():
    print(name, c["measured"], c.get("expected_range_start"), c["worse"], c["violation"], c["prior"])

Each constraint reports: - measured: the value in this clip; - expected_range_start and worse: where real media stops, and which direction is suspicious; - violation: 0 inside the real range, rising to 1 at the end of the range; - prior: provisional (hand-set from the literature) or learned (fitted on real media).

details["timeline"] gives per-frame or per-stretch values for localizing the problem in time.

docs.title: The physdf report
docs.text:
det = forensix.load("physdf", weights_path="physdf_graph.safetensors")   # weights_path optional
pred = det.predict("interview.mp4")       # its sound track is used if present
report = pred.details["report"]
print(report["markdown"])

The report gives a verdict and confidence, then: - Findings: one claim per violated constraint, naming the physical law, the measured value, where the real range ends, whether that range is calibrated, and where and when. - Counter-evidence: the checks that passed. - What couldn't be checked, and why.

forensix.physics.report.verify_report(report, pred.details) re-derives every claim, the score and the verdict from the evidence. It returns an empty list when everything checks out. The report abstains ("inconclusive") when fewer than 5 checks apply or the strongest violation is weak, and says "low confidence" when only provisional ranges are violated.

Without a trained graph prior, physdf runs the five detectors and reports on them. With the prior, it adds cross-system residuals: the mouth predicted from the speech, the speech from the mouth, each skin region's pulse from the others, and so on (Training).

docs.title: Calibrate before you rely on it
docs.text:
The provisional ranges are hand-set, and the video ranges haven't been checked against a large set of real videos. In testing, provisional blood-flow and lighting ranges fired on real footage. Until you fit learned priors on real media like yours, treat physics output as leads for a human reviewer, not as a detector score.

Learned priors set each constraint's range from real media only, so a real clip trips any one constraint of a detector with probability about α (default 1%):

# 1. measure every constraint on real media like yours (resumable JSONL)
python scripts/calibrate_physics.py measure --media /data/real_videos --kind video --with-audio \
    --label real --source my-real --out m/real.jsonl
# 2. fit priors on real clips; reports held-out false-alarm rates, learned vs provisional
python scripts/calibrate_physics.py fit --measurements m/real.jsonl --out learned_priors.json
# 3. optional: real vs fake AUC per detector and per constraint
python scripts/calibrate_physics.py measure --media /data/fakes --kind video --with-audio --label fake --out m/fake.jsonl
python scripts/calibrate_physics.py eval --measurements m/real.jsonl m/fake.jsonl --priors learned_priors.json

Use them:

det = forensix.load("phys-bloodflow")
det.load_priors("learned_priors.json")

To make them the default for every detector, ship the file as forensix/physics/learned_priors.json (the package already declares it as package data). A constraint with fewer than 100 applicable real clips keeps its provisional range; details["constraints"][k]["prior"] tells you which applied.

Suggested real data with commercially usable licenses: LibriSpeech (CC BY 4.0) for audio and VoxCeleb2 test (CC BY 4.0; video copyright stays with the owners) for video with sound.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• rPPG needs a steady face: heavy compression, makeup, low light and fast motion weaken the pulse signal.
  • Weak cues: noise-colour changes and spliced rooms score low even when present, because blind RT60 from a few decays is noisy.
  • Pitch continuity: at this tracker quality, it can't separate fast genuine pitch moves from an octave-jumping synthetic voice.
  • No attribution: the priors know real media only, so the system says that physics was violated, not which generator did it.

docs.title: Training models
docs.text:
To adapt a pretrained detector (image, audio, or the GenD video models) to your own data, see Fine-tuning on your data. This page covers the models that ship without weights.

Most ForensiX models ship with pretrained weights. Five ship without, because no commercially usable weights exist and ForensiX trains its own:

Model Learns From Training script Where to run avcons Whether audio and lips belong together Real talking-face videos only train_avcons.py Colab GPU avid Whether the voice belongs to the face Real talking-face videos, many speakers train_avid.py Colab GPU id-motion A person's motion and expression style Real videos, several per person train_id_motion.py Colab (CPU extract, GPU train) physdf graph prior How face, pulse, light and voice relate Real talking-face videos train_physdf.py Colab (CPU extract, GPU train) physics priors Real ranges of each physics constraint Real media calibrate_physics.py Anywhere person-detector One person That person's media train_person_model.py or Python Your laptop (CPU, seconds)

All of them train on real media only, with negatives synthesized from it. They learn what real looks like rather than one generator's fingerprints, and they avoid deepfake datasets, most of which have non-commercial terms.

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
VoxCeleb2 (CC BY 4.0) fits most of these models: talking faces with sound, from thousands of speakers. Video copyright stays with the YouTube owners.

Split Speakers Use for VoxCeleb2 dev 5,994 avid, id-motion (the number of people matters more than hours) VoxCeleb2 test 118 avcons, physdf, physics priors

Lay it out as <person>/<video>/<clip>.mp4 (VoxCeleb's own layout). The scripts split train and held-out sets by person, so held-out results measure unseen people.

docs.title: The two-step pattern
docs.text:
Every training script has two subcommands:

  1. extract runs the slow, frozen parts (face tracking, SyncNet, ECAPA, MediaPipe) once per clip and caches compact features. It's resumable: rerun the same command after a disconnect.
  2. train trains the small model on the cache, reports held-out metrics, and writes a .safetensors checkpoint.

Keep the cache on Google Drive or another persistent disk: extraction is the expensive part.

docs.title: avcons
docs.text:
python scripts/train_avcons.py extract --media /content/voxceleb2_test/mp4 \
    --out /content/drive/MyDrive/avcons_cache --max-files 5000 --device cuda
python scripts/train_avcons.py train --cache /content/drive/MyDrive/avcons_cache \
    --out avcons.safetensors --steps 20000 --device cuda
  • Extraction drops clips with unclear sync (SyncNet confidence under 3, e.g. off-screen speech) and re-aligns the rest to their own sync.
  • Negatives: constant offsets of 6–15 frames, 5% speed drift, another speaker's voice or face, and spliced segments.
  • train output: AUC per manipulation on held-out speakers.

docs.title: avid
docs.text:
python scripts/train_avid.py extract --media /content/voxceleb2/mp4 \
    --out /content/drive/MyDrive/avid_cache --max-files 20000 --device cuda
python scripts/train_avid.py train --cache /content/drive/MyDrive/avid_cache \
    --out avid.safetensors --device cuda
  • Speaker split: speakers are divided three ways: heads (contrastive voice–face space), scorer (calibrated against swaps and splices), and a report split.
  • train output: AUC per negative kind, and 1:2 voice-to-face matching accuracy (about 80% is the published level for this task).

docs.title: id-motion
docs.text:
python scripts/train_id_motion.py extract --media /content/voxceleb2/mp4 \
    --out /content/drive/MyDrive/idmotion_cache --max-files 30000 --workers 8
python scripts/train_id_motion.py train --cache /content/drive/MyDrive/idmotion_cache \
    --out id_motion.safetensors --steps 20000 --device cuda
  • Extraction is CPU-bound (MediaPipe), so raise --workers to the number of CPU cores.
  • train output: the verification EER on held-out people. Its threshold becomes the model's decision threshold.

docs.title: physdf
docs.text:
python scripts/train_physdf.py extract --media /content/voxceleb2_test/mp4 \
    --out /content/drive/MyDrive/physdf_cache --max-files 3000 --workers 8
python scripts/train_physdf.py train --cache /content/drive/MyDrive/physdf_cache \
    --out physdf_graph.safetensors --steps 20000 --device cuda
  • Extraction (MediaPipe plus the ICT lighting fit) is the slow, CPU-bound part.
  • Training is masked modelling: node spans, whole nodes, the mouth or a whole modality are hidden, and the model predicts them from the rest.
  • Checkpoint: stores the feature normalization and the real residual distributions, per input condition (audio+video, audio only, video only).

Fit the physics priors too (Physics guide).

docs.title: Using your checkpoints
docs.text:
forensix.load("avcons", weights_path="avcons.safetensors")
forensix.load("avid", weights_path="avid.safetensors")
forensix.load("id-motion", weights_path="id_motion.safetensors")
forensix.load("physdf", weights_path="physdf_graph.safetensors")

Evaluation scripts take them with --weights NAME=PATH:

python scripts/eval_deepfake_eval_2024.py --data /content/de2024 --modality video \
    --models avcons syncnet avad --weights avcons=avcons.safetensors --device cuda \
    --max-per-class 250 --out results/de2024_av.json

docs.title: Before you train
docs.text:
• Run a smoke test. Before a long run, run with --max-files 50 --steps 200 to check the data layout and the full pipeline in a few minutes.
  • Check the held-out report that train prints. If held-out AUC or EER is far worse than training, look for too few speakers or leaks between splits.
  • Record what you trained on (dataset, split, file count, steps, commit) next to the checkpoint. You'll need it for audits and for licensing questions.
  • Shipping trained weights: a checkpoint you train is yours, but check the training data's terms. VoxCeleb2's CC BY 4.0 requires attribution (Licensing).

docs.title: ForensiX
docs.text:
Catch deepfakes before they cost you, from the first file you check to a production API on any cloud.

ForensiX is an end-to-end media forensics platform. It detects manipulated and AI-generated images, video and voices, and reads the evidence a file carries: Content Credentials, generator watermarks and metadata. It adapts to your own media and runs as an API and web console on your laptop, your Kubernetes cluster, or AWS, Google Cloud and Azure. Every bundled model and weight is under a commercially usable license.

docs.title: Try it on sample files
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/anas-rz/ForensiX.git && cd ForensiX
pip install -e ".[provenance]"
python scripts/fetch_samples.py         # a small, labelled test kit of real and fake media
python -m forensix forensix-samples/images/fake/dalle3_angry_man.jpg forensix-samples/provenance/c2pa_tampered.jpg

dalle3_angry_man.jpg (image)
  commfor          FAKE   0.976  (threshold 0.5)
  c2pa             no_credentials         No Content Credentials (C2PA) in this file.
c2pa_tampered.jpg (image)
  c2pa             tampered               Content Credentials signed by C2PA Test Signing Cert no longer match the content: it was modified after signing.

(Output abridged. The first run downloads model weights.)

Try it in Colab: no install · Read the docs · Deploy to your cloud

docs.title: Why teams choose ForensiX
docs.text:
• Built for commercial use. Every bundled model and weight is under a commercially usable license, documented model by model, with the conditions to check before you ship in the licensing guide. Many published deepfake detectors release weights for research use only; those are left out, so what's here can go into a product.
  • Every modality, one API. Image generators, face swaps, cloned voices, lip-sync mismatches, physical and physiological inconsistencies, identity and provenance: 38 detectors in 8 families behind forensix.load(name).predict(file) and a single /v1/detect endpoint.
  • Decisions you can defend. Calibrate on your own data to get real probabilities, a threshold with a statistical guarantee on the false-alarm rate you choose (split conformal), and an explicit "can't tell" when the evidence is mixed. Provenance adds proof that no score can: a signed AI-generation declaration, an edit after signing, a generator's watermark.
  • Proof, not promises. A public, reproducible leaderboard with 95% confidence intervals, recomputed from raw result files (excerpt below).
  • Fairness you can show. Fairness reports give false-alarm rates by skin tone, age and gender, with confidence intervals and significance tests: the evidence buyers and regulators ask for.
  • Adapts to your media. Fine-tune any image, audio or face-video detector on your own data, including LoRA with PEFT. The result is a checkpoint of a few megabytes that serves at full speed.
  • Production-ready on day one. The API keeps models loaded, batches requests and caches results, and comes with a web console, Prometheus metrics, Docker and Kubernetes manifests, and one-command or one-click deployment to AWS, Google Cloud and Azure.

docs.title: How we measure
docs.text:
Benchmark Top models (AUC or EER, 95% interval) SDFVD face swaps: 53 real and 53 face-swapped videos gend-pe AUC 0.956 [0.919, 0.983] · gend 0.919 [0.864, 0.961] · dfdet-clip 0.916 [0.861, 0.963] ASVspoof 2019 LA subset: 2,001 trials xlsr-aasist-df EER 0.0% [0.0, 0.2] · nes2net-x-itw 0.1% [0.0, 0.2] · nes2net-x 0.2% [0.0, 0.4]

These are small public benchmarks, and the ASVspoof attacks are older ones, so treat them as a starting point, not a promise for your media. At the default threshold of 0.5, gend-pe also flags 24.5% of the real SDFVD videos, which is why ForensiX calibrates the threshold on your own data.

  • Intervals, not single numbers: bootstrap intervals for AUC and Wilson intervals for rates, with dataset sizes stated.
  • Recomputable: every number is rebuilt from saved per-item scores by python scripts/build_leaderboard.py, and each benchmark lists the command that produced it.
  • Faithful ports: each ported model is checked for parity against its upstream implementation (verification).
  • Licensed test data: only benchmarks whose license allows commercial use.

The work lines up with public standards and practice, without claiming certification: C2PA Content Credentials for provenance; transparency duties for AI-generated content such as Article 50 of the EU AI Act; and per-group error reporting, as in NIST's face recognition evaluations, for fairness.

docs.title: How it works
